false_positives.candidate:
Add/remove member failures are swallowed with no user feedback

`addMembers` and `removeMember` call into `Discourse.Group#addMembers` / `#removeMember`, neither of which attach a rejection handler. If the server responds 422 (e.g. `can_not_modify_automatic`) or 404/500 (see the RecordNotFound path in `Admin::GroupsController#remove_member`), the promise rejects silently: the member list is not refreshed and the admin gets no indication the operation failed. Add an error handler that surfaces the message (as `save`/`destroy` in this controller already do). The `// TODO: should clear the input` note is related: because `usernames` is never reset, clicking Add again re-sends the same list.

GET /groups/:name/members response shape changed from array to object

The endpoint previously rendered a bare JSON array of serialized users (`render_serialized(members.to_a, GroupUserSerializer)`); it now returns `{"members": [...], "meta": {...}}`. This is an unversioned, breaking change for any external API consumer or plugin that reads `/groups/:name/members.json` as an array (they will now see an object and silently iterate nothing). If the break is intentional it should at least be called out in the PR description/changelog; otherwise consider keeping the array for non-paginated requests.

No spec for the rewritten members endpoint

`GroupsController#members` changed substantially in this PR (new `{members:, meta:}` envelope, new default limit of 50 applied to all groups instead of automatic groups only, `total` computed with a separate count query), but the only spec touched is `spec/controllers/admin/groups_controller_spec.rb`. There is no test asserting the new response structure, that `limit`/`offset` are honoured and echoed in `meta`, or that `total` reflects the full member count — so the response-shape break and any future regression in pagination would go unnoticed.

Public group members page now silently truncated to 50 members

`model.findMembers()` requests the default page (limit 50, offset 0) and `discourse/templates/group/members.hbs` renders only `members` with no pagination controls. Previously non-automatic groups returned all members from this endpoint, so a group with more than 50 members now shows only the first 50 with no way for a user to reach the rest. Either add next/previous controls (as done in the admin template) or load all pages for this route.

Removal of the PATCH membership endpoint makes old PATCH requests silently destructive

The `update_patch` branch (incremental `changes: {add:, delete:}` membership edits) was deleted, but `resources :groups` still routes PATCH to `update`. A client still issuing `PATCH /admin/groups/:id` with `changes` now gets HTTP 200 while the membership changes are silently discarded, and because `update` unconditionally executes `group.visible = params[:visible] == "true"`, the absent `visible` param flips the group to not visible. Old callers therefore both lose their intended effect and mutate unrelated state while being told everything succeeded. Either keep handling `changes` (or reject PATCH explicitly) and only assign `visible` when the param is present.

Specs depend on hardcoded group id 1 being an automatic group

The new `.update` spec (`id: 1`) and the `.add_members` / `.remove_member` automatic-group specs (`group_id: 1`) rely on seeded data where group id 1 happens to exist and be automatic, and `.update` then calls `Group.find(1)`. If seeds change or the test database is built differently, these raise `RecordNotFound` rather than fail meaningfully, and nothing in the spec documents the assumption. Fabricate an automatic group explicitly (`Fabricate(:group, automatic: true)`) as the `.destroy` spec does.

add_members assumes usernames is a String and silently ignores unknown users

`usernames.split(",")` raises `NoMethodError` (HTTP 500) if the parameter arrives as an array (`usernames[]=a&usernames[]=b`), which is a natural shape for API clients. Also, usernames that do not resolve to a `User` are skipped and the action still returns `success_json`, so an admin who mistypes a username sees a successful save and no member added, with no error reported. Normalize the parameter (`Array(usernames).join(",").split(",")` or similar) and report unknown usernames back to the caller.

create ignores alias_level sent by the client

`create` only assigns `name` and `visible`, but the client (`Discourse.Group#asJSON`, used by `create()`) always sends `alias_level` as well. A group created with a non-default alias level in the admin UI is silently saved with the default level, and the UI then shows the value the admin picked, so the discrepancy is invisible until a page reload. `update` does assign `alias_level`; `create` should do the same. Note also that this change switches the create/update payload from nested `group[...]` params to flat params and drops support for `usernames`, which breaks any existing API client of `POST/PUT /admin/groups`.

members endpoint does not validate limit/offset

`limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` and `offset = params[:offset].to_i` are passed straight to `.limit()/.offset()`. A request with `?offset=-1` or `?limit=-1` produces `OFFSET -1` / `LIMIT -1`, which PostgreSQL rejects (`ERROR: OFFSET must not be negative`), turning a bad query string into a 500. There is also no upper bound on `limit`, so `?limit=1000000` on a large automatic group (e.g. trust_level_0) will serialize every member in one unauthenticated-reachable request, an easy way to burn server CPU/memory. Clamp both values (e.g. `limit` to 1..100, `offset` to >= 0) server-side; the JS clamping in `Discourse.Group#findMembers` protects nothing against direct requests.

remove_member deletes join rows with delete_all, skipping callbacks and user_count maintenance

`group.users.delete(user_id)` goes through the `has_many :users, through: :group_users` association. For a `has_many :through` association without a `:dependent` option, `delete` removes the join rows with `delete_all`, so no `GroupUser` is instantiated and no ActiveRecord callbacks / counter-cache updates run. Consequences: the cached `groups.user_count` column (exposed by `BasicGroupSerializer` and used by the admin group list and group index) is never decremented and drifts permanently, and any `GroupUser` destroy-time bookkeeping (e.g. clearing `primary_group`/badge title that was granted by the group) is skipped. The removal should go through the model API that destroys the join record, e.g. `group.remove(user)` or `group.group_users.where(user_id: user_id).destroy_all`. Additionally, passing an id that is not a member makes the association call `find(id)` and raise `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`, turning a no-op removal into a 404 instead of a clean response.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`@loaded_locales ||= []` in ensure_loaded! runs outside LOAD_MUTEX

`ensure_loaded!` lazily initialises the shared `@loaded_locales` array outside the `LOAD_MUTEX` that `load_locale` uses. Two threads calling `ensure_loaded!` concurrently on a fresh process can each create a separate array; one of them is then discarded together with the locales it recorded, so locales get re-loaded (and the `@loaded_locales.include?` fast path in `translate` can be defeated) under load. Initialise the array inside the mutex (or at module load time) to keep the bookkeeping consistent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Every request depends on I18n.fallbacks being the custom FallbackLocaleList

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` assumes `I18n.fallbacks` is the `FallbackLocaleList` defined in `config/initializers/i18n.rb`. `ensure_loaded!` does not exist on the stock `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks`. Rails' I18n railtie configures fallbacks from `config.i18n.fallbacks` inside `config.after_initialize`, i.e. *after* `config/initializers/*` have run, and assigns `I18n.fallbacks = I18n::Locale::Fallbacks.new(...)`. This PR removed `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` from production/profile/cloud66 only; if it is still set in any other environment file (development/test) or by any plugin/host config, the custom list is replaced at boot and then *every* request raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'ensure_loaded!'` in a before_filter — a complete outage. Either guard the call (`respond_to?`) or install the fallback list from an `after_initialize`/railtie hook that runs after Rails' own i18n setup.

Fallback locales are never loaded outside of HTTP requests, so fallbacks silently fail in jobs/mailers

The translate accelerator only loads the YAML for `config.locale` (`load_locale(config.locale)` in `translate`), and the patched `I18n::Backend::Base#load_translations` deliberately does nothing when called without filenames, so `Simple#init_translations` will not autoload anything either. With `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` now mixed in, a lookup that misses falls back to `SiteSetting.default_locale` and `:en`, but those locales' translations are only in memory if something explicitly called `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for them. The only caller added in this PR is `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any translation performed outside a controller request — Sidekiq jobs (e.g. digest/notification emails rendered with the recipient's locale via `I18n.with_locale`), rake tasks, console, console-driven exports — will therefore still produce “translation missing” for keys absent from the user's locale, which is exactly the case fallbacks are supposed to fix. The ensure-loaded logic should be hooked into `load_locale`/`translate` (or into `I18n.locale=`) rather than into a single before_filter.

LRU translation cache key ignores the fallback chain (stale strings after default_locale change)

The cache key is `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`. Now that a lookup result can come from `SiteSetting.default_locale` via the new fallback chain, the cached value depends on the site default locale, which is not part of the key and does not change the backend object. After an admin changes `default_locale`, every already-cached fallback translation for other locales keeps serving strings from the old default locale until the process is restarted or `I18n.reload!` is called. Include the fallback chain (or the default locale) in the cache key, or clear the LRU cache when `default_locale` changes.

No tests for the new fallback behaviour

This PR changes how every translation is resolved (custom fallback chain, on-demand loading of fallback locales, removal of `config.i18n.fallbacks`) but adds no specs. There is nothing verifying that (a) the fallback order is user locale → `SiteSetting.default_locale` → `:en`, (b) `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` actually loads the fallback locales' YAML so a key missing from the user locale resolves instead of returning “translation missing”, and (c) the chain is recomputed when `SiteSetting.default_locale` changes. Regressions here degrade silently into missing-translation strings, so at minimum a spec exercising a key present only in `en` while `I18n.locale` is a partial locale is needed.

`SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` can raise and `.compact` cannot protect against it

`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` calls `to_sym` on the site setting before the array is built, so a nil/blank `default_locale` raises `NoMethodError` instead of being removed by `compact` (`compact` after `uniq` only removes a nil `locale`). More importantly, this method is invoked by `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` on every missed translation, including during boot, migrations and `rake assets:precompile`, where `SiteSetting` may be unavailable (no DB / missing table) — turning a harmless missing-translation lookup into an exception. Resolve the default locale defensively (e.g. `SiteSetting.default_locale.presence&.to_sym` inside a rescue) and build the list as `[locale, default, :en].compact.uniq`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not match the declared signature

`UsernameForm.authenticate()` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` without arguments, but the only declaration in the hierarchy is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (added in this PR, UsernamePasswordForm.java:160); neither `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` nor `AbstractFormAuthenticator` declares a no-arg variant. As written this does not compile. Either add a no-arg overload that only checks `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()` (which appears to be the intent here, since the user is already known to be non-null in this branch) or pass `context.getUser()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() requires a non-null user, disabling conditional passkeys for normal (first-time) login

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Both new call sites use it with `context.getUser()`: in `authenticate()` (line 115) and in `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137). On a regular login the authentication context has no user yet, so the condition is false and `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is never invoked. Consequences: the `ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI` attribute, the WebAuthn challenge (`AUTH_CHALLENGE_NOTE`), RP id and timeout are never put on the login form, so passkey/conditional-UI login from the initial login page stops working entirely (previously it was enabled exactly in the `context.getUser() == null` case). This also contradicts the existing assertions in `PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey` and `passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey`, which expect the `webauth` form and `username webauthn` autocomplete on the first login page. The user check should be dropped (the method should only test that the webauthn authenticator exists and passkeys are enabled).

false_positives.candidate:
New shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() hook decouples the branch from the null-user guard

The branch that builds `new WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean(session, realm, user, ...)` is now guarded by the overridable `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context)` instead of `user != null`, while `user` is still read from `context.getUser()` above. Any subclass that overrides the hook to return `true` for an unidentified user will pass a `null` user into `WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean`, causing an NPE while rendering the login form. Since this is a new protected extension point, the null check on `user` should be kept inside the branch (or documented as a precondition of the hook).

Re-authentication now always renders the username form when realm passkeys are enabled, even for users with no passkey

The new condition only checks the realm-level passkeys flag, not whether the already-known user actually has a passkey credential. With passkeys enabled on the realm, any re-authentication (e.g. `prompt=login`) will no longer short-circuit the username step; instead the username form is rendered with `usernameHidden=true`, i.e. a page with no input field and just a submit button, for every user including those who have only a password. That is a pointless extra click/step and a confusing screen for all password-only users. Consider also checking that the user has a passwordless WebAuthn credential (as `WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm` used to do by returning null when the user has no registered authenticators) before keeping the form.

reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey does not cover a password-only user in a passkeys-enabled realm

The test name suggests coverage for re-authenticating a user that has no passkey, but it disables passkeys for the whole realm (`setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(FALSE)`), so it only verifies that WebAuthn markup is absent when the realm feature is off. The behaviour actually changed by this PR - passkey/conditional-UI markup is now rendered during re-authentication whenever the realm has passkeys enabled, regardless of whether the known user owns a passkey credential (see `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` returning `false`, which removes the previous "no registered authenticators" short-circuit) - remains untested. Add a case with passkeys enabled on the realm and a user holding only a password.

try/catch(Exception) around findElement can silently pass on unrelated WebDriver errors

The 'webauthn elements not available' checks are implemented as `try { assertThat(driver.findElement(...), nullValue()); fail(...); } catch (Exception nsee) { }`. Any exception other than `NoSuchElementException` (e.g. `StaleElementReferenceException`, `TimeoutException`, a session error) is swallowed and the assertion silently passes, so the test can report success without having verified anything. Use `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))` as done elsewhere in these tests.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises ValueError (500)

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices the queryset with a negative start: `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing; this raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The endpoint's `paginate()` helper only converts `BadPaginationError` into a 400, so any client that supplies a cursor with a negative offset (cursors are user-supplied strings and `Cursor.from_string` happily parses `-5`) gets an unhandled 500. The inline comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong and should not be used to justify this branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member can be None -> AttributeError 500

`organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated whenever `request.user.is_superuser` is false. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional and is `None` for requests that are not made by an org member (e.g. token/integration or org-auth-token authenticated requests, or a user acting through superuser without membership). In that case this line raises `AttributeError` and the endpoint returns a 500 instead of the audit log. The attribute access also needs verification that `has_global_access` exists on the RPC member model at all, since it is a property of the Django `OrganizationMember` model rather than a field of the RPC payload.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator key handling is numeric-only but is used with a datetime order_by

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `math.floor/ceil(getattr(item, self.key))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged (the integer/float `Paginator` semantics). The only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`, uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`. Consequences: (1) `math.ceil(datetime)` raises `TypeError` for any non-empty result page, so the first optimized request 500s; (2) even if that were fixed, `value_from_cursor` would feed a raw number into the raw SQL comparison built by `build_queryset` (`"datetime" <= %s`), which fails/compares wrongly against a timestamp column. For a datetime sort key the class must derive from `DateTimePaginator` (or override these two methods with the timestamp-multiplier logic).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
Comment claims a behaviour change that the code does not make

The added comment in `Cursor.__init__` states "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but the code is unchanged (`self.offset = int(offset)`) - no validation was removed or added, and nothing in `Cursor` makes negative offsets usable (consumers slice QuerySets, which reject negative starts). A comment that describes a non-existent feature will mislead future readers into assuming negative offsets are a supported, safe input. Remove it or replace it with an accurate note (ideally a validation that rejects negative offsets).

Cursor values become incompatible depending on an undeclared query parameter

The new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter switches between `DateTimePaginator` (cursor values are millisecond timestamps) and `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (cursor values are raw numeric keys). Cursors returned by one paginator are therefore meaningless to the other, so a client that follows a `Link` header but drops/keeps the flag inconsistently (or a cached/bookmarked cursor) will silently page to the wrong position rather than erroring. The parameter is also not declared in `AuditLogQueryParamSerializer`, so it is undocumented and unvalidated (any value other than the exact string "true" silently falls back). Either encode the mode in the cursor/Link headers or drop the request-level switch.

Inconsistent and silent clamping of negative offsets in BasePaginator

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behaviour for every paginator derived from `BasePaginator`. For forward cursors an invalid negative offset is now silently clamped to 0, so a malformed/tampered cursor returns page 1 instead of surfacing an error - and the `next`/`prev` cursors are then built from `cursor.offset` (still negative) in `build_cursor`, producing further inconsistent cursors. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed straight into `queryset[offset:stop]`, which raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` and yields a 500. Negative offsets should be rejected explicitly (e.g. `raise BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`, as `OffsetPaginator` and `ChainPaginator` already do) rather than half-clamped; the comment claiming "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is incorrect.

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint branch

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including the negative-offset branch and the `enable_advanced_features` flag) and the new conditional path in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` are added with no accompanying tests. Nothing exercises the optimized path, which is why the datetime/`math.ceil` TypeError and the negative-slice ValueError went unnoticed; there is also no test asserting that unprivileged callers cannot activate the path. Tests covering: optimized path with results, cursor round-tripping, negative offsets, and the authorization gate are needed before merging.

Privilege gate uses request.user.is_superuser and member.has_global_access

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is described as gating "authorized administrators", but neither condition expresses that. Sentry requires superuser mode to be actively elevated for a request; the correct check is `is_active_superuser(request)` (or an explicit scope check). Reading `request.user.is_superuser` grants the privileged code path to any staff account with a normal, non-elevated session. Additionally, `has_global_access` on an org member only means "access to all teams" and is implicitly true for every member of an organization with open membership, so the second clause makes the gate effectively 'any member', not 'admin'. If the advanced pagination path is meant to be restricted, gate it on an explicit permission/scope instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offsets are passed straight into a Django queryset slice and raise ValueError

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects this with `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for any slice whose start or stop is negative, so the request ends in an unhandled exception / HTTP 500. The inline comment “The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically” is factually wrong, and the comment “enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds … safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level” documents behaviour that does not exist. Since `Cursor.from_string` accepts any integer offset from the `cursor` query parameter, this is a user-triggerable error path. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silently clamping negative cursor offsets masks invalid cursors and is inconsistent for prev cursors

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` in `BasePaginator.get_result` silently rewrites an invalid (negative) forward cursor offset to 0, so the caller gets page 1 data while `build_cursor` still derives the next/prev cursors from the original negative `cursor.offset` (e.g. `next_offset = offset + limit`), producing further bogus cursors. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still handed to the Django slice, which raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so the fix is only half applied. Other paginators in this file (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`) raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`; `BasePaginator` should do the same rather than clamp.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is an integer paginator but is used with a datetime sort key

The endpoint sorts by `-datetime` (a `DateTimeField`). `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — i.e. the integer semantics of `Paginator`, not the millisecond-timestamp conversion that `DateTimePaginator` implements. Consequently, when `optimized_pagination=true` is honored, `build_cursor` calls `get_item_key` on a `datetime` and raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, and any follow-up cursor value is injected raw into the `WHERE datetime >= %s` clause built by `build_queryset`, comparing an integer against a timestamp column. The optimized path therefore cannot work for this endpoint at all; it only produces 500s (and would silently mis-page if it did not crash).

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member` can be None, causing a 500 on every audit-log request

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET, before it is known whether the optimized path is even requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` and is None whenever the caller is not an organization member of record — e.g. requests authenticated with an organization auth token / API token that carries `org:write`/`org:admin`, which `OrganizationAuditPermission` accepts. For those callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False (AnonymousUser), so the right-hand side is evaluated and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working endpoint into a hard 500. At minimum the check must be guarded (`organization_context.member and ...`) and only evaluated when `use_optimized` is true.

false_positives.candidate:
Misleading comment added to Cursor.__init__

The added comment claims that `self.offset = int(offset)` is a “performance optimization” that “allows negative offsets … enables efficient reverse pagination”. No code changed here; `int(offset)` has always accepted negative values, and negative offsets are not a supported feature — most paginators reject them and Django refuses negative slices. The comment documents a non-existent and unsafe capability and will mislead the next reader into thinking negative offsets are intentional and handled.

Module docstring still describes plain Redis sets and no eviction

The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted on insert once a segment exceeds 1000 members, but the module docstring was not updated: step 3 still says “Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`” and the glossary still says “span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys”. Nothing documents that spans can now be silently dropped from a segment, which is the most important semantic change in this PR for anyone debugging missing spans.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a brand-new public paginator wired into a production endpoint, but no tests were added in this PR (neither for the paginator itself nor for the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch of `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`). As a result the broken datetime key handling and the negative-offset ValueError path described in the other findings would not be caught by CI. Tests should cover: default behaviour parity with `DateTimePaginator` for the audit log ordering, and the behaviour for negative/invalid cursor offsets.

No test covers the new eviction-on-insert behaviour

The PR's headline change is trimming segments to 1000 spans during insert (`zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua) and the switch from sets to sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, yet the only test changes are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to existing fixtures. There is no test that pushes more than the limit of spans into one segment and asserts that the oldest-ending spans are the ones dropped, nor any test that the score is preserved correctly across the `zunionstore` merges. The previously-tested-by-implication span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed with no replacement coverage, so a regression in the eviction logic (wrong aggregate, wrong pop count, off-by-one on the threshold) would go unnoticed.

Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the explanatory comment deleted

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence (“theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly”) was removed. With the lower bound, traces whose redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to their real root set and will be emitted as separate, incorrectly split segments. This is a behavioural change unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (eviction on insert), is not mentioned in the description, and now has no comment documenting the limitation.

Segment span limit hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, conflicting with the now-dead max_segment_spans setting

The new eviction uses the literal `1000` in two places (`if span_count > 1000` / `zpopmin set_key, span_count - 1000`), while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still exposes `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, which this PR leaves completely unused after removing the span-count check in `_load_segment_data`. The effective limit is therefore no longer configurable, differs from the previous 1001 threshold, and the stale constructor parameter will mislead operators who try to tune it. Either pass the configured limit into the script as an ARGV, or remove `max_segment_spans` from the buffer.

max_segment_spans is now dead code and the over-size-segment metric/log was dropped

`_load_segment_data` no longer checks `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, so the constructor parameter `max_segment_spans` is unused, and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric plus the accompanying `logger.error` are gone. Any dashboards/alerts built on that metric will silently go to zero, and there is no longer any signal when a segment is truncated — trimming now happens silently inside the Lua script. Add an equivalent metric for evicted spans (e.g. the `zpopmin` count) and remove or honor the unused parameter.

zunionstore defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting the end-timestamp scores used for eviction

Both merge steps use `redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` without an `AGGREGATE` option, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both sorted sets. Scores here are `end_timestamp_precise` values, so a span payload that happens to exist in both the destination set and the merged set (e.g. a duplicate delivery, or a span already zadd'ed under the top-most parent key by `process_spans` and also present under its own span key) ends up with a score of roughly 2×1.7e9. That value is no longer a timestamp, and because the new trimming logic uses `zpopmin` (lowest score evicted first), duplicated spans become effectively un-evictable while legitimate newer spans are dropped. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep scores meaningful.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility computed from outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument and runs the query against it, but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)`. In the dashboard discover-split path (`get_event_stats_factory.fn`) `_get_event_stats` is deliberately called with a different dataset (`discover` for the errors-only probe, `split_dataset`, etc.), so the decision whether to rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count()` is made for the wrong dataset. Result: the errors-only split probe against `discover` will not be upsampled when the request dataset is metrics/transactions, and conversely a transform decided for `errors` can be applied to a query actually executed against another dataset. Use `scoped_dataset` for the check.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
60s eligibility cache with no invalidation path returns stale upsampling decisions

`cache.set(cache_key, is_eligible, 60)` caches the allowlist decision for 60 seconds, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (defined below at line 67) is never called from anywhere in the codebase — nothing hooks option updates for `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. Consequently, after a project is removed from the allowlist, event-stats responses keep returning upsampled (inflated by 1/sample_rate) counts for up to a minute, and after a project is added the counts stay un-upsampled. Given `options.get` is already option-cached in Sentry, the extra cache buys little while introducing a correctness window; either drop the cache or wire the invalidation to option changes.

Accidental git submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed

This PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d2909 (the PR's own base commit) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. A gitlink without submodule configuration leaves the repository in a broken state: `git submodule update --init --recursive` fails or silently leaves an empty directory, tooling that walks the worktree sees a phantom directory, and CI checkouts can fail. This is clearly an accidental artifact of local development and must be removed from the PR.

Added lines contain trailing whitespace that will fail lint/black checks

Several newly added lines consist of or end with trailing whitespace (e.g. line 223 after the `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)` call, line 234 after the first `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling(...)` assignment, and line 278 in the RPC branch); the same pattern exists in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` docstrings/blank lines. The repository enforces black and flake8 via pre-commit, so CI will reject these as formatting failures until the files are reformatted.

Cache key built from `hash()` of project ids and omits the allowlist value

The cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}"`. Two different project-id sets in the same organization that hash to the same value will share a cache entry, which can make a query over non-allowlisted projects be treated as eligible and silently multiply reported error counts by the sample weight (or vice versa, suppressing upsampling). The key also does not incorporate the allowlist option value, so the cached answer is not tied to the input that produced it. Use the explicit sorted project id list (or a stable digest such as md5 of the joined ids) in the key, and include an allowlist version/hash.

Comment claims cached/consistent decision, but eligibility is re-evaluated per call and can flip mid-request

The comments say "Early upsampling eligibility check ... This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution" and "Store the upsampling decision to apply later", but `should_upsample` is recomputed on every invocation of `_get_event_stats`, and the helper's cache has a 60s TTL. In the discover-split flow `_get_event_stats` is called 2–3 times per request (errors-only probe, original query, transactions-only probe). If the cached entry expires or the allowlist option changes between those calls, one series will be `sum(sample_weight)` based and another plain `count()`, so `check_if_results_have_data` / `save_split_decision` compares incomparable magnitudes and the widget split decision is made on inconsistent data. The decision should be computed once per request and passed down.

Docstring states allowlist is read fresh every call, contradicting the new cache

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`'s docstring says the function "reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time ... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state", but its only caller caches the result for 60 seconds, so callers do not see the latest configuration. The docstring will mislead the next person debugging stale upsampling behaviour and should be corrected or removed.

No test covers the new public entry point or its caching logic

The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The actually new and risky behaviour introduced by this PR — `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` with its cache key derivation, 60s TTL staleness, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` — has no coverage at all, so regressions such as a cached `True` being returned after a project is removed from the allowlist, or a cache key collision, would not be caught. Note also that cached entries persist across tests in the same process, so any future test of this function must clear the cache in `setUp`.

Upsampling end-to-end tests only cover the default discover dataset

`OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` only issues requests without `dataset` (discover) plus one `dataset=discover` transaction case. The `errors` dataset — for which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` unconditionally returns True and which is the primary production path for error charts — is never exercised, nor is the `topEvents` branch where the transform is also applied. This matters because the `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction was registered only in the discover dataset config; if the errors dataset config does not inherit that registry, every upsampled errors-dataset request would fail with an unknown-function error and no test would notice. Add coverage for `dataset=errors` and for a `topEvents` request.

`_is_error_focused_query` substring match also matches negated/unrelated queries

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the lowercased raw query string contains the substring `event.type:error`. A query such as `!event.type:error` (an explicitly non-error query) or a free-text/message search that happens to contain that substring also matches, so `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (i.e. `sum(sample_weight)`) for a result set that includes transactions/other event types. That yields wrong numbers, and on entities where `sample_weight` is unavailable it can fail the Snuba query outright. Parse the search query (e.g. with the event search parser) and require a positive `event.type:error` term instead of a substring check.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` swallows all exceptions, silently dropping the sample rate

Both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion are wrapped in bare `except Exception: pass`. If a test supplies `client_sample_rate` in an unexpected shape (string, nested differently, typo'd context key), the sample rate is silently not set, the event is stored with weight 1, and the upsampling assertions in tests degrade to asserting the non-upsampled path without any signal that the fixture was wrong. Validate/convert explicitly and let bad fixture data raise, or at minimum narrow the exception types.

`upsampled_count` declares `default_result_type="number"` for an integer aggregate

The aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` and it replaces `count()` (which declares `integer`), yet it declares `default_result_type="number"`. The declared result type is echoed in the response `meta`, so the frontend will format the upsampled count as a float/number rather than an integer, making charts and tables render differently depending on whether upsampling was applied. Use `"integer"`.

`upsampled_count` is exposed publicly in the discover function registry

Unlike the neighbouring internal helper functions, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, so it immediately becomes a user-callable aggregate on every endpoint using the discover dataset config (events, events-stats, dashboards, alerts). Users can request `upsampled_count()` for projects that are not allowlisted (producing meaningless or inflated numbers), and for queries that include transaction events, where `sample_weight` is not available — the very case `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` deliberately avoids — which surfaces as a Snuba error rather than a validation error. Mark it `private=True` since the only intended caller is the internal column transform.

`upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` with no null/zero fallback

The new SnQLFunction resolves to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no `ifNull`/default. Events in an allowlisted project that were ingested without a client sample rate (older events already in retention, SDKs that don't emit `contexts.error_sampling`, or server-side generated events) have no sample weight, so they contribute 0 to the sum and vanish from the chart entirely — an undercount that looks like data loss. The helper docstring in error_upsampling.py ("We rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, so no additional null checks are needed") is an assumption, not an enforced invariant. Use something like `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` or an explicit default.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error IDs are zipped against unordered nodestore results

`fetch_error_details()` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` and then pairs them with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi()` returns a mapping keyed by node id; its iteration order is an implementation detail (several backends merge cache hits and DB fetches into a new dict), so `events.values()` is not guaranteed to be in the same order as `error_ids`. Worse, missing events are filtered with `if data is not None` *after* zipping, so a single missing event shifts every subsequent pairing. The result is `ErrorEvent.id` values attached to the wrong title/message/timestamp, which is then fed to Seer for summarization. Pair explicitly instead, e.g. iterate `for error_id, node_id in zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and look up `events.get(node_id)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged table widget renders hardcoded empty data

When `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, the widget renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`, completely ignoring the `result` that was just fetched. Any organization with this flag enabled will see every dashboard table widget render as an empty table with no columns and no rows, with no error or loading state to explain it. Either wire the real `result`/`fields` into the new component or keep the branch out of the shipped code path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
age/timestamp mutual-exclusion validation is incomplete and falsy-sensitive

The serializer is meant to accept exactly one of `age` (Editor's Draft) or `timestamp` (Working Draft), but: (1) both fields are `required=False` with no object-level check, so a report containing *neither* passes validation; and (2) the cross-checks use truthiness (`if self.initial_data.get("age")` / `.get("timestamp")`), so `age: 0` (a perfectly valid age for a freshly generated report) or `timestamp: 0` bypasses the mutual-exclusion check and both fields are accepted together. Use `is not None` checks and add a `validate()` that requires exactly one of the two fields.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics event recorded before feature gate and payload validation

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is the first statement in `post()`, before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before schema validation. Every request from an org without the feature (which gets a 404) and every malformed request is counted as an assemble event, so the metric no longer reflects actual assemble attempts. Move the call after the feature/validation checks. Note also that with org-auth-token authentication `request.user` is anonymous, so `user_id` will be `None` for the main machine-to-machine use case.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

false_positives.candidate:
Custom cell renderers fall back on any falsy return, not just undefined

Both `renderDefaultHeadCell` and `renderDefaultBodyCell` decide to use the custom renderer with `if (cell)`. The documented contract (see the prop JSDoc in `tableWidgetVisualization.tsx` and the storybook text: 'If the function returns `undefined`, fallback renderer will run') is that only `undefined` falls through. In practice a renderer that intentionally renders nothing by returning `null`, or that returns `''`/`0`/`false` for a cell value, will be silently overridden by the default renderer. Check `cell !== undefined` instead.

Dead `enabled` condition and default refetching on an LLM-backed endpoint

`normalizeDateTimeParams(...)` always returns an object, so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always `true` and contributes nothing to the `enabled` guard — the intent (don't query without a date range) is not implemented. Additionally the query uses `staleTime: 5000` with default refetch behaviour, so the `/feedback-summary/` endpoint (which generates an LLM completion server-side) can be re-hit every few seconds on remount/refocus, multiplying model cost. Consider a substantially larger `staleTime` and an explicit guard on the date range.

Dead code left behind after removing regex experiments

With `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` deleted, the nested `_handle_regex_match` helper inside `parametrize_w_experiments` is no longer referenced by anything (the loop now always calls `experiment.run(content, _incr_counter)`), and `ParameterizationRegex.compiled_pattern` / `_compiled_pattern` were only used by the removed class. Removing them keeps the module from accumulating unreachable branches that future readers assume are live.

Error/breadcrumb merge compares timestamps in different units

`gen_request_data()` interleaves errors and replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamps come from the nodestore event payload (epoch **seconds**, e.g. 1.75e9), while the top-level timestamp of an rrweb replay event is epoch **milliseconds** (e.g. 1.75e12). The comparison is therefore always true for real data, so every error is emitted before the first breadcrumb instead of being interleaved chronologically, defeating the purpose of the merge. The new unit tests use hand-written second-based event timestamps (1.5, 2.0), which hides the mismatch. Normalize both sides to the same unit before comparing.

Hook now returns possibly-undefined attributes instead of an empty TagCollection

Previously `attributes` was derived through a `useMemo` that always produced a `TagCollection` object (`{}` when there was no data). Now it is `isFetching ? previous : data`, where both `previous` (first render) and `data` (query disabled or not yet resolved) are `undefined`. Callers that are not updated in this PR and treat the value as always-present (spreading is fine, but `Object.keys(attributes)` / `attributes[key]` is not) can now hit runtime errors, in particular when the hook is used with `enabled: false`. Fall back to an empty object (`data ?? {}`) to preserve the previous contract.

Inconsistent optional chaining on required tableData prop

`Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields)` mixes optional chaining with a non-guarded member access and an unguarded `Object.keys`. If `tableData` is ever undefined (the surrounding code defends against it with `tableData?.data ?? []`), this throws `Cannot convert undefined or null to object` instead of rendering an empty table. Either treat `tableData` as truly required (drop the `?.`) or guard the fallback column computation.

Issue list template produces blank lines and a trailing newline in PR comments

`MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE` ends with `
`, but both the GitHub and GitLab workflows join the rendered entries with `"
".join(...)`. Every bullet is therefore separated by a blank line (which Markdown renders as a 'loose' list with extra paragraph spacing) and the list ends with an extra newline immediately before the `<sub>Did you find this useful?</sub>` footer. The updated tests encode this double spacing, so the formatting regression will ship silently. Drop the trailing `
` from the template.

Tests no longer exercise the application/reports+json content type

The rewritten `test_basic` and `test_handles_multiple_reports_both_specs` post without `content_type="application/reports+json"` (the previous tests passed it explicitly). The custom `BrowserReportsJSONParser` exists precisely to accept the Browser Reporting API media type, and that is the content type real browsers send, yet it is now only covered indirectly by the negative `test_rejects_invalid_content_type` case. Keep at least one success-path test that posts with `application/reports+json`.

Unauthenticated endpoint loops over an unbounded report array

This endpoint has `permission_classes = ()` and is CSRF exempt, yet the new code iterates the entire posted array with no cap on the number of reports: it logs the full request body, logs each invalid report (`extra={"raw_report": report}`) and emits one metric per valid report at `sample_rate=1.0`. A single large request can therefore flood logs and the metrics pipeline with attacker-controlled content. Add a maximum list length (and ideally a body size limit) before processing.

get_environment_info triggers a recommended-event lookup per issue in PR comments

`get_environment_info()` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment. That helper runs a Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch per issue, so building a comment for the top 5 issues now issues up to 5 extra event lookups (each able to time out or return a stale 'recommended' event) inside the PR comment task, for a single word of decoration in the comment. Consider resolving environments from data already fetched (e.g. the group's environments or the snuba row) instead of fetching full events. Also note the `except Exception` branch logs the raw exception object in `extra={"error": e}`; `str(e)` serializes more reliably.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code comparison is case-sensitive while the input is not normalized

`backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` compares the user input literally against lowercase hex codes generated by `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`. The input field in `apps/web/components/auth/BackupCode.tsx` sets no `autoCapitalize="off"`/`autoCorrect="off"`, so mobile keyboards commonly capitalize the first character and users who type the code in upper case will be rejected with "Backup code is incorrect" even though they supplied a valid code. The same applies to `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`. Normalize with `.toLowerCase().trim()` server-side and/or disable auto-capitalization on the input.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

The code decrypts the whole array, nulls one entry and writes the re-encrypted blob back with a plain `user.update`. Two concurrent logins using the same backup code both read the un-consumed array and both succeed, so a one-time code can be used more than once; two concurrent logins using different codes will clobber each other's update, resurrecting an already-used code. Consider a transaction with a row-level check (e.g. conditional update on the previous value) or storing individual code rows that can be deleted atomically.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code state and object URL are never cleaned up

`resetState()` only clears password, error and step; `backupCodes` and `backupCodesUrl` keep holding the generated codes in component state after the dialog closes (the modal is kept mounted by the settings page). The blob URL created in `handleSetup` is only revoked when a new one is created, never on unmount or close, so each setup leaks a blob for the lifetime of the page. Clear both in `resetState()` and revoke the URL (e.g. in a cleanup effect).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

false_positives.candidate:
"missing_backup_codes" message points users to a settings feature that does not exist

The string is "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." but there is no UI anywhere in this PR to generate or regenerate backup codes — codes are only created inside the 2FA setup flow (`totp/setup`). Every user who enabled 2FA before this migration has `backupCodes = null` and will hit this message with no actionable path; the only way to obtain codes is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Either add a regenerate action or change the message to tell users to disable and re-enable two-factor authentication.

Backup code alone can authenticate without the account password

The password is only verified by the block at lines 121-129, which is guarded by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`. The new backup-code branch is entered whenever `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` is set, regardless of `totpCode`. An attacker who obtains a single backup code (e.g. the downloaded `cal-backup-codes.txt`) but does not know the password can POST to the credentials endpoint with `email`, an arbitrary `password`, any non-empty `totpCode` (e.g. "000000") and the valid `backupCode`: the password check is skipped because `totpCode` is truthy, and only the backup code is validated, so the login succeeds. Backup codes are intended to replace the second factor, not the password, so this turns them into full single-factor credentials. The backup-code branch must verify the password (or the branch selection must not depend on `totpCode` being absent).

Backup codes are unusable for Google/SAML users with 2FA

For users who reach the login page via the external TOTP flow (`totpEmail` set, i.e. Google/SAML accounts with 2FA), `ExternalTotpFooter` is rendered and the new "Lost access" button is never shown, so those users cannot use their backup codes. Even if a `backupCode` were submitted, `authorize()` in next-auth-options.ts throws `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` at the `user.identityProvider !== CAL && !credentials.totpCode` check before reaching the backup-code branch. These users have no recovery path if they lose their authenticator, which is the main purpose of the feature.

Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of hashed

Backup codes are persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`, i.e. recoverable plaintext. The server never needs to display the codes again after setup (they are only shown from the setup response), so they can and should be stored as one-way hashes like passwords. As implemented, anyone who gains read access to the users table together with the (single, global, long-lived) encryption key — which is also present in every app instance's environment — can recover every user's 2FA backup codes and bypass two-factor auth for all accounts.

Clipboard write rejection is unhandled and success toast is shown unconditionally

`navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` returns a promise that is neither awaited nor caught, and `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")` runs immediately. In contexts where the Clipboard API is unavailable or permission is denied (non-HTTPS deployments, some browsers), the user is told the codes were copied while nothing was copied, and the rejection surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection. Await the call and only show success on resolve, with an error toast/fallback otherwise.

First 2FA test asserts nothing and is not updated for the new backup-codes step

`expect(page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on the returned Promise, which is always truthy, so the step verifies nothing — the PR documents this with a FIXME instead of fixing it. This matters now: with the new flow the backup-codes dialog stays open after OTP entry and `onEnable()` is never fired, so the switch would legitimately not be checked; the test only passes because the assertion is a no-op. Use `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch][data-state="checked"]')).toBeVisible()` after dismissing the backup-codes dialog, as the second test does.

Password visibility toggle made unreachable by keyboard

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button removes it from tab order, so keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer toggle password visibility. This change affects every `PasswordField` in the app, not just the 2FA dialogs. If the intent was to keep tab order flowing to the next form field, consider other means (e.g. ordering/`aria` handling) rather than making the control unfocusable.

Submitting an empty backup code silently does nothing

The login form is rendered with `noValidate`, and the zod schema only validates `email`/`password` (`.passthrough()`), so the `required`/`minLength` attributes on the backup-code input are not enforced. Submitting the backup-code screen with an empty field sends `backupCode: ""`, the server falls through to the TOTP branch and returns `SecondFactorRequired`, which this handler maps to `setTwoFactorRequired(true)` — a no-op since the user is already on that screen — while `errorMessage` was cleared at the start of submit. The user gets no feedback at all. Validate the backup code client-side or surface an error for this case.

Unvalidated request body can crash the disable endpoint

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes the field is a string; a client sending `{"backupCode": 123}` or an object causes an uncaught `TypeError` and an opaque 500 instead of a 400. Likewise `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` on line 58 is unguarded, so a corrupted/re-keyed `backupCodes` column throws an unhandled exception rather than returning a meaningful error.
