false_negatives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar/video update uses the requester's credentials instead of the booking organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` build the EventManager from the *logged-in* user, but `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` must operate on the organizer's calendar/video integration (the references belong to `booking.user`). When an attendee or a team admin/owner adds guests, the requester has no credentials for the organizer's Google/Outlook calendar or video app, so the external calendar invite is never updated (or the wrong account is targeted) while the DB and emails say it succeeded. The handler already fetches `booking.user.credentials` (line 38) but never uses it.

CalendarEvent is built without `team`, so team hosts are never notified

The `evt` object omits `team`, yet `sendAddGuestsEmails` loops over `calendarEvent.team?.members` to notify co-hosts. Because `team` is always undefined here, that loop is dead code and additional hosts of team/round-robin events never learn that guests were added. Populate `evt.team` (as `editLocation`/booking flows do) or drop the loop.

Component inside packages/ui imports the package's own barrel, creating a circular dependency

`import { Button, EmailField, Icon, Tooltip } from "@calcom/ui";` is a self-import of the package root, which `packages/ui/index.tsx` in turn re-exports (`export { default as MultiEmail } from "./form/MultiEmailLazy"`). Circular barrel imports can resolve to `undefined` component references depending on module evaluation order and bloat the lazy chunk this file is meant to keep small. Import from the relative component paths (`../components/button`, `../components/form`, `../components/icon/Icon`, `../components/tooltip`) as other internal files do.

Email failures are swallowed with console.log and the error is discarded

`catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` drops `err` entirely and uses `console.log` instead of the shared `logger` used elsewhere in the codebase. If guest notification emails fail there is no actionable signal (no stack, no bookingId), making production incidents undebuggable while the mutation still reports success.

Error toast shows raw tRPC error codes and the fallback message is unreachable

`const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`` is always a non-empty string, so `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` can never fall back to the friendly copy, and users are shown technical strings such as "FORBIDDEN: you_do_not_have_permission" or "undefined: ..." when `err.data` is missing. Translate known message keys and fall back to `t("unable_to_add_guests")` when the code/message is not user-facing.

Guests added to seated bookings get no BookingSeat record and bypass seatsPerTimeSlot

Attendees are inserted directly with `attendees.createMany` without creating the corresponding `BookingSeat` row and without checking `eventType.seatsPerTimeSlot`. For seated events the rest of the product (seat-reference based cancel/reschedule links, seat availability counting, success page) keys off `BookingSeat`; attendees created here will have no seat reference, so they cannot cancel/reschedule their seat and the seat capacity can be exceeded. Either reject seated bookings in this handler or create the seat references.

Label `htmlFor="emails"` points at a non-existent input id

The `<label htmlFor="emails">` has no matching element with `id="emails"` (the rendered `EmailField`s get generated ids and are passed `label={<></>}`), so clicking the label does nothing and screen readers announce the inputs without a label. Either give the first input that id or associate labels per field.

New mutation that mutates bookings and sends email has no tests

`addGuestsHandler` contains non-trivial authorization logic (organizer / attendee / team admin), filtering/blacklisting, attendee creation and email+calendar side effects, but no unit or integration test is added in this PR. The permission bug on line 46 (AND vs OR) and the unfiltered `guests` passed to `sendAddGuestsEmails` are exactly the kind of regressions a handler test would catch.

Newly added guests receive the full attendee list even when seatsShowAttendees is false

`new AttendeeScheduledEmail(calendarEvent, attendee)` is called without the `showAttendees` argument (compare `sendScheduledSeatsEmails`, which passes it). For seated event types with `seatsShowAttendees: false`, the email/ICS sent to a newly added guest will disclose the names and email addresses of all other attendees, leaking personal data that the event type is configured to hide.

No upper bound on the number of guests allows mass-mail abuse

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` accepts an unbounded array. Any authenticated user is the organizer of their own bookings, so they can call `bookings.addGuests` with thousands of arbitrary addresses; the handler then creates an Attendee row per address and `sendAddGuestsEmails` sends a Cal.com-branded confirmation email with an ICS invite to each one. This turns the endpoint into an email relay/spam vector from Cal.com's sending domain and can also blow up the single DB write and the email queue. Add a `.max(...)` limit (and ideally rate limiting).

No validation of booking status; guests can be added to cancelled/rejected/past bookings

The handler only checks existence and permissions. A cancelled, rejected or already-finished booking will still get new attendees, a calendar-attendee update and "your event" confirmation emails to the new guests. The UI hides the action for cancelled bookings, but the tRPC mutation is reachable directly. Reject bookings whose status is not ACCEPTED/PENDING (and optionally bookings in the past).

Stale "emails must be unique and valid" error persists after a successful add

`onSuccess` resets `multiEmailValue` and closes the dialog but never clears `isInvalidEmail`. If the user first submits an invalid entry and then a valid one, the error banner stays in state and is displayed again the next time the dialog is opened, even though the input is empty. Reset `setIsInvalidEmail(false)` in `onSuccess` (and on successful validation in `handleAdd`).

findFirstOrThrow with `booking.userId || 0` yields an opaque 500 for bookings without a user

When `booking.userId` is null (e.g. dynamic group bookings or bookings whose user was deleted), the query looks up user id 0 and `findFirstOrThrow` raises a Prisma error that surfaces as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of a meaningful tRPC error. Handle the null-userId case explicitly (or use the already-included `booking.user` relation).

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany `retryCount > 1` arm is not scoped to SMS reminders

The new OR branch in the `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany()` call matches `retryCount > 1` for *every* row in `WorkflowReminder`, with no `method` filter. This SMS cron therefore deletes EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders too as soon as anything starts incrementing `retryCount` for them (e.g. when the same retry logic is added to `scheduleEmailReminders`/`scheduleWhatsappReminders`, or if a future writer sets the field). It also deletes rows that are already `scheduled: true` with a `referenceId`, losing the record needed to cancel the scheduled message later. The branch should be scoped with `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and arguably `scheduled: false`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

false_positives.candidate:
Comment no longer describes what the delete query does

The comment `//delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date` now sits above a query that also deletes any reminder (of any method) whose `retryCount` exceeds 1. A reader relying on the comment will not realise rows are being removed for retry exhaustion, which is the main new behaviour here. Update the comment to mention the retry-count deletion.

No retry accounting when message is empty or sendTo is missing

The retryCount increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. When `sendTo` is null (e.g. `booking.smsReminderNumber` not set for an SMS_ATTENDEE step) or the rendered `message` is empty, the loop body falls through without touching the row: `scheduled` stays `false` and `retryCount` stays unchanged, so this reminder is re-selected and re-processed (including the `prisma.profile.findFirst` and `getBookerBaseUrl` queries) on every cron invocation until `scheduledDate` passes. That is precisely the endless-rescheduling behaviour this PR is meant to eliminate, and it remains unfixed for these cases.

No tests for the new retry/delete behaviour

The PR introduces behaviour that permanently deletes user-facing reminders (increment on failure, delete when `retryCount > 1`) and no test covers it: there is no assertion that a failed `twilio.scheduleSMS` increments `retryCount`, that a falsy (non-throwing) return also increments it, that a successful schedule leaves the row intact, or that the delete threshold yields exactly two attempts. Given the data-loss consequence of an off-by-one here (threshold `gt: 1` vs `gte: 1`), a unit test around the handler with a mocked twilio provider would be worth adding.

OR on unindexed retryCount forces a full scan of WorkflowReminder on every cron run

The rewritten `deleteMany` produces `WHERE (method = 'SMS' AND scheduledDate <= now) OR retryCount > 1`. There is no index on `retryCount` (the schema only has `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` and `[cancelled, scheduledDate]`), so the OR prevents an index-only plan and Postgres will sequentially scan the whole `WorkflowReminder` table each time this cron runs. On a table of this size (one row per reminder per booking) that is a noticeable repeated cost. Splitting into two `deleteMany` calls (one per condition, with the retry one scoped to `method: SMS`) and/or indexing the retry predicate would keep the existing index usable.

Transient failures cause permanent deletion of pending SMS reminders

`retryCount` is incremented for every failure path without distinguishing permanent errors (invalid phone number, which is the motivating case) from transient ones (Twilio outage/5xx, network timeout, DB hiccup, rate limiting). Since the cron processes all reminders due within the next 7 days on every run, two consecutive bad runs are enough to push `retryCount` to 2 for the entire backlog, and the next run's `deleteMany` silently deletes all of them — reminders that would have sent fine are lost permanently with no notification. Consider only counting non-retryable Twilio errors, or using a time-based backoff/last-attempt timestamp so retries are spread out rather than consumed within minutes/hours of each other.

retryCount update inside catch can abort the whole cron run

The `prisma.workflowReminder.update()` added at the top of the `catch` block is not itself protected. Before this change the catch only called `console.log`, so any error for one reminder was swallowed and the loop continued. Now, if this update throws (row deleted concurrently by the `deleteMany` of a parallel invocation → Prisma P2025 "record not found", or a DB connection error, which is exactly the kind of failure likely to have caused the original exception), the rejection propagates out of the `for` loop, every remaining unscheduled reminder in the batch is skipped, and the endpoint returns a 500 instead of the expected response. Wrap the update in its own try/catch (or `.catch()`) so a bookkeeping failure cannot abort the batch.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unreachable branches in getBaseConditions

`getAuthorizationConditions()` always resolves to a `Prisma.Sql` object (at minimum `NOTHING_CONDITION`), and objects are always truthy, so the `else if (filterConditions)` branch (line 76) and the final `else return NOTHING_CONDITION` (line 79) can never execute. The dead code suggests the author expected auth conditions to possibly be null/absent; if a future change makes auth conditions optional the fallback would silently drop authorization. Either drop the dead branches or make the nullability explicit.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching tests deleted although the caching logic still exists

The `describe("Caching")` block (previously asserting that `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return the same cached value on repeated calls) was removed, but the service still implements `cachedAuthConditions` / `cachedFilterConditions` memoization, including the `undefined`-vs-`null` distinction in `getFilterConditions()` (a cached `null` must not trigger a rebuild). That memoization path is now untested, so a regression such as caching `null` incorrectly or rebuilding conditions on every call would go unnoticed. The tests could simply be ported to the new `Prisma.sql` expectations instead of deleted.

New InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions weakens compile-time validation of options

The constructor parameter type changed from the zod discriminated union (`InsightsBookingServiceOptions`, which requires `teamId` when `scope === "team"`) to the hand-written `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` with `scope: "user" | "org" | "team"` and optional `teamId`. A caller can now pass `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` without `teamId` and it type-checks; at runtime `safeParse` fails, `this.options` becomes `null`, and the service silently returns `1=0`, i.e. an empty result set with no error or log. The previous typing made this a compile error. Keep the discriminated union as the constructor type (or at least log/throw when validation fails) so misuse is caught instead of producing silently empty insights.

Org/team scope assertions depend on unspecified DB row ordering

The org-scope expectation hard-codes the parameter arrays as `[org.id, team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`. These come from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId` and `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, which issue queries without an `ORDER BY`, so PostgreSQL does not guarantee the returned order. With `toEqual` on the `Prisma.Sql` object the `values` arrays are compared element-by-element, so any reordering (e.g. after a vacuum, index-only scan or parallel plan) fails the test even though the generated SQL is semantically equivalent. Sort the ids in the service (or sort before comparison in the test) to make the assertion deterministic.

Public findMany() removed without updating any callers

The public method `findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)`, which ran `prisma.bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany` with the authorization and filter where-clauses applied, is deleted and replaced by `getBaseConditions()` returning a raw `Prisma.Sql`. No other file in the repository is touched by this PR, so any existing consumer of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` will no longer compile, and consumers must now hand-write raw SQL (taking on responsibility for parenthesization, column quoting and result typing). Either keep a `findMany`-style convenience wrapper or update the call sites in this PR. The PR description also states that only the tests changed and that the service was already converted, which hides this breaking change from reviewers.

Returned SQL fragments contain top-level OR without enclosing parentheses

`getBaseConditions()` returns the authorization fragment verbatim when no filters are set (line 75), and for `org`/`team` scope that fragment is built by the reduce as `(A AND "isTeamBooking" = true) OR (B AND "isTeamBooking" = false)` with no enclosing parentheses (lines 171-174 and 204-207). The same is true for `getFilterConditions()` when only `eventTypeId` is set (`("eventTypeId" = x) OR ("eventParentId" = x)`). Because `AND` binds tighter than `OR` in SQL, any consumer that composes the fragment with extra predicates — e.g. `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "startTime" >= ${from}` — produces `A OR (B AND startTime >= ...)`, so the additional predicate constrains only one branch of the OR. The result is silently widened row sets, i.e. a potential authorization/scope bypass and wrong insights numbers. The fragments should be wrapped (`Prisma.sql`(${cond})`) before being returned. Note the only test uses `WHERE ${baseConditions}` standalone, so this failure mode is not covered.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateManyByCredentialId called with an empty data object to bump updatedAt

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` relies on Prisma implicitly writing the `@updatedAt` column when `data` is empty. This is implicit/undocumented behaviour — if Prisma emits no SET clause the call is a pure no-op write — and even when it works it issues an extra UPDATE over every SelectedCalendar row of the credential on every cache refresh (including rows that were not refreshed), which runs on the cache cron for every watched credential. The PR description itself notes `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is not consumed by the frontend (the UI uses `cacheUpdatedAt`), so this write appears unnecessary; if it is needed, pass an explicit `{ updatedAt: new Date() }`.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is BSD/macOS-only and breaks on Linux

`sed -i '' -E "s|...|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses the BSD syntax where `-i` takes a separate (empty) suffix argument. With GNU sed (Linux CI/dev containers) the empty string is parsed as the script/first file operand and the command fails with "can't read : No such file or directory", leaving `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` un-updated while the script still reports success. Use `sed -i.bak`/a temp-file approach, or branch on the platform.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteCache throws a plain Error instead of TRPCError

When the credential does not exist or does not belong to the caller the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. tRPC maps non-TRPCError exceptions to `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` (HTTP 500), so an authorization failure is reported as a server fault, gets logged/reported to error tracking as a crash, and the client cannot distinguish it from a real failure. Use `throw new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" | "FORBIDDEN", message: ... })` as the other handlers in this router do.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is hard-coded to en-US formatting

`new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })` ignores the user's locale and 12h/24h `timeFormat` preference stored on the user, so non-US users see MM/DD/YYYY and AM/PM dates inside an otherwise localized UI (the surrounding string is translated via `cache_last_updated`). Use the user's locale/time-format (e.g. the existing dayjs/`useTimePreferences` helpers) instead of a literal "en-US".

false_positives.candidate:
Cache deletion does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query

`deleteCacheMutation.onSuccess` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop. Unlike the disconnect mutation (which invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`), nothing invalidates the query that produced `cacheUpdatedAt`. In `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` the `onChanged` prop is optional and is not always supplied, and the query is configured with `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`, so after deleting the cache the dropdown keeps showing the old "Last updated" timestamp and the "Delete cached data" entry until a full page reload, making it look like the deletion failed.

Cache status lookup bypasses the calendar-cache feature flag

The handler instantiates `CalendarCacheRepository` directly instead of going through `CalendarCache.init(...)`, so the `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` added in this PR is never used and an extra `calendarCache.groupBy` query is executed on every `connectedCalendars` request even for deployments/teams where calendar cache is disabled (and also when `credentialIds` is empty, producing a pointless `IN ()` query). Route through the feature-flag aware factory, or skip the query when there are no credentialIds / the feature is off.

Dev script writes .env outside the repository

`ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the current working directory, not to the script location. The documented way of running repo scripts is from the repository root (`./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`), which makes the script create/modify a `.env` file in the parent directory of the checkout (and print "Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL" as if it had succeeded), while the app's real `.env` is left untouched. Resolve the path from `$(dirname "$0")/..` instead.

Migration comment contradicts the statement and backfill produces misleading timestamps

The generated warning block says the required column is added "without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty", but the statement does supply `DEFAULT NOW()`; the stale comment will mislead reviewers/operators about the migration's safety. In addition, all pre-existing rows are backfilled with the migration time, so immediately after deploy the new UI will report long-stale caches as "Last updated: <deploy time>". Consider removing/correcting the comment and documenting (or backfilling from `expiresAt - CACHING_TIME`) the known inaccuracy.

No tests for the new deleteCache authorization or cache-status query

`deleteCacheHandler` performs an ownership check that gates a destructive `calendarCache.deleteMany`, and `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` is new behaviour surfaced in the UI, yet neither has a unit test. A regression in the `userId` predicate would let a user delete another user's calendar cache, and nothing would catch it. Add tests covering: deletion for an owned credential, rejection for a credential owned by another user, and the credential→updatedAt mapping returned by the repository.

UserWithCalendars now requires updatedAt/googleChannelId that are never used

`UserWithCalendars` (an exported type consumed outside this file, e.g. by the platform API v2 calendars service and other callers of `getConnectedDestinationCalendarsAndEnsureDefaultsInDb`) was widened to require `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId` on `allSelectedCalendars` and `userLevelSelectedCalendars`, but neither field is read anywhere in this module. Any caller that selects only `externalId`/`integration`/`eventTypeId` will now fail type-check, and `UserRepository.findUnlockedUserForSession` had to be changed to fetch two extra columns per selected calendar into the session payload purely to satisfy the type. Revert the type tightening unless the fields are actually needed.

dev:cron uses npx tsx but tsx is not a dependency

`"dev:cron": "npx tsx cron-tester.ts"` invokes a binary that is not declared in `devDependencies` (only `ts-node` is, and it is still used by the `check-changed-files` and `translate-locales` scripts). `npx` will download an unpinned `tsx` from the network on each run (or prompt), which fails in offline/CI environments and is inconsistent with the yarn-workspace setup. Add `tsx` to devDependencies and call it via `yarn tsx`, or leave the script on `ts-node`. This change is also unrelated to the feature in this PR.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt

The groupBy query selects `MAX(updatedAt)` for the given credentialIds without filtering on `expiresAt >= now()`, while `getCachedAvailability` only serves non-expired rows. As a result the UI will report a credential as having a cache ("Cache Status / Last updated …") and offer "Delete cached data" even when every cached row is expired and no availability request can be served from it, giving users a misleading view of cache health.

updateManyByCredentialId types data as SelectedCalendarUpdateInput

`updateMany` accepts `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput`, not `SelectedCalendarUpdateInput`. Using the single-record update type lets callers pass nested relation operations (e.g. `{ user: { connect: { id } } }`) which type-check but fail at runtime with a Prisma validation error. Change the parameter type to `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation promises are not awaited, so the cancelled flag may never be persisted

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...)`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` are async but are invoked inside a `forEach` without awaiting, and the promises are no longer collected into `prismaPromises` as the deleted `remindersToDelete` array was. The whole fix now depends on a DB write (`cancelled = true`) performed in a floating promise; in a serverless deployment the function can be frozen/terminated once the handler returns, so the update can be lost and the reminder email will still be sent. The same pattern exists in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (requestReschedule) and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx`. In `handleNewBooking.ts` the surrounding `try/catch` (lines 964-975) is additionally dead code: because the calls are not awaited, it can never catch their failures. These calls should be awaited (e.g. `await Promise.all(reminders.map(...))`).

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path has no fallback and leaves the WorkflowReminder row behind

In the `immediateDelete` branch the SendGrid cancel request is issued and the function returns without deleting the reminder row and without setting `cancelled = true`. Two problems: (1) if the request fails — which is precisely what happens when SendGrid's limit of 100 pending cancellations is hit, the scenario this PR describes — the error is swallowed by the outer `catch` and nothing records the intent to cancel, so the new cron fallback will never pick the reminder up and the reminder email is still delivered; (2) on success the row stays in the DB with `scheduled = true` and a dead `referenceId` until the cron's `deleteMany` eventually removes it, whereas the previous code deleted it. At minimum this branch should also mark/delete the row so there is a retry path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
cancelled column is nullable with no default and no index for the cron query

`cancelled Boolean?` (and the matching migration `ADD COLUMN "cancelled" BOOLEAN` with no default) gives the column three states (null/false/true) where only a boolean flag is needed, so consumers must remember that `cancelled: false` and `cancelled: null` both mean "not cancelled". In addition, `WorkflowReminder` has no index covering `(cancelled, scheduledDate)` or `scheduledDate`, and the cron now runs `findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: ... } } })` every 15 minutes over a table that grows with every booking/workflow step, forcing a sequential scan each run. Consider `Boolean @default(false)` plus an index on the fields the cron filters on.

false_positives.candidate:
Deferring cancellation to a 15-minute cron leaves reminders that are due soon uncancellable

Cancellation is now only performed by this cron for reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour, and the `deleteMany` at line 34 unconditionally removes every EMAIL reminder with `scheduledDate <= now` (including rows with `cancelled = true`) before the cancellation block runs. If a booking is cancelled or rescheduled less than one cron interval before the reminder's send time (e.g. 10 minutes before), the next run happens after `scheduledDate` has passed: the row is deleted by `deleteMany` and the reminder email is delivered. Even when the run lands a few minutes before the send time, SendGrid only honours cancellation of a scheduled send up to ~10 minutes before `send_at`, so the cancel request is rejected. This is a regression versus cancelling immediately and reintroduces exactly the symptom this PR is meant to fix for short-notice cancellations.

Import block is not prettier-formatted and an unrelated commented-out block was re-indented

`Prisma` is added to the import list without a trailing comma (line 9), and the previously type-only `import type { Prisma, PrismaPromise }` is turned into a value import even though both are only used in type positions. The same diff also re-indents the large commented-out `testAction` block (lines ~900-1010), which is unrelated to this change. The file is otherwise prettier-formatted, so the formatting check in CI will fail, and the comment reflow makes the diff hard to review.

No test covers the new cancellation flow

The new two-phase cancellation (mark `cancelled = true` on booking cancel/reschedule, then have the cron cancel at SendGrid and delete the row) is untested. The previous attempt at this fix (#6991) used the SendGrid API incorrectly and regressed silently in production; a test asserting that (a) cancelling a booking sets `cancelled = true` on its email reminders instead of deleting them and (b) the cron picks up only EMAIL reminders due within the window, cancels each and deletes the row even when one of them fails, would catch the loop-abort and filter problems noted above and prevent a repeat regression.

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation loop and prevents all row deletions

The cancellation loop (`for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)`) is wrapped in a single try/catch. The `await client.request(...)` call is the first statement in the loop body, so any failure for one reminder (invalid/expired `batch_id`, a batch that is already in `cancel` status, a 401, or SendGrid's 100-pending-cancellation cap being reached) throws out of the loop. Consequences: (a) every remaining reminder in `remindersToCancel` is skipped for this run, (b) `await Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` on line 74 is never reached, so even the reminders that *were* successfully cancelled keep `cancelled = true` in the DB, and (c) on the next run the same poison record is fetched again and fails again, so cancellation is permanently broken for every reminder behind it. Since the batch row is never deleted after a successful cancel in this scenario, re-cancelling an already-cancelled batch on the next run is itself likely to error, making the deadlock self-sustaining. Each iteration needs its own try/catch (and the delete should happen per-item), so one bad record cannot block the rest.

Reschedules still use the immediate SendGrid cancel, so rescheduled-booking reminders remain broken

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` passes `immediateDelete = true` for the reschedule path. The PR's own diagnosis is that immediate `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends { status: "cancel" }` calls accumulate as pending cancellations and start failing once 100 are pending. Rescheduling is one of the two cases named in the PR title, and it is a high-volume path, so it keeps filling that quota and keeps failing silently (the error is only `console.log`ged in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`), which both leaves the old reminder scheduled and can push the quota over the limit so that other cancellations (including the cron's) fail too. Reschedules should use the same deferred `cancelled = true` mechanism as cancellations.

client.setApiKey() is never called in this handler, so the new cancel requests may be unauthenticated

This file only calls `sgMail.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)`. `@sendgrid/mail` keeps its own internal client instance, whereas the `client` default export from `@sendgrid/client` used on line 57 (and line 188) is a separate singleton; `emailReminderManager.ts` explicitly calls `client.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` for this reason. Unless the key is set on that singleton by some other imported module, every `client.request()` here runs without an Authorization header and returns 401 — which, combined with the loop-wide try/catch, means no scheduled email is ever cancelled and the entire fix silently does nothing (only a `console.log`). Add `client.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` next to `sgMail.setApiKey`.

remindersToCancel query is not restricted to EMAIL reminders or to rows with a referenceId

`prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: ... } } })` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` filter and no `referenceId: { not: null }` filter, unlike the `deleteMany` above it. Any non-email row (or any row with a null `referenceId`) that ever ends up with `cancelled = true` will be POSTed to `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` with a Twilio SID or `null` as `batch_id`. SendGrid will reject it, and because of the single try/catch around the loop that aborts all remaining cancellations (see the loop issue), one such row permanently breaks email cancellation. There is also no `take` limit, so a large backlog is processed sequentially with one HTTP request each, risking a serverless timeout mid-loop.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
requestReschedule awaits inside `forEach`, so calendar/video cancellations are unawaited and errors are unhandled

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })` is fire-and-forget: the mutation continues to send the reschedule email, fire webhooks and return while the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls have not even been issued yet (they are now gated behind the awaited `getCalendar`). There is no try/catch here at all, so a failing credential or app import becomes an unhandled promise rejection in the tRPC server process. Iterate with `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered)` and `await`, or collect promises and `await Promise.all(...)` with a `.catch` so failures are logged.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recurring-booking calendar deletions remain fire-and-forget while the sibling branch was fixed

In the recurring branch, deletions are still issued inside `credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { ... })`. Because `forEach` ignores the returned promise, nothing ever awaits these callbacks: `apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent)` (line 467) runs long after `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 has already resolved with an empty/partial `apiDeletes`. The handler therefore returns `{ message: "Booking successfully cancelled." }` before the external calendar events are deleted; in a serverless/edge runtime the function is frozen or torn down and the remote events are orphaned, and any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The PR converted the equivalent non-credentialId branch just below (lines 480-483) to a `for ... of` loop with `await`, so this branch is now inconsistent; it needs the same treatment (collect the `deleteEvent` promises synchronously into `apiDeletes` or `await` them in a `for ... of`).

false_positives.candidate:
Template comment points at a non-existent path

The example comment was changed from `// import * as example from "./_example";` to `// example: import("./example"),`. The directory in the repo is `_example`, so a contributor copying this template line will add an import for a path that does not exist and get a build failure. It should read `example: import("./_example")` (matching whatever shape the final map uses).

`forEach(async ...)` makes the surrounding try/catch dead and turns errors into unhandled rejections

Same problem as in `vital/lib/reschedule.ts`: the `forEach` callback is now `async`, so the `try/catch` wrapping it (lines 124-139) can never catch a failure of `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` – those rejections now surface as unhandled promise rejections instead of being logged. The deletions are also no longer started synchronously, so `Reschedule` can resolve and the request finish before the external calendar/video events are cancelled. Replace with a `for ... of` loop and `await` (or `await Promise.all(map(...))`) inside the try block.

getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in `calendar`, changing the contract for all consumers

`getCalendar` became async but line 28 still calls it without awaiting, so each item returned by the exported `getCalendarCredentials` now carries `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`; every other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` (it is a public export of `@calcom/core`) that touches `.calendar` directly will now operate on a Promise and fail at runtime (`item.calendar.listCalendars is not a function`) unless TypeScript happens to flag it. All call sites need to be audited, or `getCalendarCredentials` should itself become async and resolve the calendars before returning. Related risk: the promises created here are left floating; if a dynamic app import rejects and nobody awaits that item, the rejection is unhandled and can terminate the process.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`end` is computed from slotStartTime, so the slot end is never validated against working hours

`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` duplicates the `start` expression instead of using `slotEndTime`. As a result the `end > workingHour.endTime` comparison can never detect a slot that overruns the end of a host's working hours. For a round-robin event where the fixed host works 09:00-12:00 and a round-robin host works 09:00-17:00, the aggregate working hours produce an 11:30 slot; for a 60-minute event it ends at 12:30, outside the fixed host's availability, yet this check passes it — exactly the over-booking of fixed hosts this PR is meant to prevent.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead branch: dayjs instances compared with `===`

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly-created objects by reference, which is always false, so this branch never executes. It was presumably meant to handle a zero-length override (a date marked completely unavailable) via `isSame()`/`valueOf()`. As written the "whole day blocked" case falls through to the generic range checks, making the behaviour accidental and hard to reason about; it also means the intent of the code is not actually implemented.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override check rejects slots when a date has multiple override ranges

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` predicate returns `true` as soon as *one* override entry for the slot's date does not contain the slot, and the outer `if` then returns `false` (slot unavailable). Cal.com allows several time ranges for a single date override day, and `getUserAvailability` returns one `{start,end}` entry per range. With overrides 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00 on the same date, a 09:30 slot is inside the first range but `slotEndTime.isBefore(14:00)` is true for the second range, so the slot is dropped; symmetrically the 14:30 slot is dropped by the first range. The net effect is that no slots at all are offered on days with more than one override range. The check must be "the slot is contained in none of the ranges for that date" rather than "some range does not contain the slot".

Expensive per-slot timezone offset computation in the hot slot-filtering loop

`checkIfIsAvailable` is invoked once per candidate slot per host (hundreds to thousands of times per `getSchedule` call on this public endpoint). For every invocation and every date override it calls `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset()` (Intl-backed, comparatively slow) and constructs ~5 additional dayjs objects, even though `utcOffset` and the converted override start/end are independent of the slot being tested. These values should be computed once per host/override before the slot loop (e.g. precomputed alongside `userAvailability`) rather than inside the predicate.

No test covers the main fix (fixed-host date overrides in round-robin) or the new edge cases

The only test added exercises a single-range date override for a personal event viewed from a second timezone. The headline behaviour of the PR — a fixed host's date override limiting the slots of a ROUND_ROBIN event (new `dateOverrides`/`workingHours` handling inside `checkIfIsAvailable`) — has no coverage, so the fixed-host filtering path is unverified. The new code paths that are most likely to regress are also untested: a schedule with two availability blocks on the same day (currently removes all slots, see the `workingHours.find` logic), a date with multiple override ranges, and a slot that overruns the end of an override. Adding a scenario with `hosts: [{isFixed: true,...},{isFixed: false,...}]`, `schedulingType: "ROUND_ROBIN"` and an override on the fixed host would catch these.

Override containment check ignores the slot end, allowing bookings that overrun the override window

Within the matched date override only two rejections exist: the slot ends before/at the override start, or the slot *start* is strictly after the override end. A slot that starts inside the override but finishes after it is therefore accepted: with an override of 09:00-11:00 and a 60-minute event, the 10:30 slot (ending 11:30) is reported as available. Likewise a slot starting exactly at the override end (11:00) passes because `isAfter` is not inclusive. For round-robin events this re-introduces the problem the PR fixes — the fixed host gets booked outside their date override. The condition should require `slotEndTime` to be ≤ override end (and use `isSameOrAfter` for the start comparison).

Override date comparison mixes server-local and UTC formatting

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` builds a dayjs in the *server's local* timezone, while `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is UTC (`slotStartTime = time.utc()`). On any deployment whose process timezone is not UTC the two date strings disagree near midnight, so `dateOverrideExist` is not set for the correct day: overrides are silently ignored (host booked when unavailable) or applied to the wrong day (all slots of a normal day dropped). Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` so both sides are evaluated in the same zone.

Timezone-shifted override wraps across midnight and lands on the wrong day

`startTime`/`endTime` are derived as `hour()*60 + minute()` after shifting the override by `inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset`, and are then applied relative to `startOfInviteeDay`. When the shift pushes the override past midnight the minute-of-day silently wraps and the override is applied to the wrong date. Example: organizer in UTC with an override 22:00-23:30 on day D, invitee in Asia/Kolkata (offset +330). The shifted time is 03:30-05:00 on D+1, giving startTime=210, which is added to the invitee's start of day D (18:30 UTC on D-1) producing slots at 22:00 UTC on D-1 — a full day earlier than the real override. In the opposite direction (negative offset crossing back over midnight) the wrap can make `endTime < startTime`, in which case `buildSlots` drops the range (`if (start >= end) continue;`) and the override produces no slots at all.

Working-hours check uses `find` with inverted logic, rejecting valid slots for users with more than one availability block

`checkIfIsAvailable` rejects a slot if `workingHours.find(...)` locates *any* working-hours entry for the slot's weekday that does not contain the slot (`start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime` → `return false` for the slot). `WorkingHours` is a list, and a single user routinely has several entries for the same day: a split schedule (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00 UTC) yields two entries, and `getWorkingHours` additionally splits any schedule that crosses UTC midnight into two entries. With a 09:00-12:00 / 13:00-17:00 schedule, the 10:00 slot is inside the first entry but outside the second, so the second entry makes the function return `false` and the slot disappears. Because every user of a personal event is treated as a fixed host (`isFixed: !eventType.schedulingType`), this silently removes all slots for any user with a lunch break or a schedule spanning UTC midnight. The condition must be "no entry contains the slot" (`!workingHours.some(containsSlot)`), not "some entry does not contain the slot".

`override.timeZone` is optional; a missing value silently uses dayjs' default timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` relies on the new optional `timeZone` field added to `TimeRange` in packages/types/schedule.d.ts. When a caller of `getSlots` passes date overrides without `timeZone` (the field is `timeZone?: string`), `.tz(undefined)` falls back to dayjs' default/guessed timezone (the machine's zone), so `organizerUtcOffset` is computed from an unrelated zone and the override is shifted by an arbitrary amount instead of keeping the previous UTC interpretation. Either make `timeZone` required for date overrides in this code path or default explicitly to `"UTC"`/the organizer timezone already passed into `getSlots`.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is the pipeline signature, not a per-session nonce

`state` is set to `pipeline.signature` and later compared against `request.GET["state"]`. The pipeline signature is derived from the pipeline's view set, so it is a constant value shared by every user and every organization — the tests hard-code it (`state=9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). A constant, publicly discoverable `state` provides no CSRF / authorization-code-injection protection for the OAuth callback: an attacker can always craft a callback URL with the correct `state`. The PR description lists this as one of the security checks, which overstates what it provides. Generate a random nonce per pipeline run, store it with `pipeline.bind_state(...)`, and compare that instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when integration metadata has no `sender` (500 during install)

`GitHubInstallation.dispatch` compares the pipeline-stored GitHub login against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with direct subscripting. `sender` is only ever written by `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` when the incoming state carries it (`if state.get("sender")`), i.e. only for Integrations created from the GitHub `installation` webhook. Integrations created through the install pipeline itself have no `sender` key (see `test_basic_flow`, which asserts metadata without `sender`), and all Integration rows that pre-date the webhook handler also lack it. Any time this branch is reached for such a row (Integration exists, no OrganizationIntegration — e.g. a re-install after the org integration was removed, or a self-hosted instance where webhooks are not delivered), the view raises `KeyError` and the user gets an unhandled 500 instead of the intended error page. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide explicitly how to behave when it is absent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

false_positives.candidate:
Hard-coded redirect_uri must be registered as the GitHub App callback URL

The authorize redirect sends `redirect_uri=<absolute_uri>/extensions/github/setup/`. GitHub rejects an authorize request whose `redirect_uri` is not under the callback URL registered for the app ("The redirect_uri MUST match the registered callback URL for this application"). Instances whose GitHub App/OAuth App is configured with a different callback URL (self-hosted setups are documented to point the user-authorization callback elsewhere, and single-tenant deployments use custom apps) will fail at the very first step of the integration install after this change. The PR contains no documentation or setup-instruction update for the newly required callback URL.

Identity check uses mutable GitHub login instead of immutable user id

The new authenticity check compares the OAuth-authenticated GitHub `login` string to the `login` stored in `integration.metadata["sender"]` at webhook time. GitHub usernames are renameable and, once freed, re-registerable by anyone. Consequences: (a) a legitimate installer who renames their GitHub account is permanently locked out of re-installing (generic "Invalid installation request."), and (b) an attacker who registers the installer's abandoned username passes the check. The webhook stores the sender's numeric `id` alongside the login and `get_user_info()` returns `id` as well; comparing the immutable numeric ids would close both holes.

No coverage for token-exchange failure branches

The PR introduces two new failure branches in `OAuthLoginView` — the access-token exchange returning a body without `access_token` (wrong or reused `code`) and `get_user_info` returning a payload without `login` — and both are listed as intended failure modes in the description, but no test stubs a failing `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` or `/user` response. Regressions in these paths (e.g. an exception leaking a 500 instead of the error page) would go unnoticed.

Re-install now blocked for non-ACTIVE integrations

After the `installations_exist` check, the code re-fetches the integration with `status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE` and renders the generic error if it is missing. Previously this branch (Integration row exists, no OrganizationIntegration) simply advanced the pipeline, so an Integration left in `PENDING_DELETION`/`DISABLED` with its org integrations already removed could be re-installed. Now such users get "We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request", which does not describe the real cause and gives them no actionable path. Either reuse the row already fetched on line 478 or report a status-specific message.

Unhandled exception from get_user_info on GitHub API failure

`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (from `sentry.identity.github`) performs a `GET /user` and raises on a non-2xx response rather than returning a payload. Unlike the surrounding code paths (bad state, missing access token), this call is not wrapped in try/except, so a transient GitHub 5xx, rate limit, or revoked token turns the install flow into an unhandled 500 instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." page. Wrap the call and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` (ideally with logging/metrics so these failures are observable).

User validation is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet

The GitHub-user equality check only runs in the branch where an `Integration` row for the `installation_id` already exists. If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` (line 481-482) the pipeline advances with no validation at all, so a caller who supplies someone else's `installation_id` can still bind that installation to their own Sentry org. This happens whenever the `installation` webhook has not been processed yet (race between the user finishing the pipeline and webhook delivery), was never delivered, or webhooks are not configured (self-hosted). A validation that does not depend on previously stored webhook data — e.g. calling `GET /user/installations` with the freshly obtained user access token and asserting the `installation_id` is listed — would cover this branch too.

error_short strings are not extractable for translation

`error()` takes `error_short` as a plain string and calls `_(error_short)` at runtime (line 141). Because the argument is a variable, `makemessages` cannot extract the literals ("Invalid installation request.", "GitHub installation pending deletion.", "Github installed on another Sentry organization."), so these user-facing strings will never be translated even though the code implies they are. Mark the literals with `_()` at their definition/call sites and pass the already-lazy objects through.

test_installation_not_found no longer covers the 404 path

The test passes `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which differs from the valid pipeline signature used by every other test in this file (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). The request therefore short-circuits in `OAuthLoginView` on the state-mismatch branch and the assertion `b"Invalid installation request."` passes for that reason alone. The behaviour the test is named for — `get_installation_info` returning 404 and `build_integration` raising `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")`, previously asserted — is now completely uncovered, and the 404 `responses.replace` setup is dead. Either use the correct state so the flow reaches `build_integration`, or rename the test to reflect that it only exercises state mismatch and add a separate test for the 404 case.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued` default is evaluated once at import time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass field default, so `timezone.now()` is called exactly once when the module is first imported. Every `AssignmentSource` created afterwards (including all instances built by `from_integration`) carries the process-start timestamp instead of the time the assignment was actually queued. Any logging/debugging or future staleness check based on `queued` will be wrong, and `__eq__` (which includes `queued`) will differ between processes for otherwise identical sources. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource does not survive a serialization round-trip through the task queue

`to_dict()` (via `asdict`) puts a raw `datetime` into the dict that is passed as celery task kwargs in `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, and `from_dict()` just splats the dict into the constructor with no coercion. Depending on the configured task serializer this either (a) fails to serialize the task payload, breaking all outbound assignee syncs, or (b) round-trips `queued` as an ISO string, which `from_dict` happily accepts because dataclasses perform no type validation — leaving a field annotated `datetime` holding a `str`. Tests only exercise the eager/in-process path, so neither case is covered. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()`) and parse it back in `from_dict`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
New `assignment_source` kwarg passed to duck-typed installations that may not accept it

The task resolves `installation` by `hasattr(installation, "sync_assignee_outbound")` and now always passes `assignment_source=...`. The abstract declaration in `IssueSyncIntegration` was not updated to include this parameter, so it is only tolerated by implementations that happen to declare `**kwargs`. Any installation implementing `sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=True)` without `**kwargs` will raise `TypeError`, which is not in the task's `retry(exclude=...)` list and will therefore burn 5 retries for every assignment. Declare the parameter explicitly on the abstract method (and in the implementations) rather than relying on `**kwargs`.

No test that a different integration's assignment source still syncs outbound

The new tests cover source=None and source==the same integration, but not the case the PR explicitly claims to preserve: an assignment originating from integration A must still be propagated outbound to integration B. Since the guard in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` compares `sync_source.integration_id` to `org_integration.integration_id`, a mistake there (e.g. comparing against `org_integration.id`) would silently suppress all outbound syncs for every integration and no test would catch it. Add a case with two linked integrations where the source is one of them.

Task kwarg is always sent, breaking old workers during rollout

`assignment_source_dict` is included in the `apply_async` kwargs unconditionally (as `None` when there is no source). During a rolling deploy, workers still running the previous revision of `sync_assignee_outbound` do not accept this keyword and the task will fail with `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument`, dropping assignee syncs for the duration of the rollout. Only include the key when `assignment_source` is not `None`.

`assignment_source` added to abstract sync_status_outbound but never passed or implemented

The abstract `sync_status_outbound` now declares `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but no caller passes it (the status-sync task is unchanged) and none of the concrete implementations (Jira, Jira Server, VSTS, Example, ...) were updated to accept or use it. The parameter is dead code that suggests inbound status webhooks are protected against sync cycles when they are not. Either wire the status path through (task -> `should_sync("outbound_status", source)` -> implementations) or drop the parameter.

from_dict silently returns None, disabling cycle protection

When the payload is malformed, `from_dict` swallows the error and returns `None`. In `sync_assignee_outbound` a `None` source means `should_sync("outbound_assignee", None)` falls back to the old behaviour and the change is propagated back to the originating integration — i.e. the exact sync loop this PR is meant to break — with no log line or metric to indicate it happened. At minimum log a warning here so a serialization regression is detectable.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated (abstract methods unimplemented)

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

false_positives.candidate:
Occurrence fingerprint contract with build_fingerprint is neither enforced nor documented

Resolution is emitted by the base class as a `StatusChangeMessage` whose fingerprint comes from `self.build_fingerprint(group_key)` (line 293), but the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` hook lets subclasses construct the `IssueOccurrence` fingerprint however they like, and the abstract method has no docstring stating that it must use `build_fingerprint(group_key)`. PriorityLevel(new_status) can raise ValueError for non-priority condition results

`build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))` converts the computed status to `sentry.types.group.PriorityLevel`. `new_status` is derived from `max(new_status, condition.evaluate_value(value))`, and `DataCondition.condition_result` is DB/user-configured and not constrained to `DetectorPriorityLevel` values (it can be a bool or an arbitrary int). Stale TODO comment contradicts the code

The comment "TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction" sits directly above a class that now *is* a `StatefulDetectorHandler`. Leaving it there is misleading for the next reader; it should be removed or replaced with the remaining work (implementing the abstract hooks).

get_group_key_values type annotation disallows the None group key that the code and tests use
