Federated rule-group immutability check dropped for CombinedRule abilities

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false` (the `isFederatedRuleGroup` import was removed). Previously the CombinedRule path computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which marked rules in Mimir federated groups (`source_tenants` set) as immutable and hid Edit/Delete/Duplicate. With this change the existing rule list/detail pages will offer Edit and Delete for federated rule groups; saving such a group through the UI editor can drop `source_tenants` and silently break cross-tenant federation. The federated check needs to be preserved (or re-derived from the group identifier) before merging.

Grafana-managed recording rules lose Pause/Export/DeletePermanently support in the new ability hook

In `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` the supported flags for `ModifyExport`, `Pause`, `Restore` and `DeletePermanently` are derived from `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`, i.e. alerting rules only. The ruler-based equivalent uses `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which is true for Grafana-managed recording rules as well – those rules do support pausing and modify-export. Since the list view now relies exclusively on this hook, Export (and Pause, once the menu gating is fixed) will be missing for Grafana recording rules, a regression from the current list.

Misleading test comment about skipToken behaviour

The repeated comment "Cloud rules only need useRulerRuleAbilities mock (useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gets skipToken)" is incorrect: `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` is still invoked with `skipToken` and, in production, still returns non-false abilities for some actions (see `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` with an undefined rule). The default `[false, false]` mock hides that behaviour, so the comment both misdescribes the code and conceals a gap in coverage for cloud rules.

New Grafana-Prometheus ability logic has no unit tests

`useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable`, the `skipToken` handling and the OR-combination in `AlertRuleMenu`/`RuleActionsButtons` introduce ~130 lines of new permission logic, but there are no tests for them: `RulesTable.test.tsx` mocks the whole `useAbilities` module (so the real logic never runs) and `GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx` only covers the happy path with all permissions granted plus a single "no update permission" case. Important cases are untested: provisioned rules (`provenance`), plugin-provided rules, recording rules, and `skipToken` (data-source rules) returning permissive abilities.

OR-combining ruler and Prometheus abilities can override a deny, e.g. for provisioned rules

All abilities are now computed as `(rulerSupported && rulerAllowed) || (promSupported && promAllowed)`. Because a deny from the ruler-based check is ignored when the Prometheus-based check allows, any immutability signal that exists only in the ruler DTO is lost. Concretely, provisioning is detected in the prom path via `isProvisionedPromRule`, which reads the `provenance` field that is only now being added as an *optional* property on `GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase` (no backend change in this PR). If `/api/prometheus/grafana/api/v1/rules` does not return `provenance`, provisioned (file-provisioned/Terraform) rules will show Edit/Delete/Duplicate everywhere `promRule` is available – including the rule detail page where the ruler rule correctly reports the rule as immutable – and the subsequent write will be rejected by the API. Please confirm the API actually returns `provenance` and add a test with a provisioned rule; alternatively prefer the ruler result when it is available instead of OR-ing.

Stale comment and variable name after removing the ruler prefetch

The ruler `prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)` dispatch was removed, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX ... doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded" and the variable is still called `cacheAndRulerPreload`. Both now describe behaviour that no longer exists and will mislead the next reader into thinking ruler data is still being warmed up here.

`returnTo` query param dropped from rule view links

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` built the href as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` omits it, so navigating from the (filtered) rule list into a rule detail page loses the "return to previous" context and the user is no longer sent back to the list they came from.

skipToken path still computes permissive abilities for a non-existent rule

`useGrafanaPromRuleAbility`/`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` map `skipToken` to `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined)`, which does not short-circuit: with `rule === undefined`, `loading` is `false` (see `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable`'s early return) and `isPluginProvided(undefined)` is `false`, so `MaybeSupported = AlwaysSupported` and `[AlertRuleAction.Duplicate] = [true, hasPermission(AlertingRuleCreate)]` (same for View/Explore). Since `AlertRuleMenu` OR-combines ruler and Grafana-prom abilities, a data-source (Mimir/Prometheus/Loki) rule – which always passes `skipToken` – will show "Duplicate" even when the ruler-based check says duplication is unsupported (e.g. ruler API unavailable, federated, plugin-provided rule), leading the user into a clone flow that cannot succeed. The skipToken/undefined case should return an all-`[false, false]` ability map.

true_positives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New interpolation test is unrealistic and does not cover the risk introduced

The stubbed `replace: (input = '') => input.replace('$__auto', '5m').replace('$step', '5m')` ignores `scopedVars`, whereas the real Loki `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately strips `__auto`/`__interval`/`__range` from the scoped vars so that these are interpolated by the backend; so in production `$__auto` is still present in the expression at this point and the assertion `expr === 'count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])'` does not reflect real behavior. More importantly, the actual risk of this change — the target being interpolated again by `DataSourceWithBackend.query` inside `runQuery`, duplicating ad hoc filters from `request.filters` and re-expanding variable values that contain `$` — is untested. Add a test with `request.filters` set asserting the ad hoc filter appears exactly once in the final expression sent to `runQuery`, and one with a variable value containing `$`/`${}` to assert it is not re-expanded.

false_positives.candidate:
Queries are now interpolated twice (runSplitQuery + DataSourceWithBackend.query)

`runSplitQuery` now maps every target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`, but each resulting sub-request is executed via `datasource.runQuery(subRequest)` → `super.query()` (`DataSourceWithBackend.query`), which already calls `applyTemplateVariables` on every target. So each split query is interpolated at least twice. Two concrete consequences: (1) ad hoc filters (`request.filters`) are applied by `addAdHocFilters()` a second time to an expression that already contains them, which can duplicate label matchers / pipeline stages (e.g. `| key="value" | key="value"`); (2) `templateSrv.replace()` runs again over values that were already substituted, so any variable whose value contains `$name`, `${name}` or `[[name]]` is expanded a second time and the final LogQL is wrong. If the interpolated query is only needed to make splitting decisions (step parsing, logs-vs-metric classification, `$__range` detection), keep it locally for those decisions and send the original targets downstream, or mark the request/targets as already interpolated so the backend data source layer skips the second pass.

Shard splitting path now interpolates each query three times

`runShardSplitQuery` interpolates all targets here; `splitQueriesByStreamShard` then builds `subRequest` from those interpolated + shard-annotated targets and hands it to `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which after this PR interpolates again, and `runQuery`/`DataSourceWithBackend.query` interpolates a third time. Besides the correctness problems of repeated interpolation (ad hoc filters re-appended to an expression that already carries them, template values containing `$`/`${}`/`[[]]` re-expanded), the expression handed to the 2nd/3rd pass already contains the injected `__stream_shard__=~"..." | drop __stream_shard__`, so `addAdHocFilters()` re-parses and re-modifies a mutated query whose stage ordering is no longer the user's. There is also avoidable cost: `addAdHocFilters` parses the LogQL expression per target, now once per shard group in addition to the per-sub-request pass.

Test asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times for a single target, locking in redundant interpolation

`expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` is for a request with a single target. The 5 calls come from one interpolation in `runShardSplitQuery` plus one per sub-request created by `runSplitQuery`, i.e. the assertion codifies that the same query is interpolated repeatedly instead of exactly once. This makes the test both a brittle magic number (it changes whenever the shard grouping or the number of split requests changes) and a guard that prevents noticing the double/triple interpolation problem. The intent of the test ("Interpolates queries before running") would be better expressed by asserting interpolation happened once per user target.

applyTemplateVariables mock mutates the query and is idempotent, masking repeated interpolation

The new mock `datasource.applyTemplateVariables = jest.fn().mockImplementation((query) => { query.expr = query.expr.replace('$SELECTOR', '{a="b"}'); return query; })` mutates the target object in place and performs a replacement that is a no-op the second time it runs. The real implementation returns a new object and is *not* idempotent (it re-applies ad hoc filters and re-runs template replacement). Because of this mock, the tests cannot detect that the same target is now interpolated multiple times, and they also silently mutate the shared `request.targets` fixture used by subsequent assertions in the same test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, discarding recorded logs

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver (or a logger sharing its `Logs` state). `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now emits its only log line via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so any test that injects a `*TestLogger` and then asserts on `InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`/`Ctx` will observe zero calls, because the log is recorded on a throwaway instance. This makes the fake unusable for verifying the middleware's logging behaviour and will silently pass tests that are meant to catch regressions. Return `f` (or a logger that writes into the same `Logs` fields).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface breaks out-of-tree implementations

`log.Logger` in `pkg/plugins/log` is an exported interface that is passed around the plugin management code (e.g. `NewLoggerMiddleware`). Adding the `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method is a breaking change for any implementation outside this package (Grafana Enterprise, other modules, custom fakes), which will fail to compile until updated. If these implementations exist, they must be updated in lockstep; consider documenting this in the PR or providing an embeddable default implementation.

LoggerMiddleware still uses the stale "plugin.instrumentation" logger name

After the rename, there is no instrumentation middleware any more, yet the logger handed to `NewLoggerMiddleware` is still created as `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")`, so every plugin egress log line is emitted with `logger=plugin.instrumentation`. This is misleading for anyone grepping logs for the middleware that produced them. If the name is kept for backwards compatibility with existing log queries/dashboards, that should be stated in a comment; otherwise rename it to match the middleware.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware is untested and the ordering dependency it creates is unguarded

The log fields `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, `uname` and `traceID` were removed from `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` and are now expected to come from contextual attributes injected by this new middleware (plus the tracing contextual log provider). No test exercises `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`, and no test asserts that the "Plugin Request Completed" log line still contains those fields. If this middleware is omitted from a chain, or ordered after `NewLoggerMiddleware` in `CreateMiddlewares`, every plugin egress log line silently loses all plugin/datasource/user identification and nothing fails. Add a test that runs the real middleware chain (or at least ContextualLogger + Logger) and asserts the emitted log parameters.

Test function name not renamed along with the middleware

The file and the type under test were renamed to `MetricsMiddleware`/`metrics_middleware_test.go`, but the test is still called `TestInstrumentationMiddleware`. Since the whole point of the PR is consistent naming, leaving the old name makes the test harder to locate by name (`go test -run TestMetricsMiddleware` finds nothing).

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check-then-insert on device count allows exceeding the configured limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` reads the device count and then performs the upsert as two separate statements with no transaction, locking, or unique constraint on the aggregate. Concurrent requests (and in HA setups, concurrent Grafana instances) can all observe `count < deviceLimit` and then each insert a new row, so the number of tracked anonymous devices can exceed `auth.anonymous.device_limit`. If the limit is meant to be an enforced cap (it is used to reject authentication), the count and insert need to be done atomically, e.g. inside a single transaction with appropriate locking or an `INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(...)) < limit` style statement.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`rowsAffected == 0` is reported as "device limit reached" for unrelated cases

`updateDevice` maps any update that matched no rows to `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. Besides the intended "this device is not among the tracked devices" case, zero affected rows also occurs when the row exists but its `updated_at` falls outside the `[now-30d, now+1m]` window used in the WHERE clause (e.g. a device last seen 31 days ago, or clock skew between HA instances pushing a stored timestamp past the +1m bound), and — on MySQL connections without CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS — when the update is a no-op. In those cases the caller/user is told the device limit was reached, which is misleading and makes debugging and metrics harder. Distinguish "no matching device" from the limit condition, e.g. by checking existence explicitly.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit rejection is cached, so the limit is bypassed on the next request

`tagDeviceUI` writes the cache key (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) *before* calling `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. With the new behaviour, when the device limit is reached `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, which now propagates out of `TagDevice` and makes `Anonymous.Authenticate` fail. But the cache entry stays in place for the cache lifetime (29 min). On the very next request with the same `X-Grafana-Device-Id`, `tagDeviceUI` hits the cache, returns nil, `TagDevice` returns nil, and the anonymous identity is granted even though the device was never persisted and the limit is exceeded. Net effect: the device limit can be trivially bypassed by reloading the page once, and the device is invisible to `ListDevices`/usage stats. The cache key must be removed (or only written after a successful store call) when `CreateOrUpdateDevice` fails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
DI signatures changed but wire registration/generated code not updated in this PR

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` no longer accepts `anonstore.AnonStore` (it now takes `db.DB` and constructs the store itself), and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a required `deviceLimit int64` parameter. Both functions are wired via Google Wire (`pkg/server/wire.go` / `wire_gen.go`), which is not part of this changeset: the generated code still calls the old signature, and if `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` is still in a provider set, wire now has to resolve a bare `int64` dependency, which it cannot. This will break the build / wire generation unless the provider sets and generated files are updated in the same PR. Constructing the store inside the service also removes the ability to inject an alternative `AnonStore` implementation (e.g. for tests or enterprise).

Device-limit error returned as an untyped error, producing an opaque failure for the user

`Authenticate` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` (a plain `fmt.Errorf` value) straight to the authn broker. Grafana's authn layer expects `errutil`-typed errors to derive an HTTP status and a user-facing message; an untyped error yields a generic internal/unauthenticated failure with no indication that the anonymous device limit was hit. Given this PR also ships `anonymousDeviceLimit` to the frontend (presumably to display a message), the error should be wrapped in an `errutil` error with an explicit status (e.g. 403/429) and message id so the UI and API clients can react meaningfully.

Device-limit tests omit the main success path and the limit-bypass scenario

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device is rejected once the limit is hit. There is no test that an already-tracked device can still be refreshed while the store is at the limit (the whole point of the `updateDevice` branch — a regression there would lock out every existing anonymous user), no test for `deviceLimit` boundary values (e.g. count exactly equal to vs. below the limit, negative/0 limit), and no test at the `AnonDeviceService`/client level covering the new error propagation from `TagDevice` or the local-cache interaction, which is where the limit is currently bypassable.

New `auth.anonymous.device_limit` option is undocumented

`cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read from `auth.anonymous.device_limit`, but the option is not added to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini`, or the configuration reference docs. Grafana users discover configuration through defaults.ini and the docs page; an option that silently rejects anonymous authentication once the limit is reached is especially important to document (including that 0 means unlimited and what happens to users beyond the limit).

Unauthenticated requests now trigger a synchronous COUNT(*) plus write on the auth path

When `deviceLimit > 0`, every `CreateOrUpdateDevice` first runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?`, and since `client.go` no longer performs tagging in a background goroutine, this query plus the upsert/update now runs inline during authentication of the request. The device id comes from the attacker-controllable `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header, and the in-memory dedup cache is keyed by that header, so an unauthenticated client can force a fresh COUNT + UPDATE round-trip (and a new 29-minute cache entry) on every single request. On an instance with many anonymous devices this adds unbounded DB load and request latency on the hot auth path. Consider caching/throttling the count or enforcing the limit without a per-request aggregate query.

`anonymousDeviceLimit` is inferred as type `undefined`, making it unusable from TypeScript

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` is an initializer without a type annotation, so TypeScript infers the field type as `undefined` on `GrafanaBootConfig` (unlike the neighbouring `googleAnalyticsId: undefined;` declarations, which are annotations). Any consumer writing `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0` will fail to compile, even though the backend always serialises a number (`AnonymousDeviceLimit int64`, 0 when unset) — so the value is in fact never `undefined` at runtime. Annotate it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` (or just `number`) to match the `GrafanaConfig` interface and the actual payload.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Leftover debug logging at Error level, including full ID lists

`CleanAnnotations` and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` log six messages per batch via `r.log.Error(...)` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)`. These are informational/debug messages, not errors: they will fire on every cleanup batch for every healthy installation, polluting error logs and triggering alerting on error-level log volume. They also serialize the entire ID slice into the log line — with the documented batch sizes (e.g. the 32767 used in the new test) each line can be hundreds of kilobytes. In addition, the `"err", err` field is always nil at these call sites because the error path returns earlier. These calls should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the full ID slice.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The background cleanup loop's ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This makes every cleanup job (temp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) run ten times more often in production, which is a significant and unrelated change in DB/IO load for all Grafana installations. Note also that `clean()` has a 9-minute timeout, so a long-running cleanup cycle will be immediately followed by another one. This looks like a leftover from local reproduction of the deadlock and should be reverted to 10 minutes (or made configurable) before merge.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-subtest data cleanup is registered after the assertions that can abort the subtest

`createTestAnnotations` is called, then `assertAnnotationCount`/`assertAnnotationTagCount` run (both use `require`, which calls `FailNow`), and only afterwards is `t.Cleanup` registered to delete from `annotation`/`annotation_tag`. If either pre-condition assertion fails, the subtest aborts before the cleanup is registered, so the inserted rows stay in the shared `fakeSQL` database and every subsequent subtest (which now assumes an empty table and asserts exact counts) fails with confusing cascading errors. Register the `t.Cleanup` immediately after creating the annotations, before asserting.

Placeholder-limit workaround only covers SQLite and keys off config instead of actual ID count

`deleteByIDs` only avoids bind parameters when `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`. MySQL and Postgres have their own hard limit of 65535 placeholders per statement, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above 65535 will get every cleanup batch failing with a driver error on those backends. The condition also tests the configured batch size rather than `len(ids)`, which couples correctness of the statement to a config value instead of the data actually being deleted. Consider branching on `len(ids)` and applying a placeholder cap for all dialects (or chunking the delete).

Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite

In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite path builds the IN-list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over all IDs. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so building the list is O(n^2) in bytes copied. With a batch size such as the 32767 exercised by the new test, this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch and allocates 32k intermediate strings, for every delete batch of the cleanup job. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done elsewhere in this file) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses `d.Log` rather than the `log` built one line above with name/kind/method values. Any downstream code that pulls the logger from the context (`klog.FromContext`) loses the request identifying fields for deletes only, making delete failures hard to correlate. Should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name in the `kind` metric label (unbounded cardinality)

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Each deleted object therefore creates a new time series in the duration histogram, which is an unbounded-cardinality label and will blow up the Prometheus registry/scrape payload on any workload that deletes many objects. It also makes the metric unusable for per-kind aggregation. Should be `options.Kind`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request finishes

All four background goroutines (Create l.51, Delete l.110, Update l.135, DeleteCollection l.163) build their timeout context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. A child context is cancelled as soon as its parent is cancelled, and the apiserver cancels the request context the moment the handler returns — which happens immediately after `return created, err`. So in practice the legacy write will frequently (often always, for fast handlers) be aborted with `context.Canceled` before or during execution, which silently defeats the whole point of mode 3 (writing a safety copy to legacy). Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) as the parent before applying the timeout, so the write survives the request lifecycle.

DeleteCollection goroutine records legacy latency as storage latency

Inside the async goroutine of `DeleteCollection` the legacy call's duration is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` using `startLegacy`. This means the legacy DeleteCollection duration/errors appear under the unified-storage metric, double-counting storage samples for the same request and leaving the legacy metric with no data for delete-collection. Should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`.

Errors from the asynchronous legacy writes are never logged

In Create (l.55-56), Delete (l.112-113), Update (l.139-140) and DeleteCollection (l.165-166) the error returned by the legacy storage is only fed into a duration histogram and then dropped. The previous implementation logged these failures. Since mode 3 reads exclusively from unified storage, a failing legacy write produces a silent divergence between the two stores with no diagnostic trail (no object name, no error message), making it impossible to reconcile later. Log the error with the object identity (and the timeout cause when the ctx expired).

Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object actually persisted in storage

The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so that legacy received exactly the object that was written to unified storage. Now the raw `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update`, so legacy recomputes the updated object from *its own* stored copy. For PATCH/Apply requests, or when the client sent a resourceVersion precondition (the RV now belongs to unified storage, not legacy), this either fails with a conflict or writes a different object than the one in unified storage, producing a silent divergence between the two stores. Pass the storage result through `updateWrapper` as before.

Request-scoped object and validation callbacks are used from a goroutine after the request completed

The goroutines pass the caller-owned `obj` (Create, l.55) and the request's `createValidation`/`updateValidation`/`deleteValidation` funcs (l.55, 112, 139, 165) into the legacy store after the handler has returned. `obj` has already been mutated in place by the unified-storage create path and is still reachable from the handler, and the validation closures run admission, which writes audit annotations onto the request's audit event — an event the audit backend may be serializing concurrently once the request finished. This is a real data race / mutation-after-response hazard. Deep-copy the object before handing it to the goroutine and avoid re-running request-scoped validation/admission on the async path.

Storage failures are recorded in the legacy duration metric

In `Create`, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. The same mistake exists in `Update` (l.129). This attributes unified-storage latency/failures to the legacy histogram, so the storage histogram never records any failures and the legacy histogram is polluted with samples for an operation legacy never performed. Both should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Storage-failure test case is configured through setupLegacyFn and only works because both mocks share one mock.Mock

In the "error when creating object in the unified store fails" case the failing `Create` expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` while `setupStorageFn` is nil. It only produces the expected error because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` are constructed around the same `*mock.Mock`, so the storage call matches the legacy expectation. The test therefore cannot distinguish a legacy failure from a storage failure and is misleading for anyone adding cases later; register the expectation on the storage setup function.

Tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy writes

Every mode 3 test only asserts on the value returned from the unified store; no test waits for or asserts that `Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` was invoked (e.g. via `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` after synchronization). Because the legacy goroutine is fire-and-forget, the core behaviour added by this PR — the safety write to legacy — is completely untested, and the regression described above (the goroutine's context being cancelled with the request) would not be caught. The goroutines also outlive the subtest, so the mock is exercised after the test function returns, which makes any future expectation mismatch surface as a panic in a background goroutine rather than a test failure.

go.work.sum contains a duplicated entry and unrelated dependency hashes

The added block re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` which already exists two lines above, and adds hashes for modules unrelated to this change (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel versions). This looks like a locally dirty workspace file committed by accident rather than a regenerated one; it will churn/conflict on the next `go work sync`. Regenerate the file or drop these lines from the PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No double-check after acquiring the write lock: duplicate loads and a valid cache can be clobbered with nil

`GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, and then takes the write lock without re-checking whether another goroutine has already populated `entryPointAssetsCache` in the meantime. Two consequences on a cold start where many requests arrive concurrently (the common case, e.g. several browser tabs hitting the index page):

1. Every goroutine that observed `ret == nil` re-runs the full manifest load (disk read / JSON decode, and the CDN HTTP fetch if `cdn` is ever non-empty), serialized one after another behind the exclusive lock, instead of just reusing the value the first goroutine stored.
2. More importantly, line 69 unconditionally assigns `entryPointAssetsCache = result`. If a later goroutine's reload fails (file transiently unreadable, truncated manifest during a rebuild, CDN error), `result` is nil and the already-published, valid cache is overwritten with nil, so subsequent callers fall back to re-reading from disk again.

Fix by re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` right after acquiring the write lock, and by only assigning to the cache when `err == nil`/`result != nil`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No double-check after acquiring the write lock: duplicate loads and a valid cache can be clobbered with nil

`GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, and then takes the write lock without re-checking whether another goroutine has already populated `entryPointAssetsCache` in the meantime. Two consequences on a cold start where many requests arrive concurrently (the common case, e.g. several browser tabs hitting the index page):

1. Every goroutine that observed `ret == nil` re-runs the full manifest load (disk read / JSON decode, and the CDN HTTP fetch if `cdn` is ever non-empty), serialized one after another behind the exclusive lock, instead of just reusing the value the first goroutine stored.
2. More importantly, line 69 unconditionally assigns `entryPointAssetsCache = result`. If a later goroutine's reload fails (file transiently unreadable, truncated manifest during a rebuild, CDN error), `result` is nil and the already-published, valid cache is overwritten with nil, so subsequent callers fall back to re-reading from disk again.

Fix by re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` right after acquiring the write lock, and by only assigning to the cache when `err == nil`/`result != nil`.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock is held across blocking I/O (file read and CDN HTTP request)

The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via `defer`) for the whole duration of `readWebAssetsFromCDN` (an HTTP request whose only bound is the request context) and `readWebAssetsFromFile` (open + JSON decode). All other callers of `GetWebAssets` block on the mutex during that time. In `setting.Dev` mode the early return is skipped, so *every* index-page request takes the exclusive lock and does a disk read + JSON decode while holding it, fully serializing page loads. Consider loading outside the lock (or using `sync.Once`/`singleflight`) and only taking the lock for the pointer assignment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions() contains dead and inverted logic

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` on both branches, so the computed value and the `if` are dead code and the function is a constant `false`. Two problems: (1) the polarity is inverted — `enabled` is true when the flag is *disabled* — so if anyone later re-enables the feature by deleting the trailing `return false`, SQL expressions would be permitted exactly when the toggle is off and rejected when it is on; (2) static analysis / linters commonly flag the unreachable branch and unused assignment, which can fail CI. Since this is the kill-switch for CVE-2024-9264, it should be written unambiguously (e.g. `return false` with a comment explaining that SQL expressions are disabled for security reasons), or the flag check removed entirely.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead DuckDB-specific SQL string interpolation left behind in parser

`TablesList` still builds `SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')` by interpolating the user-supplied `rawSQL` after only replacing `'` with `''`. This is unreachable today (the stubbed `DB.RunCommands` always errors), but it is the exact pattern that made arbitrary SQL/DuckDB execution possible, and the escaping is engine-specific and incomplete (it does not handle backslash escapes or dollar-quoting). Leaving it in place means that whenever a real `DB` implementation is wired back into `NewInMemoryDB`, the injection surface is restored silently. Consider deleting the DuckDB AST parsing code along with the dependency, or at minimum parameterising the statement and adding a comment that this code is intentionally inert.

Error text "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading for an intentionally disabled feature

When a query of type `QueryTypeSQL` arrives, the reader returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. The feature *is* implemented in the codebase and the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle still exists and is documented as enabling it; the code path is deliberately disabled for security. Users who enable the toggle will get an error claiming the feature does not exist, with no hint that it was disabled on purpose, making the behaviour hard to diagnose and contradicting the toggle documentation. Either reword the error (e.g. "SQL expressions are currently disabled") or update/remove the toggle documentation accordingly.

No tests guard the newly disabled SQL-expression path

This PR disables SQL expressions (the fix for CVE-2024-9264) by stubbing `sql.DB` so every method returns "not implemented" and by short-circuiting `QueryTypeSQL` in `pkg/expr/reader.go`, but it adds no test. There is nothing that asserts that `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` rejects a `sql` query (including when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled) or that `NewSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` fail, so a future refactor could silently re-enable the vulnerable path. Conversely, any pre-existing unit tests that exercise `sql.TablesList` or the SQL command end-to-end will now fail because `RunCommands` always errors — those need to be updated in this PR as well.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No per-key build guard: concurrent BuildIndex for the same key can corrupt a file-backed index

Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its entire body, which serialized index creation. With the lock now only held around the cache write, two concurrent callers that both saw `GetIndex() == nil` (e.g. two Search requests for the same namespace/group/resource, or a watch event racing with a search) can run `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory at the same time when `size > FileThreshold`. That means two processes/goroutines writing the same on-disk bleve index concurrently (undefined behaviour/corruption, or a spurious "path already exists" error), plus duplicated full re-index work and a cache entry that is overwritten by the loser. The TODO in `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` acknowledges this; a per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed now that the global lock is gone.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads the index cache map without holding cacheMu

`bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` iterates `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes to the same map under `cacheMu` (lines 137-139). Concurrent map read + write is a fatal, unrecoverable Go runtime error (`concurrent map read and map write`), i.e. a process crash. This PR makes it reachable: `searchSupport.init` starts the watch-event goroutine (search.go line 207) and then calls `s.search.TotalDocs()` in the new log line (search.go line 216); a watch event handled in that goroutine can trigger `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex` -> cache write at the same moment. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs` (and copy out the indexes before calling `DocCount`).

false_positives.candidate:
BuildIndex still discards the span context, breaking trace nesting

The PR's stated goal is fixing trace propagation, but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` keeps `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and never passes the span context to `builder(idx)` (line 126). The builder closure in `searchSupport.build` uses the caller's context, so the `sql.resource.List`/`GetResourceStats` spans produced while populating the index become siblings of the `BuildIndex` span instead of children, which makes the index-build timing breakdown unreadable in traces. Either plumb the new context into `builder` (changing the callback signature) or document why the span is intentionally a leaf.

Data race and lost errors in the index-build errgroup

In `searchSupport.init`, the goroutines started via `group.Go` all write to the function-scoped variables `err` (line 190: `_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and `totalBatchesIndexed` (line 189) without synchronization. Up to `initWorkers` goroutines run concurrently, so these are genuine data races (detectable by `-race`, and the counter will under-count). Worse, each goroutine returns the shared `err`, so one goroutine can observe another goroutine's value: a real build failure can be clobbered by a concurrent `nil` assignment (startup then proceeds with a partially built index) or a successful goroutine can return someone else's error (startup aborts spuriously). This was largely masked before because `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its whole body and serialized the builds; this PR removes that lock, so the goroutines now really overlap. Use goroutine-local variables (`if err := s.build(...); err != nil { return err }`) and an atomic counter.

Init failure in constructor leaks the cancel func and background watcher

`ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created at line 229, but the new error path `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err }` returns without calling `cancel()`. Anything already started during `Init` (the sql backend poller started by `search.init`'s `WatchWriteEvents`, and `initWatcher`'s broadcaster goroutine if it got that far) keeps running for the lifetime of the process, and the context is leaked (this is also what `go vet`'s lostcancel check flags). Call `cancel()` (or `s.Stop`) before returning the error.

Postgres storage-server integration test silently skipped with no tracking issue

The only integration test that boots the `StorageServer` module target is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." This is the exact code path changed by this PR (unified storage now initializes - including the full index build - inside `NewResourceServer`, before the module reports running), so disabling the test may be hiding a regression introduced here rather than a pre-existing CI quirk. At minimum the skip needs a linked issue and an explanation of the failure mode; ideally the failure should be root-caused before merging, otherwise postgres deployments of the storage server have no coverage of startup at all.

Requests are no longer rejected after Stop(): initErr is now write-only

`Stop()` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", but every RPC handler's `s.Init(ctx)` guard was deleted, so nothing reads `initErr` any more. After `Stop()` cancels the background context, `Create`/`Update`/`Delete`/`List`/`Watch`/`Search` etc. will happily keep executing against a backend whose watcher/poller has been shut down: writes still reach the DB but no write events are broadcast or indexed, and watchers silently receive nothing. Previously these calls returned an error. Either keep an explicit "stopped" check at the entry of the handlers or drop the now-dead `initErr` mutations in `Stop` and document the new contract.

Synchronous, unbounded index build now blocks/aborts server construction

Moving `s.Init(ctx)` into `NewResourceServer` makes the full search-index build (all namespaces, via `searchSupport.init`) part of object construction, with no timeout and no way to serve traffic while it runs. Two consequences the PR should address explicitly: (1) startup latency - the PR itself states the build exceeds a gRPC request deadline, so Grafana/the storage-server target will not accept any request (not even `/metrics` via the gRPC health service) until indexing finishes; (2) a single transient failure (DB not reachable yet, one namespace failing to index) now aborts `NewResourceServer` and therefore the whole process startup, whereas previously only the first request failed and the next one retried via `sync.Once`... note that with `sync.Once` a retry was never possible either, but at least the server existed. Consider building the index asynchronously and gating readiness/search on it rather than blocking construction.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers the literal alias "alias", so the 21 IDPs created by the new test are never removed

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425) references a hard-coded alias `"alias"` instead of the alias that was just created (`idp-alias-<i>` / `idp-alias-20`). At cleanup time the admin client targets a non-existent provider, so either the cleanup throws `NotFoundException` or it silently does nothing; in both cases none of the 21 identity providers created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` are deleted, and `idp-alias-20` stays linked to organization `orga`.

Because the test realm is imported once per class, this leaks state into the other methods of this class: `testCacheIDPByOrg` asserts exact counts (`assertEquals(6, ...)`, `assertEquals(2/4, ...)`) for the IDPs of orga/orgb, and `testCacheIDPForLogin` itself asserts exact counts (5/5/10, 6/5/11, 5/6/11) that are only valid in a clean realm. Depending on JUnit's method order, one of the two tests will fail or produce misleading results. (The same mistake exists in the pre-existing line 303 and should be fixed there too.)

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation decision uses the organization-aware wrapper, so updates can be silently skipped

`update()` obtains `original` from `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which (when the ORGANIZATION feature is on) returns the anonymous wrapper created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the realm's organization support) is disabled, while `updated` is the raw model. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` therefore compares a model whose enabled state depends on *external* org state against a raw model, and bails out of invalidating when both sides fail the login predicate.

Concrete failure: organization X is disabled; IDP `idp1` is linked to X with `BROKER_PUBLIC=true`, raw `enabled=true`, `hideOnLogin=false`. The login caches were populated from the JPA query (which filters on the raw DB columns), so `idp1`'s id is in the `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL` entries. An admin now sets `hideOnLogin=true`: `test(original)` is false (org disabled ⇒ wrapper reports disabled) and `test(updated)` is false (hidden), so the first early-return triggers and no login cache is invalidated. When organization X is re-enabled, `getForLogin` keeps returning `idp1`'s id and `getById` returns a non-null model, so the IDP that is explicitly hidden on login is rendered on the login page (the bean only re-checks `isEnabled()`, not `hideOnLogin`/`linkOnly`).

Use the unwrapped model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`) or compare the raw fields (`enabled`, `linkOnly`, `hideOnLogin`, `organizationId`, `BROKER_PUBLIC`) when deciding whether to invalidate. Note `remove()` correctly uses the raw delegate model, so the two paths are inconsistent today. There is also no test covering a disabled organization combined with a cached login list.

Single per-realm login cache entry keyed by organizationId is rebuilt/invalidated for every unseen organization

`getForLogin` uses one cache key per realm+FetchMode (`cacheKeyForLogin`) and stores the per-organization result sets inside a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` under `searchKey = organizationId`. When a request arrives with an organizationId that is not yet present in that entry, the code calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` (bumping the revision) and re-adds a merged query containing all previously cached search keys plus the new one.

On the login hot path this means: (a) the first login for each of N organizations in a realm invalidates and rebuilds the shared entry, so the realm's login IDP lookup is re-queried and the entry re-serialized O(N) times, and concurrent first-logins for different orgs will repeatedly drop each other's entry and re-hit the DB; (b) the entry grows monotonically with the number of organizations, so a realm with thousands of orgs ends up with one very large cache object that the realm cache's eviction policy treats as a single element. For `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the problem is gratuitous: `organizationId` is ignored by the query, yet it is still used as `searchKey`, so each distinct org id creates another identical result set (and another invalidate/rebuild cycle). Consider putting the organization id in the Infinispan key itself, or at least using a constant search key for `REALM_ONLY`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JDK provider, making BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER point to e.g. "SUN"

`getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. typically the JDK's `SUN`/`SunJSSE` provider, although the interface contract states it must return a BouncyCastle (FIPS or non-FIPS) provider. `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` is derived from this value, so any keycloak-core code reachable from the authz client that does `Xxx.getInstance(algorithm, BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)` will be routed to a provider that does not implement the requested algorithms and will fail with a confusing `NoSuchAlgorithmException` instead of the clear `UnsupportedOperationException` the rest of this class raises. Consider returning a provider that actually matches the contract or documenting/handling the null case in `BouncyIntegration` instead of this workaround.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead statements in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) create encoders, write into them and discard the results; the actual DER is produced by the `writeDerSeq(...)` call below with freshly created encoders. These two statements have no effect and only add confusion (a reader may believe the first encoders are the ones serialized). They should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract `order()` method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface as an abstract method. `CryptoProvider` is an SPI that is implemented outside this repository (e.g. the keycloak-client repo, adapters, custom/vendor crypto modules). Any existing implementation that is not recompiled will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` calls `CryptoProvider::order`, and sources will no longer compile. Declaring it as a `default` method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still allowing the authz-client provider to lower/raise its priority.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Malformed DER input causes unchecked exceptions instead of IOException

`readInteger()` uses the value returned by `readLength()` without validating it. `readLength()` returns `-1` for the indefinite-length form (0x80), so `read(-1)` executes `new byte[-1]` and throws `NegativeArraySizeException`; a zero-length INTEGER (`02 00`) yields an empty array and `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throws `NumberFormatException` ("Zero length BigInteger"). Both are unchecked exceptions escaping a method declared `throws IOException`, which is what callers of `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` handle. Since the input is an attacker-supplied token signature, this turns a verification failure into an unexpected runtime error propagating out of the verification path. `readInteger()` (and `readNext()`) should reject negative/zero lengths with an `IOException`.

Multiple crypto providers on classpath are no longer rejected; ties resolved nondeterministically and only logged at debug

The previous code threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found on the classpath. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used silently. All three real providers (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`) return the same order `200`, so if two of them end up on the same classpath (e.g. BC non-FIPS jar accidentally present in a FIPS deployment) the winner depends on `ServiceLoader` iteration order, and the fact that a provider was ignored is only reported via `logger.debugf` (off by default). That turns a previously loud, deterministic failure into a silent, non-deterministic choice of crypto backend — in a FIPS deployment it can mean silently running with non-approved crypto. At minimum, equal-order collisions should still fail (or be logged at WARN) rather than being resolved arbitrarily.

Test only round-trips through the new encoder/decoder, so a wrong DER encoding would not be detected

The test asserts `asn1der -> concat -> asn1der -> concat` self-consistency using only `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`'s own `ASN1Encoder`/`ASN1Decoder`. If `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` produced structurally wrong DER (wrong tag, wrong length form, missing leading-zero for negative-looking values), the matching custom decoder would still accept it and the assertion would pass. The produced DER should be validated against the JDK, e.g. by calling `Signature.verify(asn1Des)` with the public key (and/or comparing against the BC-based provider output). Additionally, the key pair is created with the JDK default EC curve (P-256) for all three tests, so ES384/ES512 never exercise the real r/s sizes, and the leading-zero-stripping branch of `integerToBytes` (`qLength < bytes.length`) is only hit by chance depending on the randomly generated key; the test should use P-256/P-384/P-521 keys matching each algorithm.

`logger.debugf(String)` used as a format string with no arguments and built unconditionally

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` resolves to the varargs `debugf(String format, Object... params)` overload with an empty parameter array, so the message is passed through `String.format`. Any `%` character in the message (class names normally have none, but the message is data-driven) would raise `UnknownFormatConversionException`/`MissingFormatArgumentException` from a logging call. In addition, the `StringBuilder` is populated and `toString()` is invoked even when debug logging is disabled. Use `logger.debug(...)` (optionally guarded by `isDebugEnabled()`), or a proper format string with parameters.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Listener guard checks the V1 feature, so client removal still hits V2 code paths

The provider-event listener body is now guarded by `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)`, but the code inside calls `management(session, realm)` which dispatches to `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled. If both preview features are enabled at the same time (nothing prevents this), removing a client executes `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false)`, which now throws `UnsupportedOperationException` (ClientPermissionsV2), aborting client deletion with an internal error. The guard should also exclude the V2 feature (or the listener should explicitly use the V1 `MgmtPermissions`). Additionally, gating cleanup on the V1 feature means that when the feature is turned off, previously created V1 permission policies for removed roles/clients/groups are left behind as orphans.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the resource-type name and misses per-client grants

`getClientsWithPermission` iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` and adds `resource.getName()` to the result. Per-client resources are created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)` without ever setting a resource type, so they are never returned by `findByType`. The only resource with type `Clients` is the "all clients" resource created in `init()`, whose name is the literal string `"Clients"`. Consequently this method returns either an empty set or `{"Clients"}` — never real client ids — while callers of `ClientPermissionEvaluator.getClientsWithPermission(scope)` expect a set of client ids (the V1 implementation strips the `client.resource.` prefix and returns ids). Grants on individual clients are invisible to those callers and the bogus `"Clients"` entry can be mistaken for a client id.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE when the 'Clients' resource-type resource does not exist

In `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)`, when no per-client resource is found the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` and immediately passes the result to `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` without a null check. `getResourceTypeResource` returns `null` in several reachable cases: the realm has an admin-permissions client but `realm.isAdminPermissionsEnabled()` is false (so `supportsAuthorizationSchema` returns false), or the `Clients` resource simply does not exist (e.g. a realm whose admin-permissions client was created before this schema change, see the `init()` early-return). Also, if `findByResource` happens to be non-empty while `resource` is null, `new ResourcePermission(resource, resource.getScopes(), server)` dereferences null. The result is a NullPointerException in authorization checks, i.e. HTTP 500 on ordinary admin client endpoints instead of a clean allow/deny. Add a null check that returns `false` when the fallback resource is missing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code and unused imports left from copy/paste

The class contains a private, never-called `getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken)` method (line 262), an unused `logger` field (line 51) and unused imports/static imports (`Scope`, `ClientModelIdentity`, `DefaultEvaluationContext`, `EvaluationContext`, `AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE`). This is leftover from copying the V1 implementation; it produces compiler warnings and suggests an evaluation-context customization that is not actually applied. It should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Javadoc on require* methods describes a return value for void methods

`requireView()` (line 98) is documented as "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}." and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 103) as "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}." Both methods are `void` and, consistently with the other `require*` methods in this interface, throw `ForbiddenException` when the corresponding `can*` check fails. The Javadoc therefore documents behaviour that does not exist and should read "Throws ForbiddenException if ... returns {@code false}".

Management-permissions admin endpoints return 500 with V2 enabled

`isPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel)`, `setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean)`, `getPermissions(ClientModel)` and `resource(ClientModel)` all throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. These are invoked directly by the admin REST endpoints `GET`/`PUT /admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{id}/management/permissions` (`ClientResource.getManagementPermissions`/`setManagementPermissionsEnabled`). Since `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` now returns this class, enabling `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` turns those endpoints from working (V1) responses into unhandled runtime exceptions, i.e. HTTP 500. A deliberate 400/404 (e.g. `ModelValidationException`/`NotFoundException`) would be the appropriate contract for "not supported in V2".

`AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` is added to the Clients resource type and `ClientPermissionsV2.canMapClientScopeRoles` is implemented, but no test exercises it (tests only cover `manage`, `configure`, `view`, `map-roles` and `map-roles-composite`). Likewise there is no test for the all-clients `configure` permission or for a negative-logic (deny) client permission. Without coverage, regressions in the client-scope role mapping evaluation would go unnoticed.

No migration of new scopes/resource for already initialized admin-permissions clients

`init()` returns early when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null`, so realms that already had admin permissions enabled before this change never get the newly introduced scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`) nor the `Clients` resource-type resource. On such realms, creating a Clients permission fails: `getScope()` throws `ModelValidationException("Scope [configure] does not exist.")`, and `getOrCreateResource()` throws `ModelException("No scopes found.")` when building the per-client resource (HTTP 500), and `hasPermission()` in ClientPermissionsV2 cannot find the fallback `Clients` resource. Some upgrade/initialization path is needed to add missing schema scopes and resource-type resources to existing admin-permissions clients.

canExchangeTo now throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking legacy token exchange when V2 is enabled

`ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo(...)` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. Because `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` now returns `ClientPermissionsV2` (previously it returned the V1 `ClientPermissions`), the legacy token-exchange flow, which calls `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(client, targetClient, token)`, will now blow up with an unchecked exception and return HTTP 500 whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled together with the token-exchange feature. Either keep delegating to the V1 behaviour or make the caller aware that token exchange permissions are not available in V2 and return a proper deny/400 instead of an unhandled runtime exception.

`getResourceName` resolves friendly names only for the `Users` resource type ("All users" / username). For the newly added `Clients` resource type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is null for resources created by `getOrCreateResource` (only name and owner are set). As a result, permissions created for clients will be reported without a resolvable name in representations, unlike user permissions, and there is no "All clients" label for the resource-type resource.

testManageOnlyOneClient mutates shared realm state without cleanup

`testManageOnlyOneClient` renames `myclient` (`setName("somethingNew")`), removes one of its default client scopes and adds it as an optional scope, but registers no `realm.cleanup()` task to restore it. The realm/client are shared by the other tests in this class (only scope permissions are cleaned in `@AfterEach`), so the mutated client-scope assignment and name leak into subsequent tests, making the suite order-dependent and potentially flaky (e.g. other tests index into `getDefaultClientScopes()`).

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code 4 is re-used with a different meaning while recreate moves to 3

Any existing automation or operator logic that was written against the implemented behaviour (4 == recreate) will now silently interpret "feature disabled" as "recreate required", and will not react to the new code 3 at all. Since the value is being recycled rather than a fresh code allocated, consider using an unused code (e.g. 5) for the new condition, or at minimum call out the incompatible exit-code change in the release notes / upgrade guide for this preview tool.

false_positives.candidate:
Documented command passes the build-time option `--features` at runtime

The `updatecompatibility` macro now renders every documented invocation as `bin/kc.[sh|bat] update-compatibility <args> --features=rolling-updates`. `features` is a build-time option: on a distribution/container that was already built (`kc.sh build`, or any optimized image) specifying it on a runtime command either forces a re-augmentation on every invocation (slow, and impossible on a read-only container filesystem) or is rejected when `--optimized` is in effect. The guide should instead instruct users to enable `rolling-updates` at build time (as this PR does for `operator/scripts/Dockerfile-custom-image`), otherwise the copy-pasteable commands in the guide will not work in the main production deployment style. There is also a correctness trap: the guide elsewhere insists the metadata/check commands be run with exactly the deployment's configuration, yet here it tells users to add a feature the running deployment does not have.

Feature `rolling-updates` is only enabled for the non-null update strategy in UpgradeTest

Both parameterized tests (`testImageChange`, `testCacheMaxCount`) therefore run the default/unset-strategy case with the preview feature disabled in the CR, which directly contradicts the new documentation added in this PR ("While on preview stage, the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail."). Either the default strategy path is being tested in an unsupported configuration (and may pass only by accident, e.g. because the test image happens to have the feature built in), or the documented requirement is wrong. In addition, the null and RECREATE runs now differ in two dimensions (strategy *and* feature set), making any failure ambiguous.

No test covers the changed/added exit codes (3 for recreate, 4 for feature disabled)

This PR changes `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` from 4 to 3 and introduces `FEATURE_DISABLED = 4`, and the documentation explicitly tells users to script against these exit codes. However, `testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the stderr text and never asserts `exitCode() == 4`, and `testWrongVersions` never asserts `exitCode() == 3`. Note also that `@Launch`-based tests in this suite do not validate the exit code (see the pre-existing `testMissingSubCommand` which really exits with 2). As a result, a regression in the documented exit-code contract — the only thing automation is supposed to rely on — would go unnoticed. The feature gate is also only exercised for the `metadata` subcommand; the identical gate added to `check` is untested.

Operator preview note does not cover custom images and is vague about the failure
