For users running a custom/optimized image the Operator cannot change build-time options such as `features`, so the CR snippet will not have any effect — the feature has to be baked into the image at build time (exactly what this PR does in `operator/scripts/Dockerfile-custom-image`). The doc should say this. The sentence is also inconsistent with the NOTE a few lines below, which says that during preview the default strategy just mimics 26.1 behaviour, leaving the reader unsure whether the feature is required even when `spec.update.strategy` is unset, and "will fail" gives no observable symptom (condition, event, job failure) to look for.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage rights to admins that only have the 'view' scope on all groups

`GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` (the no-argument variant) returns `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, i.e. it treats the `view` scope on the aggregate "Groups" resource as sufficient for manage. `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup()` calls `auth.groups().requireManage()`, so an admin who was only granted an all-groups *view* permission can create top-level groups. Compare with the group-scoped variant `canManage(GroupModel)` (line 79) which correctly checks only `MANAGE`, and with `UserPermissionsV2`, where manage never falls back to view. The javadoc added in `GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage()` documents the same wrong behaviour. The VIEW scope should be removed from this check.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization Resource IDs, not group IDs, and never finds per-group resources

The V2 implementation collects `groupResource.getId()` (the internal authz `Resource` id) into the returned set, but all callers treat the returned values as group IDs: `UsersResource.searchForUser()`/`BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser()` put them into `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)` and `UsersResource.getUsersCount()` passes them to `session.users().getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)`. In FGAP V2 the per-object resource *name* is the group id (see `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup`), so the ids returned here never match any group and the user query is restricted to a non-existent group – an admin that has `view-members`/`manage-members` on all groups gets an empty user list. The same wrong value is also passed back into `hasPermission(groupId, ...)` on line 122, which resolves resources via `resourceStore.findByName()`, so the per-resource lookup always misses and silently falls back to evaluating the aggregate "Groups" resource.
In addition, `resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` can only return the aggregate "Groups" resource, because `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource()` creates per-object resources without calling `setType()`. Consequently per-group view-members permissions are never reported, which makes `UsersResource.getUsersCount()` return 0 for such admins while the user list endpoint still returns users (count and list disagree). V1 (`GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission`) does this correctly by using `resource.getName()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Evaluated permissions are not filtered to the requested resource (inconsistent with UserPermissionsV2)

`GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission()` iterates all `Permission` objects returned by `root.evaluatePermission(...)` and grants access as soon as any of them carries one of the expected scopes. `UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission()` (line 123 of that file) deliberately guards this with `permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId())`. Without that guard, any permission the policy engine returns for a resource other than the one being evaluated (e.g. scope-only or resource-type expanded permissions) would grant access on the wrong group. The two implementations should use the same rule.

Javadoc of requireManageMembers refers to canManageMembership

The javadoc added for `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` states "Throws ForbiddenException if {@link #canManageMembership(GroupModel)} returns false" – it is a copy of the javadoc of `requireManageMembership` and documents the wrong predicate; the method actually delegates to `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`. Since these two scopes (`manage-membership` vs `manage-members`) grant very different privileges, wrong documentation on this security API is misleading for implementors. Also note that the javadoc of `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` says "@return Stream of IDs" while the method returns a `Set`, and the permission it actually checks is view-members/manage-members, not `view`.

NPE when the aggregate "Groups" resource cannot be resolved

In `hasPermission()`, when no per-group resource is found the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)` and immediately calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` without a null check. `getResourceTypeResource()` returns `null` in two reachable situations: (a) the resource server exists but `supportsAuthorizationSchema()` is false, e.g. a realm where the admin-permissions client was created once and `adminPermissionsEnabled` was later turned off, and (b) the "Groups" resource does not exist in the resource server (realms whose admin-permissions client was created before this resource type was added – `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` only runs when the client is first created). In both cases any group/user listing by an admin without `view-users`/`query-groups` roles ends in a NullPointerException and a 500 response instead of a plain "denied".

No coverage for all-groups view-members, for the users count endpoint, or for the group members endpoint

The new test class only exercises per-group `view-members`/`manage-members` through `users().search(...)`, which happens to work even when `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` returns nothing (the search then runs unrestricted and is filtered per user). Missing cases that would have caught the broken `GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`: (1) an *all-groups* `view-members`/`manage-members` permission followed by `users().search(...)` (currently returns nothing because an authz resource id is used as a group id filter), (2) `users().count()` for an admin whose only visibility comes from group member permissions (currently returns 0 while `search` returns users), and (3) `groups().group(id).members()` which is guarded by the new `requireViewMembers` path.

No upgrade path for realms whose admin-permissions client already exists

`init()` returns early when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null`, so the newly added "Groups" aggregate resource and the new scopes (`manage-membership`, `manage-members`, `view-members`) are only created for realms that enable admin permissions after this change. For a realm that already enabled FGAP V2 with an earlier build: creating any Groups scope permission fails because `getOrCreateResource()` (line 125) throws `ModelException("No scopes found.")` when a schema scope is missing from the resource server, and group permission evaluation hits the missing aggregate resource (see `GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission`). Either a migration that adds missing scopes/resource-type resources to existing admin-permissions clients or an idempotent re-initialisation is needed.

Removal of the global view short-circuit makes group listing evaluate policies per group

`getGroups()` previously computed `boolean canViewGlobal = groupsEvaluator.canView()` once and only evaluated `canView(group)` per group when the global check failed; the same hoisting was removed in `GroupResource.getSubGroups()`. With FGAP V2, `GroupPermissionsV2.canView(group)` performs a resource lookup by name plus a full policy evaluation for every group in the stream (and in `getSubGroups` the filter is applied over all subgroups before pagination). For a policy-based admin holding an all-groups view permission this turns one evaluation into one per listed group, which is the main use case of the new feature. Consider keeping the single global check as a short-circuit.

Admin console message switched from i18next `{{n}}` to Java MessageFormat choice syntax

The removed line in this same file used `{{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}}`, i.e. this bundle is interpolated by i18next in the Admin Console SPA. The new value `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.` uses Java MessageFormat argument syntax plus a `choice` sub-format, neither of which i18next understands, so the administrator will see the raw placeholders and the raw choice expression instead of the min/max values. Diff trimming can produce substring(begin > end) and crash the verifier The common-prefix (`start`) and common-suffix (`end`) counters are computed independently, so `start + end` can exceed `sanitized.length()`. Example: a translation with a stray closing tag, `value = "

text

"` sanitizes to `"

text

"`; then `start = 11` and `end = 4`, and `sanitized.substring(11, 11 - 4)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Java MessageFormat/choice syntax put into an i18next message bundle

This bundle is served to the Account Console SPA and resolved with i18next, which interpolates `{{0}}`-style placeholders only (see line 27 `error-invalid-length-too-short='{{0}}' must have minimal length of {{1}}.` and line 3 `backTo=Back to {{app}}`), and has no support for Java MessageFormat `choice` sub-formats. true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Copy-paste in constructor validation leaves rawTokenId unchecked

`Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` checks `grantType` for the second time instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result a `null` raw token id passes validation and later produces an access-token id literally ending in ":null" (`encodeTokenId` concatenates it), instead of failing fast at construction. The message is also misleading if `grantType` is the actual null argument. Should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher checks the wrong characters and inverts the comparison

The new matcher is supposed to assert that an access-token id looks like `<session><token><grant>:<uuid>` and that the grant shortcut matches `expectedGrantShortcut`. Two defects make the check useless (and potentially wrong):

1. Wrong offset: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4 and 5 of the 6-char prefix (`on`+`rt`+`ac`), so it must be read with `substring(4, 6)`. `substring(3, 5)` reads the last char of the token-type plus the first char of the grant type (e.g. "ta" for "onrtac").
2. Inverted condition: `if (items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` fails the match when the shortcut *equals* the expectation; it should be `if (!....equals(...)) return false;`.

Combined, the matcher currently always skips the grant check (the garbled 2-char slice never equals a real shortcut), so `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` no longer verify anything about the encoded grant type — the main thing this PR introduces. Conversely, if `expectedGrantShortcut` ever happened to equal the garbled slice, every such assertion would fail. Additionally, `substring(3,5)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException (instead of returning false) for a prefix shorter than 5 chars, turning a mismatch into an error.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grant shortcut length is never validated, yet decoding hard-codes a 6-char prefix

`getTokenContextFromTokenId()` requires the prefix before ':' to be exactly 6 characters (2 for session type + 2 for token type + 2 for grant type) and throws `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise, while `encodeTokenId()` happily concatenates whatever `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` returns. Nothing validates that a shortcut is exactly 2 characters — and the Javadoc of `getShortcut()` even states "usually like 3-letters shortcut", which actively invites 3-character values. A provider (or a future built-in grant) returning a shortcut of any other length will produce access-token IDs that this very provider can never decode, i.e. permanently undecodable tokens in the wild. Validate the shortcut length in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` (fail fast at startup) and fix the Javadoc to state the exact required length.

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative test accepts any RuntimeException and ignores the result

`testIncorrectGrantType` catches `RuntimeException`, so the test would also pass if the code threw an unrelated `NullPointerException` instead of the intended `IllegalArgumentException` about an unknown grant shortcut; the declared `ctx` variable is unused. Assert the expected exception type (and ideally the message) so the test actually pins the contract of `getTokenContextFromTokenId`.

false_positives.candidate:
Decoding a malformed token id throws instead of degrading to UNKNOWN

`getTokenContextFromTokenId()` returns an all-UNKNOWN context for ids without ':' (legacy tokens), but throws `IllegalArgumentException` for ids that contain ':' with an unexpected prefix length or unknown shortcuts. Token ids come from client-supplied tokens (the stated goal is to call this from introspection/userinfo/admin endpoints), so once wired up any crafted or foreign `jti` turns into an unhandled runtime exception, i.e. an HTTP 500 instead of an invalid-token response. Treating unparseable prefixes the same way as legacy ids (UNKNOWN context) or wrapping the call in explicit error handling at the call sites is needed before these endpoints start consuming it.

Format change of access-token jti is not documented in upgrading/release notes

Access tokens no longer carry a plain UUID in `jti`; the value becomes `<6 chars>:<uuid>` (and `Details.TOKEN_ID` in events changes accordingly). This is an externally visible, behaviour-changing contract: resource servers, log/SIEM pipelines and client libraries that parse or store `jti` as a UUID (fixed 36-char column, `UUID.fromString(...)`) will break on upgrade. The PR contains no upgrading/release-note documentation for this change, nor any statement that the prefix is opaque and must not be relied upon by third parties.

New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

`getShortcut()` is added to the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` SPI interface without a `default` implementation. Any existing implementation of this SPI (third-party grant providers, and any grant factory in the repo/testsuite that was not updated in this PR) will no longer compile, and a pre-compiled provider JAR deployed into the server will fail at runtime. The failure is not localized to the grant itself: `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates over *all* `OAuth2GrantType` factories, casts them to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` and calls `getShortcut()`, so a single stale provider throws `AbstractMethodError` during server startup. Providing a `default` implementation (e.g. returning a neutral/unknown shortcut) and handling that value in the encoder would keep the SPI backwards compatible.

The previous code threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found on the classpath. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used silently. All three real providers (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`) return the same order `200`, so if two of them end up on the same classpath (e.g. BC non-FIPS jar accidentally present in a FIPS deployment) the winner depends on `ServiceLoader` iteration order, and the fact that a provider was ignored is only reported via `logger.debugf` (off by default). That turns a previously loud, deterministic failure into a silent, non-deterministic choice of crypto backend — in a FIPS deployment it can mean silently running with non-approved crypto. At minimum, equal-order collisions should still fail (or be logged at WARN) rather than being resolved arbitrarily.

`logger.debugf(String)` used as a format string with no arguments and built unconditionally

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` resolves to the varargs `debugf(String format, Object... params)` overload with an empty parameter array, so the message is passed through `String.format`. Any `%` character in the message (class names normally have none, but the message is data-driven) would raise `UnknownFormatConversionException`/`MissingFormatArgumentException` from a logging call. In addition, the `StringBuilder` is populated and `toString()` is invoked even when debug logging is disabled. Use `logger.debug(...)` (optionally guarded by `isDebugEnabled()`), or a proper format string with parameters.

Malformed DER input causes unchecked exceptions instead of IOException

`readInteger()` uses the value returned by `readLength()` without validating it. `readLength()` returns `-1` for the indefinite-length form (0x80), so `read(-1)` executes `new byte[-1]` and throws `NegativeArraySizeException`; a zero-length INTEGER (`02 00`) yields an empty array and `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throws `NumberFormatException` ("Zero length BigInteger"). Both are unchecked exceptions escaping a method declared `throws IOException`, which is what callers of `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` handle. Since the input is an attacker-supplied token signature, this turns a verification failure into an unexpected runtime error propagating out of the verification path. `readInteger()` (and `readNext()`) should reject negative/zero lengths with an `IOException`.

Test only round-trips through the new encoder/decoder, so a wrong DER encoding would not be detected

The test asserts `asn1der -> concat -> asn1der -> concat` self-consistency using only `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`'s own `ASN1Encoder`/`ASN1Decoder`. If `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` produced structurally wrong DER (wrong tag, wrong length form, missing leading-zero for negative-looking values), the matching custom decoder would still accept it and the assertion would pass. The produced DER should be validated against the JDK, e.g. by calling `Signature.verify(asn1Des)` with the public key (and/or comparing against the BC-based provider output). Additionally, the key pair is created with the JDK default EC curve (P-256) for all three tests, so ES384/ES512 never exercise the real r/s sizes, and the leading-zero-stripping branch of `integerToBytes` (`qLength < bytes.length`) is only hit by chance depending on the randomly generated key; the test should use P-256/P-384/P-521 keys matching each algorithm.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is never true for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed

`self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` creates `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances, which subclass `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, *not* `multiprocessing.context.Process` (what `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to). Therefore the guard `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` in `_ensure_processes_alive` is always False and `kill()` is never executed. Consequences: (a) a process detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`, i.e. it is still alive but has not updated `healthy_since`) is left running while a replacement process is spawned for the *same* shards — two flushers then flush/produce the same shard set, risking duplicate and/or fragmented segments on `buffered-segments`; (b) dead processes are never reaped (no `kill`/`join`/`close`), leaving zombies; (c) the same broken check at line 346 in `join()` means `terminate()` is never called on shutdown. false_positives.candidate:
No validation of flusher process count; 0/negative values silently disable flushing

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` followed by `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` has two bad edge cases reachable from the new `--flusher-processes` CLI option: passing `0` falls through the `or` and silently means "one process per shard" (the opposite of what the help text 'Maximum number of processes ... Defaults to 1' implies), and passing a negative number yields `num_processes <= 0`, so `process_to_shards_map` is empty and **no flusher process is started at all**. In that case spans keep being written to Redis but no segments are ever flushed or produced, until Redis memory backpressure stalls the consumer. The same happens if `assigned_shards` is empty. Validate the option (require >= 1) and/or clamp `num_processes` to at least 1.

New multi-process flusher test only asserts internal bookkeeping, not that all shards are flushed

`test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and `sum(len(shards)) == 4`, then immediately joins without submitting any spans. It never verifies the behaviour the PR introduces: that spans landing on each of the 4 shards are actually flushed and produced by the two flusher workers, and that shards are partitioned without overlap (the `sum == 4` assertion would also pass for a duplicated mapping such as `{0: [0, 0], 1: [1, 1]}`, which would cause double-production). It also exercises only the thread path (`produce_to_pipe` is set), so the real spawn-process path with multiple workers remains untested. Add a test that writes spans for several shards, advances the drift, and asserts every segment is produced exactly once, plus an assertion that the union of `process_to_shards_map` values equals `assigned_shards` with no duplicates.

Dead method _create_process_for_shard is unused

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere after the refactor (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` in `_ensure_processes_alive`). Leaving it in place is confusing — it suggests per-shard restart is supported, and if someone later calls it, it restarts the whole process group for the shard without resetting the restart counter bookkeeping that `_ensure_processes_alive` relies on. Remove it.

A new parent-side SpansBuffer (and Redis client) is created on every process restart and never released

`_create_process_for_shards` constructs `shard_buffer = SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent process and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, replacing the previous instance without closing it. Each restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per worker) therefore leaks the Redis client/connection pool of the discarded buffer in the consumer process. In addition, the parent now holds one buffer per worker group on top of the buffer passed in from the factory, so `submit()` performs N `record_stored_segments()`/`get_memory_info()` round trips per call instead of one. Consider reusing a single parent-side buffer for stats/memory checks and only creating per-shard buffers for the children.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error IDs are zipped against unordered nodestore results

`fetch_error_details()` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` and then pairs them with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi()` returns a mapping keyed by node id; its iteration order is an implementation detail (several backends merge cache hits and DB fetches into a new dict), so `events.values()` is not guaranteed to be in the same order as `error_ids`. The result is `ErrorEvent.id` values attached to the wrong title/message/timestamp, which is then fed to Seer for summarization. false_positives.candidate:
Error/breadcrumb merge compares timestamps in different units

`gen_request_data()` interleaves errors and replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamps come from the nodestore event payload (epoch **seconds**, e.g. 1.75e9), while the top-level timestamp of an rrweb replay event is epoch **milliseconds** (e.g. 1.75e12). The comparison is therefore always true for real data, so every error is emitted before the first breadcrumb instead of being interleaved chronologically, defeating the purpose of the merge. The new unit tests use hand-written second-based event timestamps (1.5, 2.0), which hides the mismatch. Normalize both sides to the same unit before comparing.

get_environment_info triggers a recommended-event lookup per issue in PR comments

`get_environment_info()` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment. That helper runs a Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch per issue, so building a comment for the top 5 issues now issues up to 5 extra event lookups (each able to time out or return a stale 'recommended' event) inside the PR comment task, for a single word of decoration in the comment. Consider resolving environments from data already fetched (e.g. the group's environments or the snuba row) instead of fetching full events. Also note the `except Exception` branch logs the raw exception object in `extra={"error": e}`; `str(e)` serializes more reliably.

`MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE` ends with `

".join(...)`. Every bullet is therefore separated by a blank line (which Markdown renders as a 'loose' list with extra paragraph spacing) and the list ends with an extra newline immediately before the `<sub>Did you find this useful?</sub>` footer. The updated tests encode this double spacing, so the formatting regression will ship silently. Drop the trailing `
` from the template.

Hook now returns possibly-undefined attributes instead of an empty TagCollection

Previously `attributes` was derived through a `useMemo` that always produced a `TagCollection` object (`{}` when there was no data). Now it is `isFetching ? previous : data`, where both `previous` (first render) and `data` (query disabled or not yet resolved) are `undefined`. Callers that are not updated in this PR and treat the value as always-present (spreading is fine, but `Object.keys(attributes)` / `attributes[key]` is not) can now hit runtime errors, in particular when the hook is used with `enabled: false`. Fall back to an empty object (`data ?? {}`) to preserve the previous contract.

Both `renderDefaultHeadCell` and `renderDefaultBodyCell` decide to use the custom renderer with `if (cell)`. The documented contract (see the prop JSDoc in `tableWidgetVisualization.tsx` and the storybook text: 'If the function returns `undefined`, fallback renderer will run') is that only `undefined` falls through. In practice a renderer that intentionally renders nothing by returning `null`, or that returns `''`/`0`/`false` for a cell value, will be silently overridden by the default renderer. Check `cell !== undefined` instead.

`Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields)` mixes optional chaining with a non-guarded member access and an unguarded `Object.keys`. If `tableData` is ever undefined (the surrounding code defends against it with `tableData?.data ?? []`), this throws `Cannot convert undefined or null to object` instead of rendering an empty table. Either treat `tableData` as truly required (drop the `?.`) or guard the fallback column computation.

Unauthenticated endpoint loops over an unbounded report array

This endpoint has `permission_classes = ()` and is CSRF exempt, yet the new code iterates the entire posted array with no cap on the number of reports: it logs the full request body, logs each invalid report (`extra={"raw_report": report}`) and emits one metric per valid report at `sample_rate=1.0`. Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its entire body, which serialized index creation. With the lock now only held around the cache write, two concurrent callers that both saw `GetIndex() == nil` (e.g. two Search requests for the same namespace/group/resource, or a watch event racing with a search) can run `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory at the same time when `size > FileThreshold`. That means two processes/goroutines writing the same on-disk bleve index concurrently (undefined behaviour/corruption, or a spurious "path already exists" error), plus duplicated full re-index work and a cache entry that is overwritten by the loser. The TODO in `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` acknowledges this; a per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed now that the global lock is gone.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

`bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` iterates `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes to the same map under `cacheMu` (lines 137-139). Concurrent map read + write is a fatal, unrecoverable Go runtime error (`concurrent map read and map write`), i.e. a process crash. This PR makes it reachable: `searchSupport.init` starts the watch-event goroutine (search.go line 207) and then calls `s.search.TotalDocs()` in the new log line (search.go line 216); a watch event handled in that goroutine can trigger `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex` -> cache write at the same moment. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs` (and copy out the indexes before calling `DocCount`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same data race: `TotalDocs()` iterates over `b.cache` without synchronization, which can race with `BuildIndex` writing to `b.cache` triggered by the watch-event goroutine started just before calling `TotalDocs()` in `init`, leading to a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race and lost errors in the index-build errgroup

In `searchSupport.init`, the goroutines started via `group.Go` all write to the function-scoped variables `err` (line 190: `_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and `totalBatchesIndexed` (line 189) without synchronization. Up to `initWorkers` goroutines run concurrently, so these are genuine data races (detectable by `-race`, and the counter will under-count). Worse, each goroutine returns the shared `err`, so one goroutine can observe another goroutine's value: a real build failure can be clobbered by a concurrent `nil` assignment (startup then proceeds with a partially built index) or a successful goroutine can return someone else's error (startup aborts spuriously). This was largely masked before because `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its whole body and serialized the builds; this PR removes that lock, so the goroutines now really overlap. Use goroutine-local variables (`if err := s.build(...); err != nil { return err }`) and an atomic counter.

`Stop()` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", but every RPC handler's `s.Init(ctx)` guard was deleted, so nothing reads `initErr` any more. After `Stop()` cancels the background context, `Create`/`Update`/`Delete`/`List`/`Watch`/`Search` etc. will happily keep executing against a backend whose watcher/poller has been shut down: writes still reach the DB but no write events are broadcast or indexed, and watchers silently receive nothing. Previously these calls returned an error. Either keep an explicit "stopped" check at the entry of the handlers or drop the now-dead `initErr` mutations in `Stop` and document the new contract.

`ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created at line 229, but the new error path `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err }` returns without calling `cancel()`. Anything already started during `Init` (the sql backend poller started by `search.init`'s `WatchWriteEvents`, and `initWatcher`'s broadcaster goroutine if it got that far) keeps running for the lifetime of the process, and the context is leaked (this is also what `go vet`'s lostcancel check flags). Moving `s.Init(ctx)` into `NewResourceServer` makes the full search-index build (all namespaces, via `searchSupport.init`) part of object construction, with no timeout and no way to serve traffic while it runs. Two consequences the PR should address explicitly: (1) startup latency - the PR itself states the build exceeds a gRPC request deadline, so Grafana/the storage-server target will not accept any request (not even `/metrics` via the gRPC health service) until indexing finishes; (2) a single transient failure (DB not reachable yet, one namespace failing to index) now aborts `NewResourceServer` and therefore the whole process startup, whereas previously only the first request failed and the next one retried via `sync.Once`... note that with `sync.Once` a retry was never possible either, but at least the server existed. false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of the implemented behaviour and passes only by timing

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages" but then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing is committed. In the implementation the worker catches the exception and still calls `complete_offset()` in its `finally` block, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable and the 1-second commit loop will commit them. The test only passes because its wait loop exits after ~0.3s, before the first commit tick. So it asserts behaviour the code does not have, is timing-dependent (will fail whenever the commit thread ticks early / CI is slow), and provides no real coverage of failure handling.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly points out that `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` has a docstring ('errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages') that directly contradicts its test implementation (asserting that nothing is committed), which matches the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Queue pool is permanently shut down on the first rebalance, then reused

`create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` hands the single, factory-owned `self.queue_pool` to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` it creates. Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops all worker threads and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The factory still holds a non-None reference, so the next `create_with_partitions()` after the rebalance returns a strategy backed by a dead pool: `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`, where the offset is immediately marked added+complete and therefore committed. The result is that after the first rebalance the consumer silently drops every message while advancing offsets, i.e. permanent data loss. The pool needs to be created per strategy (or recreated on assignment) rather than shared across the factory lifetime.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `Commit` callback (`StreamProcessor.__commit` -> `consumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets`). That callback and the underlying consumer state are only safe to touch from the thread running the processor loop; calling it concurrently with `poll()`/`submit()`/rebalance handling can corrupt the staged-offset bookkeeping or raise (e.g. staging an offset for a partition that was just revoked). Because the exception is caught and only logged in the loop, such failures would be invisible and offsets would silently stop advancing. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread (e.g. collected in `poll()`) instead of committed from the commit thread.

Shutdown drops all queued work instead of draining it; join() ignores timeout

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` *before* calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Each worker checks `self.shutdown` at the top of its loop, so after finishing its current item it exits immediately and never drains the remaining queued items, defeating the point of `immediate=False`. Combined with `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` which just delegates to `close()` and ignores the timeout entirely, a normal shutdown or rebalance discards everything still queued. Those offsets stay uncommitted so the messages are re-delivered, but arroyo's `join(timeout)` contract (flush outstanding work within the timeout) is broken and every restart/rebalance causes a burst of duplicate processing proportional to the queue depth.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring claim

Each queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever fills up: if a result processor is slower than the Kafka consumption rate, the strategy will keep accepting messages and grow memory without bound. Each `WorkItem` also retains the full `Message[KafkaPayload]` (field `message`, which is never read anywhere), so the retained payload bytes are kept alive as well, plus one entry per offset in `OffsetTracker.all_offsets`. A bounded queue plus `MessageRejected` (or an explicit limit) is needed to get real backpressure.

OffsetTracker state is never reset across partition assignments

`OffsetTracker` lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool` and keeps `last_committed`/`all_offsets` forever; `create_with_partitions()` never resets it for the newly assigned partition set. If a partition is revoked and later re-assigned to this consumer at a lower offset (rewind, other consumer committed less far, offset reset), `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` from the stale `last_committed`, finds no offsets at or above it, and therefore never produces a committable offset for that partition again - the consumer processes messages but silently stops committing, so the lag grows without bound and everything is reprocessed on restart. The tracker should be reset (or scoped per assignment) when partitions are assigned/revoked.

Offset-gap test does not actually verify gap blocking and is timing-dependent

`test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` submits offsets 100, 102, 103 and asserts that no commit ever exceeds 101. The tracker blocks at the gap only for the first commit tick: after `mark_committed(100)` removes offsets <= 100, the next call to `get_committable_offsets()` uses `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset) = 102` and will therefore commit 103 (reported as 104). The test passes only because the wait loop breaks ~0.2s after the first commit, before the next 1-second tick, making it flaky; and the `for commit in all_commits: assert <= 101` loop gives a false sense that committing past gaps is prevented. Either the skip-the-gap behaviour should be asserted explicitly, or the loop should keep observing commits for more than one tick.

Strategy docstring guarantees do not match behaviour

The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring claims "No item is lost or processed out of order", "Natural backpressure when queues fill up" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing". None of those hold: queues are unbounded (no backpressure), items still queued at close are discarded, and the worker marks an offset complete in its `finally` block even when `result_processor` raised, so failed items are committed and never retried. Leaving these claims in place will mislead operators about the delivery semantics of the new mode.

FilteredPayload messages are funneled through the generic exception handler

`ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload` starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, and that assert is outside its try/except. When this strategy is wrapped by something that emits `FilteredPayload` (e.g. the stale-message DLQ wrapper used via `--stale-threshold-sec`), every filtered message raises an AssertionError that lands in `submit()`'s `except Exception`, logging "Error submitting message to queue" at exception level for each one. Offsets are still advanced, so this is noise rather than data loss, but it will flood error logs/Sentry. `submit()` should handle `FilteredPayload` explicitly (track and complete the offset) instead of relying on the catch-all.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offsets are passed straight into a Django queryset slice and raise ValueError

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects this with `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for any slice whose start or stop is negative, so the request ends in an unhandled exception / HTTP 500. The inline comment “The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically” is factually wrong, and the comment “enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds … safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level” documents behaviour that does not exist. Since `Cursor.from_string` accepts any integer offset from the `cursor` query parameter, this is a user-triggerable error path. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` where a negative `cursor.offset` is passed as `start_offset` into a Django queryset slice when `enable_advanced_features` is True.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silently clamping negative cursor offsets masks invalid cursors and is inconsistent for prev cursors

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` in `BasePaginator.get_result` silently rewrites an invalid (negative) forward cursor offset to 0, so the caller gets page 1 data while `build_cursor` still derives the next/prev cursors from the original negative `cursor.offset` (e.g. `next_offset = offset + limit`), producing further bogus cursors. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still handed to the Django slice, which raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so the fix is only half applied. Other paginators in this file (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`) raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`; `BasePaginator` should do the same rather than clamp.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly points out the exact problem described in the golden comment: in `BasePaginator.get_result`, when `cursor.is_prev` is True, `start_offset = offset` without clamping, which passes a negative offset to the Django queryset slice.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is an integer paginator but is used with a datetime sort key

The endpoint sorts by `-datetime` (a `DateTimeField`). `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — i.e. the integer semantics of `Paginator`, not the millisecond-timestamp conversion that `DateTimePaginator` implements. Consequently, when `optimized_pagination=true` is honored, `build_cursor` calls `get_item_key` on a `datetime` and raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, and any follow-up cursor value is injected raw into the `WHERE datetime >= %s` clause built by `build_queryset`, comparing an integer against a timestamp column. The optimized path therefore cannot work for this endpoint at all; it only produces 500s (and would silently mis-page if it did not crash).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` uses `math.floor` on a datetime key (`-datetime`), which raises a `TypeError`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member` can be None, causing a 500 on every audit-log request

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET, before it is known whether the optimized path is even requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` and is None whenever the caller is not an organization member of record — e.g. requests authenticated with an organization auth token / API token that carries `org:write`/`org:admin`, which `OrganizationAuditPermission` accepts. For those callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False (AnonymousUser), so the right-hand side is evaluated and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working endpoint into a hard 500. At minimum the check must be guarded (`organization_context.member and ...`) and only evaluated when `use_optimized` is true.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: accessing `.has_global_access` on `organization_context.member` will raise an `AttributeError` when the user is neither a superuser nor an organization member (causing `.member` to be `None`). Note: The golden comment has a slight typo saying 'when organization_context is None' while immediately clarifying 'for non-superuser non-member users' after mentioning `organization_context.member`, which clearly aligns with the candidate's explanation of `organization_context.member` being `None`.

false_positives.candidate:
New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a brand-new public paginator wired into a production endpoint, but no tests were added in this PR (neither for the paginator itself nor for the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch of `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`). As a result the broken datetime key handling and the negative-offset ValueError path described in the other findings would not be caught by CI. Tests should cover: default behaviour parity with `DateTimePaginator` for the audit log ordering, and the behaviour for negative/invalid cursor offsets.

Misleading comment added to Cursor.__init__

The added comment claims that `self.offset = int(offset)` is a “performance optimization” that “allows negative offsets … enables efficient reverse pagination”. No code changed here; `int(offset)` has always accepted negative values, and negative offsets are not a supported feature — most paginators reject them and Django refuses negative slices. The comment documents a non-existent and unsafe capability and will mislead the next reader into thinking negative offsets are intentional and handled.

zunionstore defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting the end-timestamp scores used for eviction

Both merge steps use `redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` without an `AGGREGATE` option, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both sorted sets. Scores here are `end_timestamp_precise` values, so a span payload that happens to exist in both the destination set and the merged set (e.g. a duplicate delivery, or a span already zadd'ed under the top-most parent key by `process_spans` and also present under its own span key) ends up with a score of roughly 2×1.7e9. That value is no longer a timestamp, and because the new trimming logic uses `zpopmin` (lowest score evicted first), duplicated spans become effectively un-evictable while legitimate newer spans are dropped. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep scores meaningful.

Segment span limit hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, conflicting with the now-dead max_segment_spans setting

The new eviction uses the literal `1000` in two places (`if span_count > 1000` / `zpopmin set_key, span_count - 1000`), while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still exposes `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, which this PR leaves completely unused after removing the span-count check in `_load_segment_data`. The effective limit is therefore no longer configurable, differs from the previous 1001 threshold, and the stale constructor parameter will mislead operators who try to tune it. Either pass the configured limit into the script as an ARGV, or remove `max_segment_spans` from the buffer.

Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the explanatory comment deleted

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence (“theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly”) was removed. With the lower bound, traces whose redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to their real root set and will be emitted as separate, incorrectly split segments. This is a behavioural change unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (eviction on insert), is not mentioned in the description, and now has no comment documenting the limitation.

max_segment_spans is now dead code and the over-size-segment metric/log was dropped

`_load_segment_data` no longer checks `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, so the constructor parameter `max_segment_spans` is unused, and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric plus the accompanying `logger.error` are gone. Any dashboards/alerts built on that metric will silently go to zero, and there is no longer any signal when a segment is truncated — trimming now happens silently inside the Lua script. Add an equivalent metric for evicted spans (e.g. the `zpopmin` count) and remove or honor the unused parameter.

Module docstring still describes plain Redis sets and no eviction

The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted on insert once a segment exceeds 1000 members, but the module docstring was not updated: step 3 still says “Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`” and the glossary still says “span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys”. Nothing documents that spans can now be silently dropped from a segment, which is the most important semantic change in this PR for anyone debugging missing spans.

No test covers the new eviction-on-insert behaviour

The PR's headline change is trimming segments to 1000 spans during insert (`zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua) and the switch from sets to sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, yet the only test changes are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to existing fixtures. There is no test that pushes more than the limit of spans into one segment and asserts that the oldest-ending spans are the ones dropped, nor any test that the score is preserved correctly across the `zunionstore` merges. The previously-tested-by-implication span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed with no replacement coverage, so a regression in the eviction logic (wrong aggregate, wrong pop count, off-by-one on the threshold) would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key built from `hash()` of project ids and omits the allowlist value

The cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}"`. Two different project-id sets in the same organization that hash to the same value will share a cache entry, which can make a query over non-allowlisted projects be treated as eligible and silently multiply reported error counts by the sample weight (or vice versa, suppressing upsampling). The key also does not incorporate the allowlist option value, so the cached answer is not tied to the input that produced it. Use the explicit sorted project id list (or a stable digest such as md5 of the joined ids) in the key, and include an allowlist version/hash.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the problematic use of Python's `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))` in the cache key and recommend using an explicit sorted list or stable digest of `project_ids` instead. However, the candidate argues the problem is hash collisions and missing allowlist values, whereas the golden comment points out that Python's built-in `hash()` is non-deterministic across processes (PYTHONHASHSEED randomization), breaking cross-worker caching and invalidation. While the reasoning differs, the specific code location, anti-pattern (`hash()`), and suggested fix are identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility computed from outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument and runs the query against it, but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)`. In the dashboard discover-split path (`get_event_stats_factory.fn`) `_get_event_stats` is deliberately called with a different dataset (`discover` for the errors-only probe, `split_dataset`, etc.), so the decision whether to rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count()` is made for the wrong dataset. Result: the errors-only split probe against `discover` will not be upsampled when the request dataset is metrics/transactions, and conversely a transform decided for `errors` can be applied to a query actually executed against another dataset. Use `scoped_dataset` for the check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer `dataset` variable instead of `scoped_dataset`, causing incorrect behavior in paths like the dashboard discover-split where the executed dataset differs from the original dataset.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental git submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed

This PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d2909 (the PR's own base commit) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. A gitlink without submodule configuration leaves the repository in a broken state: `git submodule update --init --recursive` fails or silently leaves an empty directory, tooling that walks the worktree sees a phantom directory, and CI checkouts can fail. This is clearly an accidental artifact of local development and must be removed from the PR.

Comment claims cached/consistent decision, but eligibility is re-evaluated per call and can flip mid-request

The comments say "Early upsampling eligibility check ... This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution" and "Store the upsampling decision to apply later", but `should_upsample` is recomputed on every invocation of `_get_event_stats`, and the helper's cache has a 60s TTL. In the discover-split flow `_get_event_stats` is called 2–3 times per request (errors-only probe, original query, transactions-only probe). If the cached entry expires or the allowlist option changes between those calls, one series will be `sum(sample_weight)` based and another plain `count()`, so `check_if_results_have_data` / `save_split_decision` compares incomparable magnitudes and the widget split decision is made on inconsistent data. The decision should be computed once per request and passed down.

60s eligibility cache with no invalidation path returns stale upsampling decisions

`cache.set(cache_key, is_eligible, 60)` caches the allowlist decision for 60 seconds, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (defined below at line 67) is never called from anywhere in the codebase — nothing hooks option updates for `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. Consequently, after a project is removed from the allowlist, event-stats responses keep returning upsampled (inflated by 1/sample_rate) counts for up to a minute, and after a project is added the counts stay un-upsampled. Given `options.get` is already option-cached in Sentry, the extra cache buys little while introducing a correctness window; either drop the cache or wire the invalidation to option changes.

Docstring states allowlist is read fresh every call, contradicting the new cache

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`'s docstring says the function "reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time ... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state", but its only caller caches the result for 60 seconds, so callers do not see the latest configuration. The docstring will mislead the next person debugging stale upsampling behaviour and should be corrected or removed.

`_is_error_focused_query` substring match also matches negated/unrelated queries

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the lowercased raw query string contains the substring `event.type:error`. A query such as `!event.type:error` (an explicitly non-error query) or a free-text/message search that happens to contain that substring also matches, so `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (i.e. `sum(sample_weight)`) for a result set that includes transactions/other event types. That yields wrong numbers, and on entities where `sample_weight` is unavailable it can fail the Snuba query outright. Parse the search query (e.g. with the event search parser) and require a positive `event.type:error` term instead of a substring check.

`upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` with no null/zero fallback

The new SnQLFunction resolves to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no `ifNull`/default. Events in an allowlisted project that were ingested without a client sample rate (older events already in retention, SDKs that don't emit `contexts.error_sampling`, or server-side generated events) have no sample weight, so they contribute 0 to the sum and vanish from the chart entirely — an undercount that looks like data loss. The helper docstring in error_upsampling.py ("We rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, so no additional null checks are needed") is an assumption, not an enforced invariant. Use something like `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` or an explicit default.

`upsampled_count` is exposed publicly in the discover function registry

Unlike the neighbouring internal helper functions, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, so it immediately becomes a user-callable aggregate on every endpoint using the discover dataset config (events, events-stats, dashboards, alerts). Users can request `upsampled_count()` for projects that are not allowlisted (producing meaningless or inflated numbers), and for queries that include transaction events, where `sample_weight` is not available — the very case `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` deliberately avoids — which surfaces as a Snuba error rather than a validation error. Mark it `private=True` since the only intended caller is the internal column transform.

`upsampled_count` declares `default_result_type="number"` for an integer aggregate

The aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` and it replaces `count()` (which declares `integer`), yet it declares `default_result_type="number"`. The declared result type is echoed in the response `meta`, so the frontend will format the upsampled count as a float/number rather than an integer, making charts and tables render differently depending on whether upsampling was applied. Use `"integer"`.

Added lines contain trailing whitespace that will fail lint/black checks

Several newly added lines consist of or end with trailing whitespace (e.g. line 223 after the `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)` call, line 234 after the first `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling(...)` assignment, and line 278 in the RPC branch); the same pattern exists in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` docstrings/blank lines. The repository enforces black and flake8 via pre-commit, so CI will reject these as formatting failures until the files are reformatted.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` swallows all exceptions, silently dropping the sample rate

Both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion are wrapped in bare `except Exception: pass`. If a test supplies `client_sample_rate` in an unexpected shape (string, nested differently, typo'd context key), the sample rate is silently not set, the event is stored with weight 1, and the upsampling assertions in tests degrade to asserting the non-upsampled path without any signal that the fixture was wrong. Validate/convert explicitly and let bad fixture data raise, or at minimum narrow the exception types.

No test covers the new public entry point or its caching logic

The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The actually new and risky behaviour introduced by this PR — `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` with its cache key derivation, 60s TTL staleness, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` — has no coverage at all, so regressions such as a cached `True` being returned after a project is removed from the allowlist, or a cache key collision, would not be caught. Note also that cached entries persist across tests in the same process, so any future test of this function must clear the cache in `setUp`.

Upsampling end-to-end tests only cover the default discover dataset

`OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` only issues requests without `dataset` (discover) plus one `dataset=discover` transaction case. The `errors` dataset — for which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` unconditionally returns True and which is the primary production path for error charts — is never exercised, nor is the `topEvents` branch where the transform is also applied. This matters because the `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction was registered only in the discover dataset config; if the errors dataset config does not inherit that registry, every upsampled errors-dataset request would fail with an unknown-function error and no test would notice. Add coverage for `dataset=errors` and for a `topEvents` request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every denied Check now triggers a full permission re-query from the DB

The cache read was removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` and `Check` now only returns early from the cache when the cached scope map *allows* the request. Any request that is not allowed by the cached permissions falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which always queries the permission store. Combined with a denial cache that is keyed per (action, name, parentFolder), this means every distinct resource a user is denied on causes a fresh DB round-trip (user permissions, and on a cold cache basic roles and teams) once per 30s TTL window. Deny-heavy workloads (UI browsing/filtering that issues many per-resource Checks) will see a large increase in authz DB queries compared to before this change. false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are never loaded outside of HTTP requests, so fallbacks silently fail in jobs/mailers

The translate accelerator only loads the YAML for `config.locale` (`load_locale(config.locale)` in `translate`), and the patched `I18n::Backend::Base#load_translations` deliberately does nothing when called without filenames, so `Simple#init_translations` will not autoload anything either. With `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` now mixed in, a lookup that misses falls back to `SiteSetting.default_locale` and `:en`, but those locales' translations are only in memory if something explicitly called `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for them. The only caller added in this PR is `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any translation performed outside a controller request — Sidekiq jobs (e.g. digest/notification emails rendered with the recipient's locale via `I18n.with_locale`), rake tasks, console, console-driven exports — will therefore still produce “translation missing” for keys absent from the user's locale, which is exactly the case fallbacks are supposed to fix. The ensure-loaded logic should be hooked into `load_locale`/`translate` (or into `I18n.locale=`) rather than into a single before_filter.

Every request depends on I18n.fallbacks being the custom FallbackLocaleList

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` assumes `I18n.fallbacks` is the `FallbackLocaleList` defined in `config/initializers/i18n.rb`. `ensure_loaded!` does not exist on the stock `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks`. Rails' I18n railtie configures fallbacks from `config.i18n.fallbacks` inside `config.after_initialize`, i.e. *after* `config/initializers/*` have run, and assigns `I18n.fallbacks = I18n::Locale::Fallbacks.new(...)`. This PR removed `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` from production/profile/cloud66 only; if it is still set in any other environment file (development/test) or by any plugin/host config, the custom list is replaced at boot and then *every* request raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'ensure_loaded!'` in a before_filter — a complete outage. Either guard the call (`respond_to?`) or install the fallback list from an `after_initialize`/railtie hook that runs after Rails' own i18n setup.

`SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` can raise and `.compact` cannot protect against it

`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` calls `to_sym` on the site setting before the array is built, so a nil/blank `default_locale` raises `NoMethodError` instead of being removed by `compact` (`compact` after `uniq` only removes a nil `locale`). More importantly, this method is invoked by `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` on every missed translation, including during boot, migrations and `rake assets:precompile`, where `SiteSetting` may be unavailable (no DB / missing table) — turning a harmless missing-translation lookup into an exception. Resolve the default locale defensively (e.g. `SiteSetting.default_locale.presence&.to_sym` inside a rescue) and build the list as `[locale, default, :en].compact.uniq`.

LRU translation cache key ignores the fallback chain (stale strings after default_locale change)

The cache key is `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`. Now that a lookup result can come from `SiteSetting.default_locale` via the new fallback chain, the cached value depends on the site default locale, which is not part of the key and does not change the backend object. After an admin changes `default_locale`, every already-cached fallback translation for other locales keeps serving strings from the old default locale until the process is restarted or `I18n.reload!` is called. Include the fallback chain (or the default locale) in the cache key, or clear the LRU cache when `default_locale` changes.

No tests for the new fallback behaviour

This PR changes how every translation is resolved (custom fallback chain, on-demand loading of fallback locales, removal of `config.i18n.fallbacks`) but adds no specs. There is nothing verifying that (a) the fallback order is user locale → `SiteSetting.default_locale` → `:en`, (b) `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` actually loads the fallback locales' YAML so a key missing from the user locale resolves instead of returning “translation missing”, and (c) the chain is recomputed when `SiteSetting.default_locale` changes. Regressions here degrade silently into missing-translation strings, so at minimum a spec exercising a key present only in `en` while `I18n.locale` is a partial locale is needed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, discarding recorded logs

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver (or a logger sharing its `Logs` state). `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now emits its only log line via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so any test that injects a `*TestLogger` and then asserts on `InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`/`Ctx` will observe zero calls, because the log is recorded on a throwaway instance. This makes the fake unusable for verifying the middleware's logging behaviour and will silently pass tests that are meant to catch regressions. Return `f` (or a logger that writes into the same `Logs` fields).
