true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce refreshes the token on every call but then connects with the old access token

`getClient()` now unconditionally POSTs a `refresh_token` grant to Salesforce on every instantiation (i.e. for every createEvent/updateEvent/deleteEvent), ignoring whether the stored token is still valid, and then builds the `jsforce.Connection` with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` — the *old* token from the credential — instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. false_positives.candidate:
Backup code alone can authenticate without the account password

The password is only verified by the block at lines 121-129, which is guarded by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`. The new backup-code branch is entered whenever `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` is set, regardless of `totpCode`. An attacker who obtains a single backup code (e.g. the downloaded `cal-backup-codes.txt`) but does not know the password can POST to the credentials endpoint with `email`, an arbitrary `password`, any non-empty `totpCode` (e.g. "000000") and the valid `backupCode`: the password check is skipped because `totpCode` is truthy, and only the backup code is validated, so the login succeeds. Backup codes are intended to replace the second factor, not the password, so this turns them into full single-factor credentials. The backup-code branch must verify the password (or the branch selection must not depend on `totpCode` being absent).

Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of hashed

Backup codes are persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`, i.e. recoverable plaintext. The server never needs to display the codes again after setup (they are only shown from the setup response), so they can and should be stored as one-way hashes like passwords. As implemented, anyone who gains read access to the users table together with the (single, global, long-lived) encryption key — which is also present in every app instance's environment — can recover every user's 2FA backup codes and bypass two-factor auth for all accounts.

onEnable() is no longer called unless the user clicks "Close", leaving stale UI after enabling 2FA

Previously `onEnable()` was invoked as soon as the enable request succeeded. Now it is only called by the "Close" button on the backup-codes step. If the user dismisses the dialog with the X / overlay / Esc (which goes through `onOpenChange`), 2FA is already enabled server-side but the parent is never notified, so the settings page never invalidates its query and the two-factor switch keeps showing "off" until a manual reload. Additionally `resetState()` is not run on that path, so `step` stays at `DisplayBackupCodes` and re-opening the modal shows the previous (now stale) backup codes screen instead of the password step. Either call `onEnable()` when the enable request succeeds, or handle `onOpenChange` to invoke `onEnable()`/`resetState()`.

First 2FA test asserts nothing and is not updated for the new backup-codes step

`expect(page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on the returned Promise, which is always truthy, so the step verifies nothing — the PR documents this with a FIXME instead of fixing it. This matters now: with the new flow the backup-codes dialog stays open after OTP entry and `onEnable()` is never fired, so the switch would legitimately not be checked; the test only passes because the assertion is a no-op. Use `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch][data-state="checked"]')).toBeVisible()` after dismissing the backup-codes dialog, as the second test does.

"missing_backup_codes" message points users to a settings feature that does not exist

The string is "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." but there is no UI anywhere in this PR to generate or regenerate backup codes — codes are only created inside the 2FA setup flow (`totp/setup`). Every user who enabled 2FA before this migration has `backupCodes = null` and will hit this message with no actionable path; the only way to obtain codes is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Either add a regenerate action or change the message to tell users to disable and re-enable two-factor authentication.

Submitting an empty backup code silently does nothing

The login form is rendered with `noValidate`, and the zod schema only validates `email`/`password` (`.passthrough()`), so the `required`/`minLength` attributes on the backup-code input are not enforced. Submitting the backup-code screen with an empty field sends `backupCode: ""`, the server falls through to the TOTP branch and returns `SecondFactorRequired`, which this handler maps to `setTwoFactorRequired(true)` — a no-op since the user is already on that screen — while `errorMessage` was cleared at the start of submit. The user gets no feedback at all. Validate the backup code client-side or surface an error for this case.

Unvalidated request body can crash the disable endpoint

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes the field is a string; a client sending `{"backupCode": 123}` or an object causes an uncaught `TypeError` and an opaque 500 instead of a 400. Likewise `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` on line 58 is unguarded, so a corrupted/re-keyed `backupCodes` column throws an unhandled exception rather than returning a meaningful error. Validate/parse the body (e.g. with zod) and wrap the decrypt/parse in a try/catch.

Clipboard write rejection is unhandled and success toast is shown unconditionally

`navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` returns a promise that is neither awaited nor caught, and `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")` runs immediately. In contexts where the Clipboard API is unavailable or permission is denied (non-HTTPS deployments, some browsers), the user is told the codes were copied while nothing was copied, and the rejection surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection. Await the call and only show success on resolve, with an error toast/fallback otherwise.

Password visibility toggle made unreachable by keyboard

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button removes it from tab order, so keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer toggle password visibility. This change affects every `PasswordField` in the app, not just the 2FA dialogs. If the intent was to keep tab order flowing to the next form field, consider other means (e.g. ordering/`aria` handling) rather than making the control unfocusable.

Backup codes are unusable for Google/SAML users with 2FA

For users who reach the login page via the external TOTP flow (`totpEmail` set, i.e. Google/SAML accounts with 2FA), `ExternalTotpFooter` is rendered and the new "Lost access" button is never shown, so those users cannot use their backup codes. Even if a `backupCode` were submitted, `authorize()` in next-auth-options.ts throws `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` at the `user.identityProvider !== CAL && !credentials.totpCode` check before reaching the backup-code branch. These users have no recovery path if they lose their authenticator, which is the main purpose of the feature.

Dynamic imports are started eagerly, so nothing is actually lazy-loaded (and 28 floating promises are created)

Every value in `appStore` is the *result* of calling `import(...)` during module evaluation, not a thunk. As soon as anything imports `@calcom/app-store`, all 28 app packages begin loading exactly as before – the only difference is that the caller now has to `await`. The stated goal (deferring app loading) requires storing factories, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, and invoking them on demand (optionally memoising).

Second, this creates 28 promises with no handler attached. If any single app module throws while being evaluated (missing env var, broken transitive dep, etc.), the resulting rejection stays unhandled until some code happens to `await` that specific key. Under Node's default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` (Node >= 15) that terminates the server process, even though the failing app may never be used by the request. With the previous static imports a broken app failed loudly and synchronously at import time; now it can crash an unrelated request path at an arbitrary later moment.

`forEach(async ...)` makes the surrounding try/catch dead and turns errors into unhandled rejections

The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` was made `async` so it can `await getCalendar(...)`. `forEach` discards the returned promise, so the enclosing `try { ... } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }` can no longer observe anything that happens inside: previously a synchronous throw from `getCalendar` was caught and logged, now it (and any `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` rejection) escapes as an unhandled promise rejection, which under Node's default unhandled-rejection handling can kill the process. In addition, the remote delete calls are no longer even *issued* before `Reschedule` returns, because they are now behind an `await`, so the calendar/video events may never be cancelled. Use `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered) { ... await ... }` inside the existing try/catch, or `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`.

`getCalendar` became async but line 28 still calls it without awaiting, so each item returned by the exported `getCalendarCredentials` now carries `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`; every other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` (it is a public export of `@calcom/core`) that touches `.calendar` directly will now operate on a Promise and fail at runtime (`item.calendar.listCalendars is not a function`) unless TypeScript happens to flag it. text

"` sanitizes to `"

text

"`; then `start = 11` and `end = 4`, and `sanitized.substring(11, 11 - 4)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Instead of reporting the illegal HTML, the plugin aborts with an opaque exception — and mismatched/duplicated closing tags are exactly the kind of defect this check is meant to find (several such files are fixed in this PR). false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

`getShortcut()` is added to the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` SPI interface without a `default` implementation. Any existing implementation of this SPI (third-party grant providers, and any grant factory in the repo/testsuite that was not updated in this PR) will no longer compile, and a pre-compiled provider JAR deployed into the server will fail at runtime. The failure is not localized to the grant itself: `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates over *all* `OAuth2GrantType` factories, casts them to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` and calls `getShortcut()`, so a single stale provider throws `AbstractMethodError` during server startup. Providing a `default` implementation (e.g. returning a neutral/unknown shortcut) and handling that value in the encoder would keep the SPI backwards compatible.

postInit can fail with a bare NPE if a grant factory returns a null shortcut

`grantsByShortcuts`/`grantsToShortcuts` are `ConcurrentHashMap`s, which reject null keys and values. If any `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` implementation returns `null` (easy to do, since the method has no contract enforcing non-null), `postInit()` throws a `NullPointerException` from inside `ConcurrentHashMap.put`, aborting server startup with a message that gives no hint about which provider is at fault. An explicit null/length check with a descriptive `IllegalStateException` naming the offending factory id (similar to the existing duplicate-shortcut check below) would make the failure diagnosable.

Session type derived from client session instead of the user session used for the token

The provider resolves the session type via `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()`, while `TokenManager.initToken` already has the authoritative `UserSessionModel` parameter that the rest of token creation uses (subject, session id, persistence state). Any code path that builds a `ClientSessionContext` whose client session is not (yet) attached to a user session, or where the passed `userSession` differs from the one on the client session, will either NPE during token issuance or encode the wrong session type into every access token of that flow. Passing the `userSession` already available in `initToken` into `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` removes this divergence.

Decoding a malformed token id throws instead of degrading to UNKNOWN

`getTokenContextFromTokenId()` returns an all-UNKNOWN context for ids without ':' (legacy tokens), but throws `IllegalArgumentException` for ids that contain ':' with an unexpected prefix length or unknown shortcuts. Token ids come from client-supplied tokens (the stated goal is to call this from introspection/userinfo/admin endpoints), so once wired up any crafted or foreign `jti` turns into an unhandled runtime exception, i.e. an HTTP 500 instead of an invalid-token response. Treating unparseable prefixes the same way as legacy ids (UNKNOWN context) or wrapping the call in explicit error handling at the call sites is needed before these endpoints start consuming it.

Format change of access-token jti is not documented in upgrading/release notes

Access tokens no longer carry a plain UUID in `jti`; the value becomes `<6 chars>:<uuid>` (and `Details.TOKEN_ID` in events changes accordingly). This is an externally visible, behaviour-changing contract: resource servers, log/SIEM pipelines and client libraries that parse or store `jti` as a UUID (fixed 36-char column, `UUID.fromString(...)`) will break on upgrade. The PR contains no upgrading/release-note documentation for this change, nor any statement that the prefix is opaque and must not be relied upon by third parties.

No test coverage for the context values actually encoded during token issuance

The only tests are unit tests that decode hand-written token ids; nothing verifies the mapping performed by `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext`, i.e. that an offline-session token really gets `of`, a transient session `tr`, a lightweight access token `lt`, and that the grant-type attribute is populated for every grant that now sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` (authorization code, refresh, password, token exchange, pre-authorized code, device, CIBA). Given that the AssertEvents matcher that was supposed to cover this in integration tests is broken (grant check never executes), the whole encoding path is effectively untested end to end.

`createRecoveryCodesCredential` delegates to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` and, as soon as some user storage provider accepts the codes (`userStorageCreated == true`), it returns without touching Keycloak's own credential store. If the user already has a `recovery-authn-codes` credential stored locally (codes configured before the federation provider supported the type, while the provider was disabled, or for a user whose provider capabilities changed), that stale credential is never removed. `SubjectCredentialManager.isValid` falls back to the local credential providers when the user-storage validator rejects an input, so the *old* codes keep authenticating the user indefinitely even after the user regenerated codes. The helper should delete existing local credentials of this type when the provider takes over (and vice versa), otherwise credential rotation can be bypassed.

The credential value handed to the user storage provider is a Jackson-serialized JSON array of the raw recovery codes (`JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)`), whereas validation of the very same credential type passes a *single* raw code (`UserCredentialModel.buildFromBackupAuthnCode(...)` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`). This asymmetric wire format is not documented anywhere (no javadoc on the new method, no provider documentation in this PR). Any existing third-party `CredentialInputUpdater` that returns true from `supportsCredentialType("recovery-authn-codes")` - which today is only needed for validation - will now silently receive the JSON blob in `updateCredential` and will most likely store it as if it were a single code, corrupting the user's credential. The contract (JSON array of raw, unhashed codes on update; single raw code on validate) must be documented, or a dedicated structured input type used.

`createRecoveryCodesCredential` receives a fully built `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` (containing the user label entered in the required-action form and the `generatedAt` timestamp validated against the auth-session note), but when delegating to user storage it only forwards the codes JSON in `new UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson)`. The provider therefore cannot store the label or creation date (the test provider in this PR invents `Time.currentTimeMillis()` and leaves the label null), so the label a user typed is silently lost and credential metadata shown in the account console differs from the local-storage behaviour.

Reference user-storage implementation never consumes a recovery code, and no test covers single use

`isValid` for `recovery-authn-codes` only checks membership in the stored list and never invalidates the matched code; `getCredentials` additionally rebuilds the credential from the raw list each time, so every code is always reported as unused and the login form always requests code #0. Recovery codes are single-use by definition, so this provider (which is the de-facto reference implementation other provider authors will copy) accepts the same code an unlimited number of times. The new `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only logs in once and therefore does not verify that a used code is rejected, nor that the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-triggered once all codes are consumed - exactly the behaviour that distinguishes recovery codes from a static secret.

`var myUser = getMyUser(user);` is used without a null check at line 235 (`myUser.recoveryCodes`), while every other method in this class (`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`) explicitly guards against `getMyUser(user) == null`. If `getCredentials` is invoked for a user that is no longer in the in-memory map (e.g. after `removeUser`, or for a cached `UserModel`), the provider throws a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream, which will surface as a server error in whatever credential listing triggered the call.

Unlike the sibling tests (`testOTPUpdateAndLogin`, `testLoginSuccess`), this test calls `testAppHelper.startLogin(...)` but never calls `testAppHelper.completeLogin()`, so the authorization code is never exchanged and the test only checks the redirect URL rather than that the login actually produced tokens. A deliberate 400/404 (e.g. `ModelValidationException`/`NotFoundException`) would be the appropriate contract for "not supported in V2".

`init()` returns early when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null`, so realms that already had admin permissions enabled before this change never get the newly introduced scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`) nor the `Clients` resource-type resource. On such realms, creating a Clients permission fails: `getScope()` throws `ModelValidationException("Scope [configure] does not exist.")`, and `getOrCreateResource()` throws `ModelException("No scopes found.")` when building the per-client resource (HTTP 500), and `hasPermission()` in ClientPermissionsV2 cannot find the fallback `Clients` resource. Some upgrade/initialization path is needed to add missing schema scopes and resource-type resources to existing admin-permissions clients.

`getResourceName` resolves friendly names only for the `Users` resource type ("All users" / username). For the newly added `Clients` resource type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is null for resources created by `getOrCreateResource` (only name and owner are set). As a result, permissions created for clients will be reported without a resolvable name in representations, unlike user permissions, and there is no "All clients" label for the resource-type resource.

Javadoc on require* methods describes a return value for void methods

`requireView()` (line 98) is documented as "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}." and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 103) as "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}." Both methods are `void` and, consistently with the other `require*` methods in this interface, throw `ForbiddenException` when the corresponding `can*` check fails. The Javadoc therefore documents behaviour that does not exist and should read "Throws ForbiddenException if ... returns {@code false}".

`AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` is added to the Clients resource type and `ClientPermissionsV2.canMapClientScopeRoles` is implemented, but no test exercises it (tests only cover `manage`, `configure`, `view`, `map-roles` and `map-roles-composite`). Likewise there is no test for the all-clients `configure` permission or for a negative-logic (deny) client permission. Without coverage, regressions in the client-scope role mapping evaluation would go unnoticed.

`testManageOnlyOneClient` renames `myclient` (`setName("somethingNew")`), removes one of its default client scopes and adds it as an optional scope, but registers no `realm.cleanup()` task to restore it. The realm/client are shared by the other tests in this class (only scope permissions are cleaned in `@AfterEach`), so the mutated client-scope assignment and name leak into subsequent tests, making the suite order-dependent and potentially flaky (e.g. other tests index into `getDefaultClientScopes()`).

Either a migration that adds missing scopes/resource-type resources to existing admin-permissions clients or an idempotent re-initialisation is needed.

`GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission()` iterates all `Permission` objects returned by `root.evaluatePermission(...)` and grants access as soon as any of them carries one of the expected scopes. `UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission()` (line 123 of that file) deliberately guards this with `permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId())`. Without that guard, any permission the policy engine returns for a resource other than the one being evaluated (e.g. scope-only or resource-type expanded permissions) would grant access on the wrong group. The two implementations should use the same rule.

Javadoc of requireManageMembers refers to canManageMembership

The javadoc added for `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` states "Throws ForbiddenException if {@link #canManageMembership(GroupModel)} returns false" – it is a copy of the javadoc of `requireManageMembership` and documents the wrong predicate; the method actually delegates to `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`. Since these two scopes (`manage-membership` vs `manage-members`) grant very different privileges, wrong documentation on this security API is misleading for implementors. Also note that the javadoc of `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` says "@return Stream of IDs" while the method returns a `Set`, and the permission it actually checks is view-members/manage-members, not `view`.

The new test class only exercises per-group `view-members`/`manage-members` through `users().search(...)`, which happens to work even when `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` returns nothing (the search then runs unrestricted and is filtered per user). Missing cases that would have caught the broken `GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`: (1) an *all-groups* `view-members`/`manage-members` permission followed by `users().search(...)` (currently returns nothing because an authz resource id is used as a group id filter), (2) `users().count()` for an admin whose only visibility comes from group member permissions (currently returns 0 while `search` returns users), and (3) `groups().group(id).members()` which is guarded by the new `requireViewMembers` path.

`getGroups()` previously computed `boolean canViewGlobal = groupsEvaluator.canView()` once and only evaluated `canView(group)` per group when the global check failed; the same hoisting was removed in `GroupResource.getSubGroups()`. With FGAP V2, `GroupPermissionsV2.canView(group)` performs a resource lookup by name plus a full policy evaluation for every group in the stream (and in `getSubGroups` the filter is applied over all subgroups before pagination). For a policy-based admin holding an all-groups view permission this turns one evaluation into one per listed group, which is the main use case of the new feature. true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract `order()` method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface as an abstract method. `CryptoProvider` is an SPI that is implemented outside this repository (e.g. the keycloak-client repo, adapters, custom/vendor crypto modules). Any existing implementation that is not recompiled will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` calls `CryptoProvider::order`, and sources will no longer compile. Declaring it as a `default` method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still allowing the authz-client provider to lower/raise its priority.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward compatibility issue: adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations that do not implement it.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple crypto providers on classpath are no longer rejected; ties resolved nondeterministically and only logged at debug

The previous code threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found on the classpath. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used silently. All three real providers (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`) return the same order `200`, so if two of them end up on the same classpath (e.g. BC non-FIPS jar accidentally present in a FIPS deployment) the winner depends on `ServiceLoader` iteration order, and the fact that a provider was ignored is only reported via `logger.debugf` (off by default). That turns a previously loud, deterministic failure into a silent, non-deterministic choice of crypto backend — in a FIPS deployment it can mean silently running with non-approved crypto. At minimum, equal-order collisions should still fail (or be logged at WARN) rather than being resolved arbitrarily.

`logger.debugf(String)` used as a format string with no arguments and built unconditionally

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` resolves to the varargs `debugf(String format, Object... params)` overload with an empty parameter array, so the message is passed through `String.format`. Any `%` character in the message (class names normally have none, but the message is data-driven) would raise `UnknownFormatConversionException`/`MissingFormatArgumentException` from a logging call. In addition, the `StringBuilder` is populated and `toString()` is invoked even when debug logging is disabled. Use `logger.debug(...)` (optionally guarded by `isDebugEnabled()`), or a proper format string with parameters.

Malformed DER input causes unchecked exceptions instead of IOException

`readInteger()` uses the value returned by `readLength()` without validating it. `readLength()` returns `-1` for the indefinite-length form (0x80), so `read(-1)` executes `new byte[-1]` and throws `NegativeArraySizeException`; a zero-length INTEGER (`02 00`) yields an empty array and `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throws `NumberFormatException` ("Zero length BigInteger"). Both are unchecked exceptions escaping a method declared `throws IOException`, which is what callers of `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` handle. Since the input is an attacker-supplied token signature, this turns a verification failure into an unexpected runtime error propagating out of the verification path. `readInteger()` (and `readNext()`) should reject negative/zero lengths with an `IOException`.

Test only round-trips through the new encoder/decoder, so a wrong DER encoding would not be detected

The test asserts `asn1der -> concat -> asn1der -> concat` self-consistency using only `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`'s own `ASN1Encoder`/`ASN1Decoder`. If `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` produced structurally wrong DER (wrong tag, wrong length form, missing leading-zero for negative-looking values), the matching custom decoder would still accept it and the assertion would pass. The produced DER should be validated against the JDK, e.g. by calling `Signature.verify(asn1Des)` with the public key (and/or comparing against the BC-based provider output). Additionally, the key pair is created with the JDK default EC curve (P-256) for all three tests, so ES384/ES512 never exercise the real r/s sizes, and the leading-zero-stripping branch of `integerToBytes` (`qLength < bytes.length`) is only hit by chance depending on the randomly generated key; the test should use P-256/P-384/P-521 keys matching each algorithm.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is never true for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed

`self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` creates `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances, which subclass `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, *not* `multiprocessing.context.Process` (what `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to). Therefore the guard `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` in `_ensure_processes_alive` is always False and `kill()` is never executed. Consequences: (a) a process detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`, i.e. it is still alive but has not updated `healthy_since`) is left running while a replacement process is spawned for the *same* shards — two flushers then flush/produce the same shard set, risking duplicate and/or fragmented segments on `buffered-segments`; (b) dead processes are never reaped (no `kill`/`join`/`close`), leaving zombies; (c) the same broken check at line 346 in `join()` means `terminate()` is never called on shutdown. The intent was clearly to distinguish processes from threads — use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: spawn-context processes are SpawnProcess instances that fail the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) check, preventing hung flushers from being killed. The additional consequences and suggested fix do not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces the attribute on the `time` module itself. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62, with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change', therefore does nothing at all. The test still depends on the flusher thread happening to flush before `step.join()` sets the stop flag, i.e. it is racy, and the comment misleads future readers into thinking a wait was added. Either don't patch `time.sleep` globally (e.g. patch it only in the flusher module) or wait on an actual condition (poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the added time.sleep in test_consumer.py does not wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched to a no-op, leaving the flusher without guaranteed processing time. Both suggest restoring sleep or using actual synchronization.

false_positives.candidate:
No validation of flusher process count; 0/negative values silently disable flushing

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` followed by `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` has two bad edge cases reachable from the new `--flusher-processes` CLI option: passing `0` falls through the `or` and silently means "one process per shard" (the opposite of what the help text 'Maximum number of processes ... Defaults to 1' implies), and passing a negative number yields `num_processes <= 0`, so `process_to_shards_map` is empty and **no flusher process is started at all**. In that case spans keep being written to Redis but no segments are ever flushed or produced, until Redis memory backpressure stalls the consumer. The same happens if `assigned_shards` is empty. Validate the option (require >= 1) and/or clamp `num_processes` to at least 1.

New multi-process flusher test only asserts internal bookkeeping, not that all shards are flushed

`test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and `sum(len(shards)) == 4`, then immediately joins without submitting any spans. It never verifies the behaviour the PR introduces: that spans landing on each of the 4 shards are actually flushed and produced by the two flusher workers, and that shards are partitioned without overlap (the `sum == 4` assertion would also pass for a duplicated mapping such as `{0: [0, 0], 1: [1, 1]}`, which would cause double-production). It also exercises only the thread path (`produce_to_pipe` is set), so the real spawn-process path with multiple workers remains untested. Add a test that writes spans for several shards, advances the drift, and asserts every segment is produced exactly once, plus an assertion that the union of `process_to_shards_map` values equals `assigned_shards` with no duplicates.

Dead method _create_process_for_shard is unused

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere after the refactor (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` in `_ensure_processes_alive`). Leaving it in place is confusing — it suggests per-shard restart is supported, and if someone later calls it, it restarts the whole process group for the shard without resetting the restart counter bookkeeping that `_ensure_processes_alive` relies on. Remove it.

A new parent-side SpansBuffer (and Redis client) is created on every process restart and never released

`_create_process_for_shards` constructs `shard_buffer = SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent process and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, replacing the previous instance without closing it. Each restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per worker) therefore leaks the Redis client/connection pool of the discarded buffer in the consumer process. In addition, the parent now holds one buffer per worker group on top of the buffer passed in from the factory, so `submit()` performs N `record_stored_segments()`/`get_memory_info()` round trips per call instead of one. Consider reusing a single parent-side buffer for stats/memory checks and only creating per-shard buffers for the children.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error IDs are zipped against unordered nodestore results

`fetch_error_details()` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` and then pairs them with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi()` returns a mapping keyed by node id; its iteration order is an implementation detail (several backends merge cache hits and DB fetches into a new dict), so `events.values()` is not guaranteed to be in the same order as `error_ids`. Worse, missing events are filtered with `if data is not None` *after* zipping, so a single missing event shifts every subsequent pairing. The result is `ErrorEvent.id` values attached to the wrong title/message/timestamp, which is then fed to Seer for summarization. Pair explicitly instead, e.g. iterate `for error_id, node_id in zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and look up `events.get(node_id)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same order-alignment bug: zipping error_ids with get_multi results' values can associate event data with the wrong IDs because mapping order may differ and missing results can disrupt alignment.

false_positives.candidate:
Error/breadcrumb merge compares timestamps in different units

`gen_request_data()` interleaves errors and replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamps come from the nodestore event payload (epoch **seconds**, e.g. 1.75e9), while the top-level timestamp of an rrweb replay event is epoch **milliseconds** (e.g. 1.75e12). The comparison is therefore always true for real data, so every error is emitted before the first breadcrumb instead of being interleaved chronologically, defeating the purpose of the merge. The new unit tests use hand-written second-based event timestamps (1.5, 2.0), which hides the mismatch. Normalize both sides to the same unit before comparing.

get_environment_info triggers a recommended-event lookup per issue in PR comments

`get_environment_info()` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment. That helper runs a Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch per issue, so building a comment for the top 5 issues now issues up to 5 extra event lookups (each able to time out or return a stale 'recommended' event) inside the PR comment task, for a single word of decoration in the comment. Also note the `except Exception` branch logs the raw exception object in `extra={"error": e}`; `str(e)` serializes more reliably.

Every bullet is therefore separated by a blank line (which Markdown renders as a 'loose' list with extra paragraph spacing) and the list ends with an extra newline immediately before the `<sub>Did you find this useful?</sub>` footer. The updated tests encode this double spacing, so the formatting regression will ship silently. Drop the trailing `

Previously `attributes` was derived through a `useMemo` that always produced a `TagCollection` object (`{}` when there was no data). Now it is `isFetching ? previous : data`, where both `previous` (first render) and `data` (query disabled or not yet resolved) are `undefined`. Both `renderDefaultHeadCell` and `renderDefaultBodyCell` decide to use the custom renderer with `if (cell)`. The documented contract (see the prop JSDoc in `tableWidgetVisualization.tsx` and the storybook text: 'If the function returns `undefined`, fallback renderer will run') is that only `undefined` falls through. In practice a renderer that intentionally renders nothing by returning `null`, or that returns `''`/`0`/`false` for a cell value, will be silently overridden by the default renderer. Inconsistent optional chaining on required tableData prop

`Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields)` mixes optional chaining with a non-guarded member access and an unguarded `Object.keys`. If `tableData` is ever undefined (the surrounding code defends against it with `tableData?.data ?? []`), this throws `Cannot convert undefined or null to object` instead of rendering an empty table. Either treat `tableData` as truly required (drop the `?.`) or guard the fallback column computation.

This endpoint has `permission_classes = ()` and is CSRF exempt, yet the new code iterates the entire posted array with no cap on the number of reports: it logs the full request body, logs each invalid report (`extra={"raw_report": report}`) and emits one metric per valid report at `sample_rate=1.0`. A single large request can therefore flood logs and the metrics pipeline with attacker-controlled content. Add a maximum list length (and ideally a body size limit) before processing.

Tests no longer exercise the application/reports+json content type

The rewritten `test_basic` and `test_handles_multiple_reports_both_specs` post without `content_type="application/reports+json"` (the previous tests passed it explicitly). The custom `BrowserReportsJSONParser` exists precisely to accept the Browser Reporting API media type, and that is the content type real browsers send, yet it is now only covered indirectly by the negative `test_rejects_invalid_content_type` case. Keep at least one success-path test that posts with `application/reports+json`.

With `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` deleted, the nested `_handle_regex_match` helper inside `parametrize_w_experiments` is no longer referenced by anything (the loop now always calls `experiment.run(content, _incr_counter)`), and `ParameterizationRegex.compiled_pattern` / `_compiled_pattern` were only used by the removed class. Removing them keeps the module from accumulating unreachable branches that future readers assume are live.

Additionally the query uses `staleTime: 5000` with default refetch behaviour, so the `/feedback-summary/` endpoint (which generates an LLM completion server-side) can be re-hit every few seconds on remount/refocus, multiplying model cost. Consider a substantially larger `staleTime` and an explicit guard on the date range.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises ValueError (500)

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices the queryset with a negative start: `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset`. The inline comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong and should not be used to justify this branch.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator applies negative slice offsets to a Django QuerySet, which does not support them and raises an exception. The differing exception type does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

`organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated whenever `request.user.is_superuser` is false. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional and is `None` for requests that are not made by an org member (e.g. token/integration or org-auth-token authenticated requests, or a user acting through superuser without membership). In that case this line raises `AttributeError` and the endpoint returns a 500 instead of the audit log. The attribute access also needs verification that `has_global_access` exists on the RPC member model at all, since it is a property of the Django `OrganizationMember` model rather than a field of the RPC payload.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unguarded access to organization_context.member.has_global_access when member is None for token-authenticated requests, resulting in an AttributeError and HTTP 500. Its additional concern about the RPC model does not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator key handling is numeric-only but is used with a datetime order_by

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `math.floor/ceil(getattr(item, self.key))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged (the integer/float `Paginator` semantics). The only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`, uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`. Consequences: (1) `math.ceil(datetime)` raises `TypeError` for any non-empty result page, so the first optimized request 500s; (2) even if that were fixed, `value_from_cursor` would feed a raw number into the raw SQL comparison built by `build_queryset` (`"datetime" <= %s`), which fails/compares wrongly against a timestamp column. For a datetime sort key the class must derive from `DateTimePaginator` (or override these two methods with the timestamp-multiplier logic).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime because the audit logs endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", causing a TypeError. Its additional cursor-conversion concern does not change this direct match.

false_positives.candidate:
Privilege gate uses request.user.is_superuser and member.has_global_access

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is described as gating "authorized administrators", but neither condition expresses that. Sentry requires superuser mode to be actively elevated for a request; the correct check is `is_active_superuser(request)` (or an explicit scope check). Reading `request.user.is_superuser` grants the privileged code path to any staff account with a normal, non-elevated session. Additionally, `has_global_access` on an org member only means "access to all teams" and is implicitly true for every member of an organization with open membership, so the second clause makes the gate effectively 'any member', not 'admin'. If the advanced pagination path is meant to be restricted, gate it on an explicit permission/scope instead.

The new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter switches between `DateTimePaginator` (cursor values are millisecond timestamps) and `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (cursor values are raw numeric keys). Cursors returned by one paginator are therefore meaningless to the other, so a client that follows a `Link` header but drops/keeps the flag inconsistently (or a cached/bookmarked cursor) will silently page to the wrong position rather than erroring. The parameter is also not declared in `AuditLogQueryParamSerializer`, so it is undocumented and unvalidated (any value other than the exact string "true" silently falls back). Either encode the mode in the cursor/Link headers or drop the request-level switch.

Inconsistent and silent clamping of negative offsets in BasePaginator

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behaviour for every paginator derived from `BasePaginator`. For forward cursors an invalid negative offset is now silently clamped to 0, so a malformed/tampered cursor returns page 1 instead of surfacing an error - and the `next`/`prev` cursors are then built from `cursor.offset` (still negative) in `build_cursor`, producing further inconsistent cursors. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed straight into `queryset[offset:stop]`, which raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` and yields a 500. Negative offsets should be rejected explicitly (e.g. `raise BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`, as `OffsetPaginator` and `ChainPaginator` already do) rather than half-clamped; the comment claiming "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is incorrect.

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint branch

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including the negative-offset branch and the `enable_advanced_features` flag) and the new conditional path in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` are added with no accompanying tests. Nothing exercises the optimized path, which is why the datetime/`math.ceil` TypeError and the negative-slice ValueError went unnoticed; there is also no test asserting that unprivileged callers cannot activate the path. Tests covering: optimized path with results, cursor round-tripping, negative offsets, and the authorization gate are needed before merging.

Comment claims a behaviour change that the code does not make

The added comment in `Cursor.__init__` states "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but the code is unchanged (`self.offset = int(offset)`) - no validation was removed or added, and nothing in `Cursor` makes negative offsets usable (consumers slice QuerySets, which reject negative starts). A comment that describes a non-existent feature will mislead future readers into assuming negative offsets are a supported, safe input. Remove it or replace it with an accurate note (ideally a validation that rejects negative offsets).

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No per-key build guard: concurrent BuildIndex for the same key can corrupt a file-backed index

Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its entire body, which serialized index creation. With the lock now only held around the cache write, two concurrent callers that both saw `GetIndex() == nil` (e.g. two Search requests for the same namespace/group/resource, or a watch event racing with a search) can run `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory at the same time when `size > FileThreshold`. That means two processes/goroutines writing the same on-disk bleve index concurrently (undefined behaviour/corruption, or a spurious "path already exists" error), plus duplicated full re-index work and a cache entry that is overwritten by the loser. The TODO in `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` acknowledges this; a per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed now that the global lock is gone.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: narrowing cacheMu protection to the final cache write allows concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key to build duplicate indexes. It adds potential file-backed corruption consequences but matches the golden issue's underlying cause and behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads the index cache map without holding cacheMu

`bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` iterates `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes to the same map under `cacheMu` (lines 137-139). Concurrent map read + write is a fatal, unrecoverable Go runtime error (`concurrent map read and map write`), i.e. a process crash. This PR makes it reachable: `searchSupport.init` starts the watch-event goroutine (search.go line 207) and then calls `s.search.TotalDocs()` in the new log line (search.go line 216); a watch event handled in that goroutine can trigger `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex` -> cache write at the same moment. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs` (and copy out the indexes before calling `DocCount`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unsynchronized iteration of b.cache in TotalDocs racing with BuildIndex writes triggered by the event watcher started before the TotalDocs call, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race and lost errors in the index-build errgroup

In `searchSupport.init`, the goroutines started via `group.Go` all write to the function-scoped variables `err` (line 190: `_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and `totalBatchesIndexed` (line 189) without synchronization. Up to `initWorkers` goroutines run concurrently, so these are genuine data races (detectable by `-race`, and the counter will under-count). Worse, each goroutine returns the shared `err`, so one goroutine can observe another goroutine's value: a real build failure can be clobbered by a concurrent `nil` assignment (startup then proceeds with a partially built index) or a successful goroutine can return someone else's error (startup aborts spuriously). This was largely masked before because `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its whole body and serialized the builds; this PR removes that lock, so the goroutines now really overlap. Use goroutine-local variables (`if err := s.build(...); err != nil { return err }`) and an atomic counter.

Requests are no longer rejected after Stop(): initErr is now write-only

`Stop()` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", but every RPC handler's `s.Init(ctx)` guard was deleted, so nothing reads `initErr` any more. After `Stop()` cancels the background context, `Create`/`Update`/`Delete`/`List`/`Watch`/`Search` etc. will happily keep executing against a backend whose watcher/poller has been shut down: writes still reach the DB but no write events are broadcast or indexed, and watchers silently receive nothing. Previously these calls returned an error. Either keep an explicit "stopped" check at the entry of the handlers or drop the now-dead `initErr` mutations in `Stop` and document the new contract.

Init failure in constructor leaks the cancel func and background watcher

`ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created at line 229, but the new error path `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err }` returns without calling `cancel()`. Anything already started during `Init` (the sql backend poller started by `search.init`'s `WatchWriteEvents`, and `initWatcher`'s broadcaster goroutine if it got that far) keeps running for the lifetime of the process, and the context is leaked (this is also what `go vet`'s lostcancel check flags). Call `cancel()` (or `s.Stop`) before returning the error.

Synchronous, unbounded index build now blocks/aborts server construction

Moving `s.Init(ctx)` into `NewResourceServer` makes the full search-index build (all namespaces, via `searchSupport.init`) part of object construction, with no timeout and no way to serve traffic while it runs. Two consequences the PR should address explicitly: (1) startup latency - the PR itself states the build exceeds a gRPC request deadline, so Grafana/the storage-server target will not accept any request (not even `/metrics` via the gRPC health service) until indexing finishes; (2) a single transient failure (DB not reachable yet, one namespace failing to index) now aborts `NewResourceServer` and therefore the whole process startup, whereas previously only the first request failed and the next one retried via `sync.Once`... note that with `sync.Once` a retry was never possible either, but at least the server existed. Consider building the index asynchronously and gating readiness/search on it rather than blocking construction.

Postgres storage-server integration test silently skipped with no tracking issue

The only integration test that boots the `StorageServer` module target is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." This is the exact code path changed by this PR (unified storage now initializes - including the full index build - inside `NewResourceServer`, before the module reports running), so disabling the test may be hiding a regression introduced here rather than a pre-existing CI quirk. true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of the implemented behaviour and passes only by timing

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages" but then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing is committed. In the implementation the worker catches the exception and still calls `complete_offset()` in its `finally` block, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable and the 1-second commit loop will commit them. The test only passes because its wait loop exits after ~0.3s, before the first commit tick. So it asserts behaviour the code does not have, is timing-dependent (will fail whenever the commit thread ticks early / CI is slow), and provides no real coverage of failure handling.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that the docstring says processing errors should not block other offset commits, while the test asserts that no offsets are committed. This matches the golden concern about the docstring not matching the test implementation, despite additional discussion of timing and worker behavior.

false_positives.candidate:
Queue pool is permanently shut down on the first rebalance, then reused

`create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` hands the single, factory-owned `self.queue_pool` to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` it creates. Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops all worker threads and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The factory still holds a non-None reference, so the next `create_with_partitions()` after the rebalance returns a strategy backed by a dead pool: `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`, where the offset is immediately marked added+complete and therefore committed. The result is that after the first rebalance the consumer silently drops every message while advancing offsets, i.e. permanent data loss. The pool needs to be created per strategy (or recreated on assignment) rather than shared across the factory lifetime.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `Commit` callback (`StreamProcessor.__commit` -> `consumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets`). That callback and the underlying consumer state are only safe to touch from the thread running the processor loop; calling it concurrently with `poll()`/`submit()`/rebalance handling can corrupt the staged-offset bookkeeping or raise (e.g. staging an offset for a partition that was just revoked). Because the exception is caught and only logged in the loop, such failures would be invisible and offsets would silently stop advancing. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread (e.g. collected in `poll()`) instead of committed from the commit thread.

Shutdown drops all queued work instead of draining it; join() ignores timeout

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` *before* calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Each worker checks `self.shutdown` at the top of its loop, so after finishing its current item it exits immediately and never drains the remaining queued items, defeating the point of `immediate=False`. Combined with `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` which just delegates to `close()` and ignores the timeout entirely, a normal shutdown or rebalance discards everything still queued. Those offsets stay uncommitted so the messages are re-delivered, but arroyo's `join(timeout)` contract (flush outstanding work within the timeout) is broken and every restart/rebalance causes a burst of duplicate processing proportional to the queue depth.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring claim

Each queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever fills up: if a result processor is slower than the Kafka consumption rate, the strategy will keep accepting messages and grow memory without bound. Each `WorkItem` also retains the full `Message[KafkaPayload]` (field `message`, which is never read anywhere), so the retained payload bytes are kept alive as well, plus one entry per offset in `OffsetTracker.all_offsets`. A bounded queue plus `MessageRejected` (or an explicit limit) is needed to get real backpressure.

OffsetTracker state is never reset across partition assignments

`OffsetTracker` lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool` and keeps `last_committed`/`all_offsets` forever; `create_with_partitions()` never resets it for the newly assigned partition set. If a partition is revoked and later re-assigned to this consumer at a lower offset (rewind, other consumer committed less far, offset reset), `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` from the stale `last_committed`, finds no offsets at or above it, and therefore never produces a committable offset for that partition again - the consumer processes messages but silently stops committing, so the lag grows without bound and everything is reprocessed on restart. The tracker should be reset (or scoped per assignment) when partitions are assigned/revoked.

Offset-gap test does not actually verify gap blocking and is timing-dependent

`test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` submits offsets 100, 102, 103 and asserts that no commit ever exceeds 101. The tracker blocks at the gap only for the first commit tick: after `mark_committed(100)` removes offsets <= 100, the next call to `get_committable_offsets()` uses `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset) = 102` and will therefore commit 103 (reported as 104). The test passes only because the wait loop breaks ~0.2s after the first commit, before the next 1-second tick, making it flaky; and the `for commit in all_commits: assert <= 101` loop gives a false sense that committing past gaps is prevented. Either the skip-the-gap behaviour should be asserted explicitly, or the loop should keep observing commits for more than one tick.

Strategy docstring guarantees do not match behaviour

The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring claims "No item is lost or processed out of order", "Natural backpressure when queues fill up" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing". None of those hold: queues are unbounded (no backpressure), items still queued at close are discarded, and the worker marks an offset complete in its `finally` block even when `result_processor` raised, so failed items are committed and never retried. Leaving these claims in place will mislead operators about the delivery semantics of the new mode.

FilteredPayload messages are funneled through the generic exception handler

`ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload` starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, and that assert is outside its try/except. When this strategy is wrapped by something that emits `FilteredPayload` (e.g. the stale-message DLQ wrapper used via `--stale-threshold-sec`), every filtered message raises an AssertionError that lands in `submit()`'s `except Exception`, logging "Error submitting message to queue" at exception level for each one. Offsets are still advanced, so this is noise rather than data loss, but it will flood error logs/Sentry. `submit()` should handle `FilteredPayload` explicitly (track and complete the offset) instead of relying on the catch-all.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.

The inline comment “The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically” is factually wrong, and the comment “enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds … safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level” documents behaviour that does not exist. Since `Cursor.from_string` accepts any integer offset from the `cursor` query parameter, this is a user-triggerable error path. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` instead.

The candidate additionally explains Django's rejection of negative slicing and suggests a fix.

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` in `BasePaginator.get_result` silently rewrites an invalid (negative) forward cursor offset to 0, so the caller gets page 1 data while `build_cursor` still derives the next/prev cursors from the original negative `cursor.offset` (e.g. `next_offset = offset + limit`), producing further bogus cursors. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still handed to the Django slice, which raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so the fix is only half applied. Other paginators in this file (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`) raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`; `BasePaginator` should do the same rather than clamp.
