true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is an integer paginator but is used with a datetime sort key

The endpoint sorts by `-datetime` (a `DateTimeField`). `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — i.e. the integer semantics of `Paginator`, not the millisecond-timestamp conversion that `DateTimePaginator` implements. Consequently, when `optimized_pagination=true` is honored, `build_cursor` calls `get_item_key` on a `datetime` and raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, and any follow-up cursor value is injected raw into the `WHERE datetime >= %s` clause built by `build_queryset`, comparing an integer against a timestamp column. The optimized path therefore cannot work for this endpoint at all; it only produces 500s (and would silently mis-page if it did not crash).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor to a datetime key from order_by='-datetime', raising TypeError. Its additional cursor-conversion concerns do not change this direct match.

false_positives.candidate:
`organization_context.member` can be None, causing a 500 on every audit-log request

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET, before it is known whether the optimized path is even requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` and is None whenever the caller is not an organization member of record — e.g. requests authenticated with an organization auth token / API token that carries `org:write`/`org:admin`, which `OrganizationAuditPermission` accepts. For those callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False (AnonymousUser), so the right-hand side is evaluated and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working endpoint into a hard 500. At minimum the check must be guarded (`organization_context.member and ...`) and only evaluated when `use_optimized` is true.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a brand-new public paginator wired into a production endpoint, but no tests were added in this PR (neither for the paginator itself nor for the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch of `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`). As a result the broken datetime key handling and the negative-offset ValueError path described in the other findings would not be caught by CI. Tests should cover: default behaviour parity with `DateTimePaginator` for the audit log ordering, and the behaviour for negative/invalid cursor offsets.

Misleading comment added to Cursor.__init__

The added comment claims that `self.offset = int(offset)` is a “performance optimization” that “allows negative offsets … enables efficient reverse pagination”. No code changed here; `int(offset)` has always accepted negative values, and negative offsets are not a supported feature — most paginators reject them and Django refuses negative slices. The comment documents a non-existent and unsafe capability and will mislead the next reader into thinking negative offsets are intentional and handled.

zunionstore defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting the end-timestamp scores used for eviction

Both merge steps use `redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` without an `AGGREGATE` option, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both sorted sets. Scores here are `end_timestamp_precise` values, so a span payload that happens to exist in both the destination set and the merged set (e.g. a duplicate delivery, or a span already zadd'ed under the top-most parent key by `process_spans` and also present under its own span key) ends up with a score of roughly 2×1.7e9. That value is no longer a timestamp, and because the new trimming logic uses `zpopmin` (lowest score evicted first), duplicated spans become effectively un-evictable while legitimate newer spans are dropped. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep scores meaningful.

Segment span limit hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, conflicting with the now-dead max_segment_spans setting

The new eviction uses the literal `1000` in two places (`if span_count > 1000` / `zpopmin set_key, span_count - 1000`), while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still exposes `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, which this PR leaves completely unused after removing the span-count check in `_load_segment_data`. The effective limit is therefore no longer configurable, differs from the previous 1001 threshold, and the stale constructor parameter will mislead operators who try to tune it. Either pass the configured limit into the script as an ARGV, or remove `max_segment_spans` from the buffer.

Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the explanatory comment deleted

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence (“theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly”) was removed. With the lower bound, traces whose redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to their real root set and will be emitted as separate, incorrectly split segments. This is a behavioural change unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (eviction on insert), is not mentioned in the description, and now has no comment documenting the limitation.

max_segment_spans is now dead code and the over-size-segment metric/log was dropped

`_load_segment_data` no longer checks `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, so the constructor parameter `max_segment_spans` is unused, and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric plus the accompanying `logger.error` are gone. Any dashboards/alerts built on that metric will silently go to zero, and there is no longer any signal when a segment is truncated — trimming now happens silently inside the Lua script. Add an equivalent metric for evicted spans (e.g. the `zpopmin` count) and remove or honor the unused parameter.

Module docstring still describes plain Redis sets and no eviction

The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted on insert once a segment exceeds 1000 members, but the module docstring was not updated: step 3 still says “Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`” and the glossary still says “span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys”. Nothing documents that spans can now be silently dropped from a segment, which is the most important semantic change in this PR for anyone debugging missing spans.

No test covers the new eviction-on-insert behaviour

The PR's headline change is trimming segments to 1000 spans during insert (`zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua) and the switch from sets to sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, yet the only test changes are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to existing fixtures. There is no test that pushes more than the limit of spans into one segment and asserts that the oldest-ending spans are the ones dropped, nor any test that the score is preserved correctly across the `zunionstore` merges. The previously-tested-by-implication span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed with no replacement coverage, so a regression in the eviction logic (wrong aggregate, wrong pop count, off-by-one on the threshold) would go unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility computed from outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument and runs the query against it, but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)`. In the dashboard discover-split path (`get_event_stats_factory.fn`) `_get_event_stats` is deliberately called with a different dataset (`discover` for the errors-only probe, `split_dataset`, etc.), so the decision whether to rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count()` is made for the wrong dataset. Result: the errors-only split probe against `discover` will not be upsampled when the request dataset is metrics/transactions, and conversely a transform decided for `errors` can be applied to a query actually executed against another dataset. Use `scoped_dataset` for the check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer dataset rather than scoped_dataset, causing discover queries in dashboard split paths to miss upsampling when the original dataset is metrics.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental git submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed

This PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d2909 (the PR's own base commit) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. A gitlink without submodule configuration leaves the repository in a broken state: `git submodule update --init --recursive` fails or silently leaves an empty directory, tooling that walks the worktree sees a phantom directory, and CI checkouts can fail. This is clearly an accidental artifact of local development and must be removed from the PR.

Comment claims cached/consistent decision, but eligibility is re-evaluated per call and can flip mid-request

The comments say "Early upsampling eligibility check ... This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution" and "Store the upsampling decision to apply later", but `should_upsample` is recomputed on every invocation of `_get_event_stats`, and the helper's cache has a 60s TTL. In the discover-split flow `_get_event_stats` is called 2–3 times per request (errors-only probe, original query, transactions-only probe). If the cached entry expires or the allowlist option changes between those calls, one series will be `sum(sample_weight)` based and another plain `count()`, so `check_if_results_have_data` / `save_split_decision` compares incomparable magnitudes and the widget split decision is made on inconsistent data. The decision should be computed once per request and passed down.

Cache key built from `hash()` of project ids and omits the allowlist value

The cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}"`. Two different project-id sets in the same organization that hash to the same value will share a cache entry, which can make a query over non-allowlisted projects be treated as eligible and silently multiply reported error counts by the sample weight (or vice versa, suppressing upsampling). The key also does not incorporate the allowlist option value, so the cached answer is not tied to the input that produced it. Use the explicit sorted project id list (or a stable digest such as md5 of the joined ids) in the key, and include an allowlist version/hash.

60s eligibility cache with no invalidation path returns stale upsampling decisions

`cache.set(cache_key, is_eligible, 60)` caches the allowlist decision for 60 seconds, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (defined below at line 67) is never called from anywhere in the codebase — nothing hooks option updates for `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. Consequently, after a project is removed from the allowlist, event-stats responses keep returning upsampled (inflated by 1/sample_rate) counts for up to a minute, and after a project is added the counts stay un-upsampled. Given `options.get` is already option-cached in Sentry, the extra cache buys little while introducing a correctness window; either drop the cache or wire the invalidation to option changes.

Docstring states allowlist is read fresh every call, contradicting the new cache

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`'s docstring says the function "reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time ... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state", but its only caller caches the result for 60 seconds, so callers do not see the latest configuration. The docstring will mislead the next person debugging stale upsampling behaviour and should be corrected or removed.

`_is_error_focused_query` substring match also matches negated/unrelated queries

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the lowercased raw query string contains the substring `event.type:error`. A query such as `!event.type:error` (an explicitly non-error query) or a free-text/message search that happens to contain that substring also matches, so `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (i.e. `sum(sample_weight)`) for a result set that includes transactions/other event types. That yields wrong numbers, and on entities where `sample_weight` is unavailable it can fail the Snuba query outright. Parse the search query (e.g. with the event search parser) and require a positive `event.type:error` term instead of a substring check.

`upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` with no null/zero fallback

The new SnQLFunction resolves to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no `ifNull`/default. Events in an allowlisted project that were ingested without a client sample rate (older events already in retention, SDKs that don't emit `contexts.error_sampling`, or server-side generated events) have no sample weight, so they contribute 0 to the sum and vanish from the chart entirely — an undercount that looks like data loss. The helper docstring in error_upsampling.py ("We rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, so no additional null checks are needed") is an assumption, not an enforced invariant. Use something like `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` or an explicit default.

`upsampled_count` is exposed publicly in the discover function registry

Unlike the neighbouring internal helper functions, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, so it immediately becomes a user-callable aggregate on every endpoint using the discover dataset config (events, events-stats, dashboards, alerts). Users can request `upsampled_count()` for projects that are not allowlisted (producing meaningless or inflated numbers), and for queries that include transaction events, where `sample_weight` is not available — the very case `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` deliberately avoids — which surfaces as a Snuba error rather than a validation error. Mark it `private=True` since the only intended caller is the internal column transform.

`upsampled_count` declares `default_result_type="number"` for an integer aggregate

The aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` and it replaces `count()` (which declares `integer`), yet it declares `default_result_type="number"`. The declared result type is echoed in the response `meta`, so the frontend will format the upsampled count as a float/number rather than an integer, making charts and tables render differently depending on whether upsampling was applied. Use `"integer"`.

Added lines contain trailing whitespace that will fail lint/black checks

Several newly added lines consist of or end with trailing whitespace (e.g. line 223 after the `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)` call, line 234 after the first `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling(...)` assignment, and line 278 in the RPC branch); the same pattern exists in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` docstrings/blank lines. The repository enforces black and flake8 via pre-commit, so CI will reject these as formatting failures until the files are reformatted.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` swallows all exceptions, silently dropping the sample rate

Both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion are wrapped in bare `except Exception: pass`. If a test supplies `client_sample_rate` in an unexpected shape (string, nested differently, typo'd context key), the sample rate is silently not set, the event is stored with weight 1, and the upsampling assertions in tests degrade to asserting the non-upsampled path without any signal that the fixture was wrong. Validate/convert explicitly and let bad fixture data raise, or at minimum narrow the exception types.

No test covers the new public entry point or its caching logic

The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The actually new and risky behaviour introduced by this PR — `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` with its cache key derivation, 60s TTL staleness, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` — has no coverage at all, so regressions such as a cached `True` being returned after a project is removed from the allowlist, or a cache key collision, would not be caught. Note also that cached entries persist across tests in the same process, so any future test of this function must clear the cache in `setUp`.

Upsampling end-to-end tests only cover the default discover dataset

`OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` only issues requests without `dataset` (discover) plus one `dataset=discover` transaction case. The `errors` dataset — for which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` unconditionally returns True and which is the primary production path for error charts — is never exercised, nor is the `topEvents` branch where the transform is also applied. This matters because the `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction was registered only in the discover dataset config; if the errors dataset config does not inherit that registry, every upsampled errors-dataset request would fail with an unknown-function error and no test would notice. Add coverage for `dataset=errors` and for a `topEvents` request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every denied Check now triggers a full permission re-query from the DB

The cache read was removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` and `Check` now only returns early from the cache when the cached scope map *allows* the request. Any request that is not allowed by the cached permissions falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which always queries the permission store. Combined with a denial cache that is keyed per (action, name, parentFolder), this means every distinct resource a user is denied on causes a fresh DB round-trip (user permissions, and on a cold cache basic roles and teams) once per 30s TTL window. Deny-heavy workloads (UI browsing/filtering that issues many per-resource Checks) will see a large increase in authz DB queries compared to before this change. Consider bounding the re-query (e.g. only re-query if the permission cache entry is older than some threshold, or a short negative-result TTL on the permission fetch itself).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same asymmetric cache behavior: cached grants return immediately, while cached denials trigger a database lookup. It emphasizes the performance impact rather than the golden comment's stale-grant security risk, but the underlying cache logic issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not actually prove the short-circuit

The subtest "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" comments "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but seeds the permission cache with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, i.e. the scope map does *not* grant access. With or without the `permDenialCache` entry the request would be denied (the default fake store returns no permissions), so the test passes even if the denial-cache short-circuit is removed. Set the scope to `true` so the test fails if the denial cache is not consulted, and additionally assert that the store was not queried (e.g. `fakeStore.calls == 0`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same mismatch: the test comment claims cached permissions allow dashboard access, but dashboards:uid:dash1 is set to false, so permission checking still denies access. The candidate additionally explains the test weakness and suggests a fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous: name/parent concatenation can collide

`userPermDenialCacheKey` builds the key as `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Because `_` is a legal character in Grafana resource/folder UIDs, different (name, parent) pairs map to the same key: e.g. name="a_b", parent="c" and name="a", parent="b_c" both yield `...action_a_b_c`. Since `Check` now short-circuits to `Allowed: false` on any hit in this cache (service.go:117), a denial recorded for one resource can silently deny access to a completely different resource the user is actually permitted to see, for up to the 30s TTL. Use an unambiguous encoding (e.g. length-prefixed or a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions, or hash the tuple).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-delimited concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey, causing collisions between distinct component tuples and incorrect permission-denial cache hits. The candidate provides a concrete example of the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial is cached even when it is caused by a stale folder tree

The fallback path re-queries permissions from the database, but `checkPermission` -> `checkInheritedPermissions` -> `buildFolderTree` still uses `folderCache` (30s TTL). If a folder was just created/moved and is missing from the cached tree, the inherited-permission check fails and the resulting denial is then written into `permDenialCache` for another 30s. So a denial caused purely by a stale folder tree gets pinned for up to ~2x the folder cache TTL, and the problem this PR is meant to fix (access to just-created folders/dashboards) still reproduces for resources whose access is inherited through a newly created folder. Either skip caching the denial when the decision depended on the (possibly stale) folder tree, or refresh/bypass the folder cache on the fallback path.

permissionCacheUsage metric no longer measures cache hit rate

`permissionCacheUsage` is incremented with "true" only when the cached permissions allow the request, and the unconditional `WithLabelValues("false", ...)` at this line is also reached when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` *succeeded* but the decision was deny. A permission-cache hit that results in a deny is therefore reported as a cache miss. In addition, a hit in the new `permDenialCache` (line 118) is reported as a `permissionCacheUsage` hit, conflating two different caches. The metric no longer reflects the permission cache hit rate, which makes it useless for tuning TTLs and for detecting cache regressions; it should either count hits/misses of the permission cache independently of the decision, or use a separate label/metric for the denial cache.

In-proc authz client loses all client-side result caching

Replacing the authlib local cache with `NoopCache` for the in-proc client means every `Check` and every `Compile`/List performed by API handlers now goes through the in-proc gRPC channel and is fully re-evaluated server-side on every request; previously results were cached for 30s on the client. Server-side caching only covers the raw permission/identity lookups, not the per-request work: building the allowed folder/item sets in `listPermission` walks the whole scope map and folder subtree on every call, and (per the server change) any denied Check falls through to a DB query. For instances with many permissions/folders this is a noticeable per-request CPU and DB cost increase. If the goal is only freshness for newly created resources, consider a very short client TTL rather than disabling the cache entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is the pipeline signature, not a per-session nonce

`state` is set to `pipeline.signature` and later compared against `request.GET["state"]`. The pipeline signature is derived from the pipeline's view set, so it is a constant value shared by every user and every organization — the tests hard-code it (`state=9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). A constant, publicly discoverable `state` provides no CSRF / authorization-code-injection protection for the OAuth callback: an attacker can always craft a callback URL with the correct `state`. The PR description lists this as one of the security checks, which overstates what it provides. Generate a random nonce per pipeline run, store it with `pipeline.bind_state(...)`, and compare that instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: OAuth state uses the static pipeline.signature rather than a random value generated for each request or pipeline run.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when integration metadata has no `sender` (500 during install)

`GitHubInstallation.dispatch` compares the pipeline-stored GitHub login against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with direct subscripting. `sender` is only ever written by `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` when the incoming state carries it (`if state.get("sender")`), i.e. only for Integrations created from the GitHub `installation` webhook. Integrations created through the install pipeline itself have no `sender` key (see `test_basic_flow`, which asserts metadata without `sender`), and all Integration rows that pre-date the webhook handler also lack it. Any time this branch is reached for such a row (Integration exists, no OrganizationIntegration — e.g. a re-install after the org integration was removed, or a self-hosted instance where webhooks are not delivered), the view raises `KeyError` and the user gets an unhandled 500 instead of the intended error page. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide explicitly how to behave when it is absent.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify direct access to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] without checking whether "sender" exists, causing a KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata.

false_positives.candidate:
Identity check uses mutable GitHub login instead of immutable user id

The new authenticity check compares the OAuth-authenticated GitHub `login` string to the `login` stored in `integration.metadata["sender"]` at webhook time. GitHub usernames are renameable and, once freed, re-registerable by anyone. Consequences: (a) a legitimate installer who renames their GitHub account is permanently locked out of re-installing (generic "Invalid installation request."), and (b) an attacker who registers the installer's abandoned username passes the check. The webhook stores the sender's numeric `id` alongside the login and `get_user_info()` returns `id` as well; comparing the immutable numeric ids would close both holes.

User validation is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet

The GitHub-user equality check only runs in the branch where an `Integration` row for the `installation_id` already exists. If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` (line 481-482) the pipeline advances with no validation at all, so a caller who supplies someone else's `installation_id` can still bind that installation to their own Sentry org. This happens whenever the `installation` webhook has not been processed yet (race between the user finishing the pipeline and webhook delivery), was never delivered, or webhooks are not configured (self-hosted). A validation that does not depend on previously stored webhook data — e.g. calling `GET /user/installations` with the freshly obtained user access token and asserting the `installation_id` is listed — would cover this branch too.

Unhandled exception from get_user_info on GitHub API failure

`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (from `sentry.identity.github`) performs a `GET /user` and raises on a non-2xx response rather than returning a payload. Unlike the surrounding code paths (bad state, missing access token), this call is not wrapped in try/except, so a transient GitHub 5xx, rate limit, or revoked token turns the install flow into an unhandled 500 instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." page. Wrap the call and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` (ideally with logging/metrics so these failures are observable).

Hard-coded redirect_uri must be registered as the GitHub App callback URL

The authorize redirect sends `redirect_uri=<absolute_uri>/extensions/github/setup/`. GitHub rejects an authorize request whose `redirect_uri` is not under the callback URL registered for the app ("The redirect_uri MUST match the registered callback URL for this application"). Instances whose GitHub App/OAuth App is configured with a different callback URL (self-hosted setups are documented to point the user-authorization callback elsewhere, and single-tenant deployments use custom apps) will fail at the very first step of the integration install after this change. The PR contains no documentation or setup-instruction update for the newly required callback URL.

Re-install now blocked for non-ACTIVE integrations

After the `installations_exist` check, the code re-fetches the integration with `status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE` and renders the generic error if it is missing. Previously this branch (Integration row exists, no OrganizationIntegration) simply advanced the pipeline, so an Integration left in `PENDING_DELETION`/`DISABLED` with its org integrations already removed could be re-installed. Now such users get "We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request", which does not describe the real cause and gives them no actionable path. Either reuse the row already fetched on line 478 or report a status-specific message.

test_installation_not_found no longer covers the 404 path

The test passes `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which differs from the valid pipeline signature used by every other test in this file (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). The request therefore short-circuits in `OAuthLoginView` on the state-mismatch branch and the assertion `b"Invalid installation request."` passes for that reason alone. The behaviour the test is named for — `get_installation_info` returning 404 and `build_integration` raising `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")`, previously asserted — is now completely uncovered, and the 404 `responses.replace` setup is dead. Either use the correct state so the flow reaches `build_integration`, or rename the test to reflect that it only exercises state mismatch and add a separate test for the 404 case.

No coverage for token-exchange failure branches

The PR introduces two new failure branches in `OAuthLoginView` — the access-token exchange returning a body without `access_token` (wrong or reused `code`) and `get_user_info` returning a payload without `login` — and both are listed as intended failure modes in the description, but no test stubs a failing `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` or `/user` response. Regressions in these paths (e.g. an exception leaking a 500 instead of the error page) would go unnoticed.

error_short strings are not extractable for translation

`error()` takes `error_short` as a plain string and calls `_(error_short)` at runtime (line 141). Because the argument is a variable, `makemessages` cannot extract the literals ("Invalid installation request.", "GitHub installation pending deletion.", "Github installed on another Sentry organization."), so these user-facing strings will never be translated even though the code implies they are. Mark the literals with `_()` at their definition/call sites and pass the already-lazy objects through.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers the literal alias "alias", so the 21 IDPs created by the new test are never removed

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425) references a hard-coded alias `"alias"` instead of the alias that was just created (`idp-alias-<i>` / `idp-alias-20`). At cleanup time the admin client targets a non-existent provider, so either the cleanup throws `NotFoundException` or it silently does nothing; in both cases none of the 21 identity providers created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` are deleted, and `idp-alias-20` stays linked to organization `orga`.

Because the test realm is imported once per class, this leaks state into the other methods of this class: `testCacheIDPByOrg` asserts exact counts (`assertEquals(6, ...)`, `assertEquals(2/4, ...)`) for the IDPs of orga/orgb, and `testCacheIDPForLogin` itself asserts exact counts (5/5/10, 6/5/11, 5/6/11) that are only valid in a clean realm. Depending on JUnit's method order, one of the two tests will fail or produce misleading results. (The same mistake exists in the pre-existing line 303 and should be fixed there too.)
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incorrect cleanup alias: the code uses the literal "alias" instead of the created provider alias "idp-alias-" + i. The candidate adds consequences but matches the underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation decision uses the organization-aware wrapper, so updates can be silently skipped

`update()` obtains `original` from `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which (when the ORGANIZATION feature is on) returns the anonymous wrapper created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the realm's organization support) is disabled, while `updated` is the raw model. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` therefore compares a model whose enabled state depends on *external* org state against a raw model, and bails out of invalidating when both sides fail the login predicate.

Concrete failure: organization X is disabled; IDP `idp1` is linked to X with `BROKER_PUBLIC=true`, raw `enabled=true`, `hideOnLogin=false`. The login caches were populated from the JPA query (which filters on the raw DB columns), so `idp1`'s id is in the `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL` entries. An admin now sets `hideOnLogin=true`: `test(original)` is false (org disabled ⇒ wrapper reports disabled) and `test(updated)` is false (hidden), so the first early-return triggers and no login cache is invalidated. When organization X is re-enabled, `getForLogin` keeps returning `idp1`'s id and `getById` returns a non-null model, so the IDP that is explicitly hidden on login is rendered on the login page (the bean only re-checks `isEnabled()`, not `hideOnLogin`/`linkOnly`).

Use the unwrapped model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`) or compare the raw fields (`enabled`, `linkOnly`, `hideOnLogin`, `organizationId`, `BROKER_PUBLIC`) when deciding whether to invalidate. Note `remove()` correctly uses the raw delegate model, so the two paths are inconsistent today. There is also no test covering a disabled organization combined with a cached login list.

Single per-realm login cache entry keyed by organizationId is rebuilt/invalidated for every unseen organization

`getForLogin` uses one cache key per realm+FetchMode (`cacheKeyForLogin`) and stores the per-organization result sets inside a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` under `searchKey = organizationId`. When a request arrives with an organizationId that is not yet present in that entry, the code calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` (bumping the revision) and re-adds a merged query containing all previously cached search keys plus the new one.

On the login hot path this means: (a) the first login for each of N organizations in a realm invalidates and rebuilds the shared entry, so the realm's login IDP lookup is re-queried and the entry re-serialized O(N) times, and concurrent first-logins for different orgs will repeatedly drop each other's entry and re-hit the DB; (b) the entry grows monotonically with the number of organizations, so a realm with thousands of orgs ends up with one very large cache object that the realm cache's eviction policy treats as a single element. For `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the problem is gratuitous: `organizationId` is ignored by the query, yet it is still used as `searchKey`, so each distinct org id creates another identical result set (and another invalidate/rebuild cycle). Consider putting the organization id in the Infinispan key itself, or at least using a constant search key for `REALM_ONLY`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` on both branches, so the computed value and the `if` are dead code and the function is a constant `false`. Two problems: (1) the polarity is inverted — `enabled` is true when the flag is *disabled* — so if anyone later re-enables the feature by deleting the trailing `return false`, SQL expressions would be permitted exactly when the toggle is off and rejected when it is on; (2) static analysis / linters commonly flag the unreachable branch and unused assignment, which can fail CI. When a query of type `QueryTypeSQL` arrives, the reader returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. The feature *is* implemented in the codebase and the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle still exists and is documented as enabling it; the code path is deliberately disabled for security. Users who enable the toggle will get an error claiming the feature does not exist, with no hint that it was disabled on purpose, making the behaviour hard to diagnose and contradicting the toggle documentation. Either reword the error (e.g. "SQL expressions are currently disabled") or update/remove the toggle documentation accordingly.

This PR disables SQL expressions (the fix for CVE-2024-9264) by stubbing `sql.DB` so every method returns "not implemented" and by short-circuiting `QueryTypeSQL` in `pkg/expr/reader.go`, but it adds no test. There is nothing that asserts that `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` rejects a `sql` query (including when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled) or that `NewSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` fail, so a future refactor could silently re-enable the vulnerable path. Conversely, any pre-existing unit tests that exercise `sql.TablesList` or the SQL command end-to-end will now fail because `RunCommands` always errors — those need to be updated in this PR as well.

This is unreachable today (the stubbed `DB.RunCommands` always errors), but it is the exact pattern that made arbitrary SQL/DuckDB execution possible, and the escaping is engine-specific and incomplete (it does not handle backslash escapes or dollar-quoting). Leaving it in place means that whenever a real `DB` implementation is wired back into `NewInMemoryDB`, the injection surface is restored silently. Consider deleting the DuckDB AST parsing code along with the dependency, or at minimum parameterising the statement and adding a comment that this code is intentionally inert.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No double-check after acquiring the write lock: duplicate loads and a valid cache can be clobbered with nil

`GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, and then takes the write lock without re-checking whether another goroutine has already populated `entryPointAssetsCache` in the meantime. Two consequences on a cold start where many requests arrive concurrently (the common case, e.g. several browser tabs hitting the index page):

1. Every goroutine that observed `ret == nil` re-runs the full manifest load (disk read / JSON decode, and the CDN HTTP fetch if `cdn` is ever non-empty), serialized one after another behind the exclusive lock, instead of just reusing the value the first goroutine stored.
2. More importantly, line 69 unconditionally assigns `entryPointAssetsCache = result`. If a later goroutine's reload fails (file transiently unreadable, truncated manifest during a rebuild, CDN error), `result` is nil and the already-published, valid cache is overwritten with nil, so subsequent callers fall back to re-reading from disk again.

Fix by re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` right after acquiring the write lock, and by only assigning to the cache when `err == nil`/`result != nil`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same incomplete double-checked locking pattern in GetWebAssets: it checks the cache under a read lock but fails to re-check it after acquiring the write lock. The additional consequences and fixes do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

This directly matches the golden issue, despite also discussing the missing double-check.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock is held across blocking I/O (file read and CDN HTTP request)

The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via `defer`) for the whole duration of `readWebAssetsFromCDN` (an HTTP request whose only bound is the request context) and `readWebAssetsFromFile` (open + JSON decode). All other callers of `GetWebAssets` block on the mutex during that time. In `setting.Dev` mode the early return is skipped, so *every* index-page request takes the exclusive lock and does a disk read + JSON decode while holding it, fully serializing page loads. Consider loading outside the lock (or using `sync.Once`/`singleflight`) and only taking the lock for the pointer assignment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Leftover debug logging at Error level, including full ID lists

`CleanAnnotations` and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` log six messages per batch via `r.log.Error(...)` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)`. These are informational/debug messages, not errors: they will fire on every cleanup batch for every healthy installation, polluting error logs and triggering alerting on error-level log volume. They also serialize the entire ID slice into the log line — with the documented batch sizes (e.g. the 32767 used in the new test) each line can be hundreds of kilobytes. In addition, the `"err", err` field is always nil at these call sites because the error path returns earlier. These calls should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the full ID slice.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The background cleanup loop's ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This makes every cleanup job (temp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) run ten times more often in production, which is a significant and unrelated change in DB/IO load for all Grafana installations. Note also that `clean()` has a 9-minute timeout, so a long-running cleanup cycle will be immediately followed by another one. This looks like a leftover from local reproduction of the deadlock and should be reverted to 10 minutes (or made configurable) before merge.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker changing from 10 minutes to 1 minute and the resulting increase in database load and potential contention from more frequent cleanup execution.

false_positives.candidate:
Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite

In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite path builds the IN-list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over all IDs. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so building the list is O(n^2) in bytes copied. With a batch size such as the 32767 exercised by the new test, this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch and allocates 32k intermediate strings, for every delete batch of the cleanup job. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done elsewhere in this file) instead.

Placeholder-limit workaround only covers SQLite and keys off config instead of actual ID count

`deleteByIDs` only avoids bind parameters when `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`. MySQL and Postgres have their own hard limit of 65535 placeholders per statement, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above 65535 will get every cleanup batch failing with a driver error on those backends. The condition also tests the configured batch size rather than `len(ids)`, which couples correctness of the statement to a config value instead of the data actually being deleted. Consider branching on `len(ids)` and applying a placeholder cap for all dialects (or chunking the delete).

Per-subtest data cleanup is registered after the assertions that can abort the subtest

`createTestAnnotations` is called, then `assertAnnotationCount`/`assertAnnotationTagCount` run (both use `require`, which calls `FailNow`), and only afterwards is `t.Cleanup` registered to delete from `annotation`/`annotation_tag`. If either pre-condition assertion fails, the subtest aborts before the cleanup is registered, so the inserted rows stay in the shared `fakeSQL` database and every subsequent subtest (which now assumes an empty table and asserts exact counts) fails with confusing cascading errors. Register the `t.Cleanup` immediately after creating the annotations, before asserting.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses `d.Log` rather than the `log` built one line above with name/kind/method values. Any downstream code that pulls the logger from the context (`klog.FromContext`) loses the request identifying fields for deletes only, making delete failures hard to correlate. Should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that klog.NewContext uses d.Log instead of the enriched log variable, preventing the name, kind, and method fields from propagating through the context.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name in the `kind` metric label (unbounded cardinality)

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Each deleted object therefore creates a new time series in the duration histogram, which is an unbounded-cardinality label and will blow up the Prometheus registry/scrape payload on any workload that deletes many objects. It also makes the metric unusable for per-kind aggregation. Should be `options.Kind`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: the Delete method passes the object name instead of options.Kind when recording metrics. The candidate additionally explains the resulting cardinality and aggregation problems.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request finishes

All four background goroutines (Create l.51, Delete l.110, Update l.135, DeleteCollection l.163) build their timeout context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. A child context is cancelled as soon as its parent is cancelled, and the apiserver cancels the request context the moment the handler returns — which happens immediately after `return created, err`. So in practice the legacy write will frequently (often always, for fast handlers) be aborted with `context.Canceled` before or during execution, which silently defeats the whole point of mode 3 (writing a safety copy to legacy). Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) as the parent before applying the timeout, so the write survives the request lifecycle.

Errors from the asynchronous legacy writes are never logged

In Create (l.55-56), Delete (l.112-113), Update (l.139-140) and DeleteCollection (l.165-166) the error returned by the legacy storage is only fed into a duration histogram and then dropped. The previous implementation logged these failures. Since mode 3 reads exclusively from unified storage, a failing legacy write produces a silent divergence between the two stores with no diagnostic trail (no object name, no error message), making it impossible to reconcile later. Log the error with the object identity (and the timeout cause when the ctx expired).

Storage failures are recorded in the legacy duration metric

In `Create`, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. The same mistake exists in `Update` (l.129). This attributes unified-storage latency/failures to the legacy histogram, so the storage histogram never records any failures and the legacy histogram is polluted with samples for an operation legacy never performed. Both should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

DeleteCollection goroutine records legacy latency as storage latency

Inside the async goroutine of `DeleteCollection` the legacy call's duration is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` using `startLegacy`. This means the legacy DeleteCollection duration/errors appear under the unified-storage metric, double-counting storage samples for the same request and leaving the legacy metric with no data for delete-collection. Should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`.

Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object actually persisted in storage

The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so that legacy received exactly the object that was written to unified storage. Now the raw `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update`, so legacy recomputes the updated object from *its own* stored copy. For PATCH/Apply requests, or when the client sent a resourceVersion precondition (the RV now belongs to unified storage, not legacy), this either fails with a conflict or writes a different object than the one in unified storage, producing a silent divergence between the two stores. Pass the storage result through `updateWrapper` as before.

Request-scoped object and validation callbacks are used from a goroutine after the request completed

The goroutines pass the caller-owned `obj` (Create, l.55) and the request's `createValidation`/`updateValidation`/`deleteValidation` funcs (l.55, 112, 139, 165) into the legacy store after the handler has returned. `obj` has already been mutated in place by the unified-storage create path and is still reachable from the handler, and the validation closures run admission, which writes audit annotations onto the request's audit event — an event the audit backend may be serializing concurrently once the request finished. This is a real data race / mutation-after-response hazard. Deep-copy the object before handing it to the goroutine and avoid re-running request-scoped validation/admission on the async path.

Tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy writes

Every mode 3 test only asserts on the value returned from the unified store; no test waits for or asserts that `Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` was invoked (e.g. via `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` after synchronization). Because the legacy goroutine is fire-and-forget, the core behaviour added by this PR — the safety write to legacy — is completely untested, and the regression described above (the goroutine's context being cancelled with the request) would not be caught. The goroutines also outlive the subtest, so the mock is exercised after the test function returns, which makes any future expectation mismatch surface as a panic in a background goroutine rather than a test failure.

Storage-failure test case is configured through setupLegacyFn and only works because both mocks share one mock.Mock

In the "error when creating object in the unified store fails" case the failing `Create` expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` while `setupStorageFn` is nil. It only produces the expected error because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` are constructed around the same `*mock.Mock`, so the storage call matches the legacy expectation. The test therefore cannot distinguish a legacy failure from a storage failure and is misleading for anyone adding cases later; register the expectation on the storage setup function.

go.work.sum contains a duplicated entry and unrelated dependency hashes

The added block re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` which already exists two lines above, and adds hashes for modules unrelated to this change (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel versions). This looks like a locally dirty workspace file committed by accident rather than a regenerated one; it will churn/conflict on the next `go work sync`. Regenerate the file or drop these lines from the PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in a list without a `key`

In the `rules.map(...)` loop the `'grafana'` branch now returns `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` without passing `key={key}`, while the `'datasource'` and `default` branches still pass it. The component previously rendered (`GrafanaRuleLoader`) did receive the key. Clicking the item updates showSilenceDrawer without rendering anything, so it has no visible effect in list views.

Delete and Pause menu items can never render without a ruler rule, so they disappear from the ruler-less list view

The menu still gates Delete on `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165) and Pause on `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123). After this change the Grafana rule list renders `RuleActionsButtons` with only `promRule` (see `GrafanaRuleListItem`), so `rulerRule` is always `undefined` there and both items are unconditionally hidden. The newly computed `grafanaDeleteAbility` / `grafanaPauseAbility` therefore have no effect (dead code), and users lose the ability to delete or pause a rule from the rule list – functionality that existed before this PR. The new test in `GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx` even asserts exactly 4 menu items with full permissions granted, codifying the loss of Delete/Pause.

skipToken path still computes permissive abilities for a non-existent rule

`useGrafanaPromRuleAbility`/`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` map `skipToken` to `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined)`, which does not short-circuit: with `rule === undefined`, `loading` is `false` (see `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable`'s early return) and `isPluginProvided(undefined)` is `false`, so `MaybeSupported = AlwaysSupported` and `[AlertRuleAction.Duplicate] = [true, hasPermission(AlertingRuleCreate)]` (same for View/Explore). Since `AlertRuleMenu` OR-combines ruler and Grafana-prom abilities, a data-source (Mimir/Prometheus/Loki) rule – which always passes `skipToken` – will show "Duplicate" even when the ruler-based check says duplication is unsupported (e.g. ruler API unavailable, federated, plugin-provided rule), leading the user into a clone flow that cannot succeed. The skipToken/undefined case should return an all-`[false, false]` ability map.

Federated rule-group immutability check dropped for CombinedRule abilities

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false` (the `isFederatedRuleGroup` import was removed). Previously the CombinedRule path computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which marked rules in Mimir federated groups (`source_tenants` set) as immutable and hid Edit/Delete/Duplicate. With this change the existing rule list/detail pages will offer Edit and Delete for federated rule groups; saving such a group through the UI editor can drop `source_tenants` and silently break cross-tenant federation. The federated check needs to be preserved (or re-derived from the group identifier) before merging.

Grafana-managed recording rules lose Pause/Export/DeletePermanently support in the new ability hook

In `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` the supported flags for `ModifyExport`, `Pause`, `Restore` and `DeletePermanently` are derived from `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`, i.e. alerting rules only. The ruler-based equivalent uses `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which is true for Grafana-managed recording rules as well – those rules do support pausing and modify-export. Since the list view now relies exclusively on this hook, Export (and Pause, once the menu gating is fixed) will be missing for Grafana recording rules, a regression from the current list.

All abilities are now computed as `(rulerSupported && rulerAllowed) || (promSupported && promAllowed)`. Because a deny from the ruler-based check is ignored when the Prometheus-based check allows, any immutability signal that exists only in the ruler DTO is lost. Concretely, provisioning is detected in the prom path via `isProvisionedPromRule`, which reads the `provenance` field that is only now being added as an *optional* property on `GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase` (no backend change in this PR). If `/api/prometheus/grafana/api/v1/rules` does not return `provenance`, provisioned (file-provisioned/Terraform) rules will show Edit/Delete/Duplicate everywhere `promRule` is available – including the rule detail page where the ruler rule correctly reports the rule as immutable – and the subsequent write will be rejected by the API. Please confirm the API actually returns `provenance` and add a test with a provisioned rule; alternatively prefer the ruler result when it is available instead of OR-ing.

Analytics `logWarning` is invoked from render and can be emitted repeatedly

`getEditableIdentifier` is called during render and calls `logWarning('Unable to construct an editable rule identifier')` whenever neither a ruler rule nor a Grafana prom rule is supplied (e.g. a data-source Prometheus rule whose ruler rule has not loaded yet). Because this is a side effect in the render body it fires on every re-render of every such row, which can flood the analytics backend when a page contains many rules. Move the logging into an effect, or log once per identifier.

`returnTo` query param dropped from rule view links

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` built the href as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` omits it, so navigating from the (filtered) rule list into a rule detail page loses the "return to previous" context and the user is no longer sent back to the list they came from.

New Grafana-Prometheus ability logic has no unit tests

`useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable`, the `skipToken` handling and the OR-combination in `AlertRuleMenu`/`RuleActionsButtons` introduce ~130 lines of new permission logic, but there are no tests for them: `RulesTable.test.tsx` mocks the whole `useAbilities` module (so the real logic never runs) and `GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx` only covers the happy path with all permissions granted plus a single "no update permission" case. Important cases are untested: provisioned rules (`provenance`), plugin-provided rules, recording rules, and `skipToken` (data-source rules) returning permissive abilities.

Misleading test comment about skipToken behaviour

The repeated comment "Cloud rules only need useRulerRuleAbilities mock (useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gets skipToken)" is incorrect: `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` is still invoked with `skipToken` and, in production, still returns non-false abilities for some actions (see `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` with an undefined rule). The default `[false, false]` mock hides that behaviour, so the comment both misdescribes the code and conceals a gap in coverage for cloud rules.

Stale comment and variable name after removing the ruler prefetch

The ruler `prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)` dispatch was removed, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX ... doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded" and the variable is still called `cacheAndRulerPreload`. Both now describe behaviour that no longer exists and will mislead the next reader into thinking ruler data is still being warmed up here.

So each split query is interpolated at least twice. Two concrete consequences: (1) ad hoc filters (`request.filters`) are applied by `addAdHocFilters()` a second time to an expression that already contains them, which can duplicate label matchers / pipeline stages (e.g. `| key="value" | key="value"`); (2) `templateSrv.replace()` runs again over values that were already substituted, so any variable whose value contains `$name`, `${name}` or `[[name]]` is expanded a second time and the final LogQL is wrong. If the interpolated query is only needed to make splitting decisions (step parsing, logs-vs-metric classification, `$__range` detection), keep it locally for those decisions and send the original targets downstream, or mark the request/targets as already interpolated so the backend data source layer skips the second pass.

`runShardSplitQuery` interpolates all targets here; `splitQueriesByStreamShard` then builds `subRequest` from those interpolated + shard-annotated targets and hands it to `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which after this PR interpolates again, and `runQuery`/`DataSourceWithBackend.query` interpolates a third time. Besides the correctness problems of repeated interpolation (ad hoc filters re-appended to an expression that already carries them, template values containing `$`/`${}`/`[[]]` re-expanded), the expression handed to the 2nd/3rd pass already contains the injected `__stream_shard__=~"..." | drop __stream_shard__`, so `addAdHocFilters()` re-parses and re-modifies a mutated query whose stage ordering is no longer the user's. There is also avoidable cost: `addAdHocFilters` parses the LogQL expression per target, now once per shard group in addition to the per-sub-request pass.

Test asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times for a single target, locking in redundant interpolation

`expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` is for a request with a single target. The 5 calls come from one interpolation in `runShardSplitQuery` plus one per sub-request created by `runSplitQuery`, i.e. the assertion codifies that the same query is interpolated repeatedly instead of exactly once. This makes the test both a brittle magic number (it changes whenever the shard grouping or the number of split requests changes) and a guard that prevents noticing the double/triple interpolation problem. The intent of the test ("Interpolates queries before running") would be better expressed by asserting interpolation happened once per user target.

The new mock `datasource.applyTemplateVariables = jest.fn().mockImplementation((query) => { query.expr = query.expr.replace('$SELECTOR', '{a="b"}'); return query; })` mutates the target object in place and performs a replacement that is a no-op the second time it runs. The real implementation returns a new object and is *not* idempotent (it re-applies ad hoc filters and re-runs template replacement). Because of this mock, the tests cannot detect that the same target is now interpolated multiple times, and they also silently mutate the shared `request.targets` fixture used by subsequent assertions in the same test.

Concurrent requests (and in HA setups, concurrent Grafana instances) can all observe `count < deviceLimit` and then each insert a new row, so the number of tracked anonymous devices can exceed `auth.anonymous.device_limit`. If the limit is meant to be an enforced cap (it is used to reject authentication), the count and insert need to be done atomically, e.g. inside a single transaction with appropriate locking or an `INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(...)) < limit` style statement.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same check-then-insert race: concurrent requests can pass the device count check and create devices beyond the configured limit. Both recommend atomic enforcement using a transaction or locking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

`updateDevice` maps any update that matched no rows to `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. Besides the intended "this device is not among the tracked devices" case, zero affected rows also occurs when the row exists but its `updated_at` falls outside the `[now-30d, now+1m]` window used in the WHERE clause (e.g. a device last seen 31 days ago, or clock skew between HA instances pushing a stored timestamp past the +1m bound), and — on MySQL connections without CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS — when the update is a no-op. In those cases the caller/user is told the device limit was reached, which is misleading and makes debugging and metrics harder. Distinguish "no matching device" from the limit condition, e.g. by checking existence explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: updateDevice incorrectly maps zero affected rows to ErrDeviceLimitReached, even though this can mean the device does not exist or is outside the update time window. The candidate's additional no-op example does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. `tagDeviceUI` writes the cache key (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) *before* calling `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. But the cache entry stays in place for the cache lifetime (29 min). On the very next request with the same `X-Grafana-Device-Id`, `tagDeviceUI` hits the cache, returns nil, `TagDevice` returns nil, and the anonymous identity is granted even though the device was never persisted and the limit is exceeded. Net effect: the device limit can be trivially bypassed by reloading the page once, and the device is invisible to `ListDevices`/usage stats. The cache key must be removed (or only written after a successful store call) when `CreateOrUpdateDevice` fails.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice, leaves it cached when ErrDeviceLimitReached occurs, and consequently allows subsequent requests to bypass the device limit during the 29-minute cache lifetime.

false_positives.candidate:
Unauthenticated requests now trigger a synchronous COUNT(*) plus write on the auth path

When `deviceLimit > 0`, every `CreateOrUpdateDevice` first runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?`, and since `client.go` no longer performs tagging in a background goroutine, this query plus the upsert/update now runs inline during authentication of the request. The device id comes from the attacker-controllable `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header, and the in-memory dedup cache is keyed by that header, so an unauthenticated client can force a fresh COUNT + UPDATE round-trip (and a new 29-minute cache entry) on every single request. On an instance with many anonymous devices this adds unbounded DB load and request latency on the hot auth path. Consider caching/throttling the count or enforcing the limit without a per-request aggregate query.

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` no longer accepts `anonstore.AnonStore` (it now takes `db.DB` and constructs the store itself), and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a required `deviceLimit int64` parameter. Both functions are wired via Google Wire (`pkg/server/wire.go` / `wire_gen.go`), which is not part of this changeset: the generated code still calls the old signature, and if `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` is still in a provider set, wire now has to resolve a bare `int64` dependency, which it cannot. This will break the build / wire generation unless the provider sets and generated files are updated in the same PR. Constructing the store inside the service also removes the ability to inject an alternative `AnonStore` implementation (e.g. for tests or enterprise).

Device-limit error returned as an untyped error, producing an opaque failure for the user

`Authenticate` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` (a plain `fmt.Errorf` value) straight to the authn broker. Grafana's authn layer expects `errutil`-typed errors to derive an HTTP status and a user-facing message; an untyped error yields a generic internal/unauthenticated failure with no indication that the anonymous device limit was hit. Given this PR also ships `anonymousDeviceLimit` to the frontend (presumably to display a message), the error should be wrapped in an `errutil` error with an explicit status (e.g. 403/429) and message id so the UI and API clients can react meaningfully.

`cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read from `auth.anonymous.device_limit`, but the option is not added to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini`, or the configuration reference docs. Grafana users discover configuration through defaults.ini and the docs page; an option that silently rejects anonymous authentication once the limit is reached is especially important to document (including that 0 means unlimited and what happens to users beyond the limit).

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device is rejected once the limit is hit. There is no test that an already-tracked device can still be refreshed while the store is at the limit (the whole point of the `updateDevice` branch — a regression there would lock out every existing anonymous user), no test for `deviceLimit` boundary values (e.g. count exactly equal to vs. below the limit, negative/0 limit), and no test at the `AnonDeviceService`/client level covering the new error propagation from `TagDevice` or the local-cache interaction, which is where the limit is currently bypassable.

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` is an initializer without a type annotation, so TypeScript infers the field type as `undefined` on `GrafanaBootConfig` (unlike the neighbouring `googleAnalyticsId: undefined;` declarations, which are annotations). Any consumer writing `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0` will fail to compile, even though the backend always serialises a number (`AnonymousDeviceLimit int64`, 0 when unset) — so the value is in fact never `undefined` at runtime. Annotate it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` (or just `number`) to match the `GrafanaConfig` interface and the actual payload.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.
