true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher checks the wrong characters and inverts the comparison

The new matcher is supposed to assert that an access-token id looks like `<session><token><grant>:<uuid>` and that the grant shortcut matches `expectedGrantShortcut`. Two defects make the check useless (and potentially wrong):

1. Wrong offset: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4 and 5 of the 6-char prefix (`on`+`rt`+`ac`), so it must be read with `substring(4, 6)`. `substring(3, 5)` reads the last char of the token-type plus the first char of the grant type (e.g. "ta" for "onrtac").
2. Inverted condition: `if (items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` fails the match when the shortcut *equals* the expectation; it should be `if (!....equals(...)) return false;`.

Combined, the matcher currently always skips the grant check (the garbled 2-char slice never equals a real shortcut), so `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` no longer verify anything about the encoded grant type — the main thing this PR introduces. Conversely, if `expectedGrantShortcut` ever happened to equal the garbled slice, every such assertion would fail. Additionally, `substring(3,5)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException (instead of returning false) for a prefix shorter than 5 chars, turning a mismatch into an error.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug in isAccessTokenId: the grant shortcut is at indices 4–5 and must be read with substring(4,6), and the equality condition is inverted so a match incorrectly returns false. The extra detail does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grant shortcut length is never validated, yet decoding hard-codes a 6-char prefix

`getTokenContextFromTokenId()` requires the prefix before ':' to be exactly 6 characters (2 for session type + 2 for token type + 2 for grant type) and throws `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise, while `encodeTokenId()` happily concatenates whatever `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` returns. Nothing validates that a shortcut is exactly 2 characters — and the Javadoc of `getShortcut()` even states "usually like 3-letters shortcut", which actively invites 3-character values. A provider (or a future built-in grant) returning a shortcut of any other length will produce access-token IDs that this very provider can never decode, i.e. permanently undecodable tokens in the wild. Validate the shortcut length in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` (fail fast at startup) and fix the Javadoc to state the exact required length.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments concern the mismatch between getShortcut() Javadoc suggesting 3-letter shortcuts and the actual 2-character shortcut requirement used by token encoding/decoding. The candidate additionally recommends startup validation, but it identifies the same documentation/length issue.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

`getShortcut()` is added to the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` SPI interface without a `default` implementation. Any existing implementation of this SPI (third-party grant providers, and any grant factory in the repo/testsuite that was not updated in this PR) will no longer compile, and a pre-compiled provider JAR deployed into the server will fail at runtime. The failure is not localized to the grant itself: `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates over *all* `OAuth2GrantType` factories, casts them to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` and calls `getShortcut()`, so a single stale provider throws `AbstractMethodError` during server startup. Providing a `default` implementation (e.g. returning a neutral/unknown shortcut) and handling that value in the encoder would keep the SPI backwards compatible.

postInit can fail with a bare NPE if a grant factory returns a null shortcut

`grantsByShortcuts`/`grantsToShortcuts` are `ConcurrentHashMap`s, which reject null keys and values. If any `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` implementation returns `null` (easy to do, since the method has no contract enforcing non-null), `postInit()` throws a `NullPointerException` from inside `ConcurrentHashMap.put`, aborting server startup with a message that gives no hint about which provider is at fault. An explicit null/length check with a descriptive `IllegalStateException` naming the offending factory id (similar to the existing duplicate-shortcut check below) would make the failure diagnosable.

Session type derived from client session instead of the user session used for the token

The provider resolves the session type via `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()`, while `TokenManager.initToken` already has the authoritative `UserSessionModel` parameter that the rest of token creation uses (subject, session id, persistence state). Any code path that builds a `ClientSessionContext` whose client session is not (yet) attached to a user session, or where the passed `userSession` differs from the one on the client session, will either NPE during token issuance or encode the wrong session type into every access token of that flow. Passing the `userSession` already available in `initToken` into `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` removes this divergence.

Decoding a malformed token id throws instead of degrading to UNKNOWN

`getTokenContextFromTokenId()` returns an all-UNKNOWN context for ids without ':' (legacy tokens), but throws `IllegalArgumentException` for ids that contain ':' with an unexpected prefix length or unknown shortcuts. Token ids come from client-supplied tokens (the stated goal is to call this from introspection/userinfo/admin endpoints), so once wired up any crafted or foreign `jti` turns into an unhandled runtime exception, i.e. an HTTP 500 instead of an invalid-token response. Treating unparseable prefixes the same way as legacy ids (UNKNOWN context) or wrapping the call in explicit error handling at the call sites is needed before these endpoints start consuming it.

Format change of access-token jti is not documented in upgrading/release notes

Access tokens no longer carry a plain UUID in `jti`; the value becomes `<6 chars>:<uuid>` (and `Details.TOKEN_ID` in events changes accordingly). This is an externally visible, behaviour-changing contract: resource servers, log/SIEM pipelines and client libraries that parse or store `jti` as a UUID (fixed 36-char column, `UUID.fromString(...)`) will break on upgrade. The PR contains no upgrading/release-note documentation for this change, nor any statement that the prefix is opaque and must not be relied upon by third parties.

Negative test accepts any RuntimeException and ignores the result

`testIncorrectGrantType` catches `RuntimeException`, so the test would also pass if the code threw an unrelated `NullPointerException` instead of the intended `IllegalArgumentException` about an unknown grant shortcut; the declared `ctx` variable is unused. Assert the expected exception type (and ideally the message) so the test actually pins the contract of `getTokenContextFromTokenId`.

No test coverage for the context values actually encoded during token issuance

The only tests are unit tests that decode hand-written token ids; nothing verifies the mapping performed by `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext`, i.e. that an offline-session token really gets `of`, a transient session `tr`, a lightweight access token `lt`, and that the grant-type attribute is populated for every grant that now sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` (authorization code, refresh, password, token exchange, pre-authorized code, device, CIBA). Given that the AssertEvents matcher that was supposed to cover this in integration tests is broken (grant check never executes), the whole encoding path is effectively untested end to end.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

The candidate adds storage-provider context but points to the same unguarded Optional access.

false_positives.candidate:
Pre-existing local recovery-codes credential is left behind when codes are written to user storage

`createRecoveryCodesCredential` delegates to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` and, as soon as some user storage provider accepts the codes (`userStorageCreated == true`), it returns without touching Keycloak's own credential store. If the user already has a `recovery-authn-codes` credential stored locally (codes configured before the federation provider supported the type, while the provider was disabled, or for a user whose provider capabilities changed), that stale credential is never removed. `SubjectCredentialManager.isValid` falls back to the local credential providers when the user-storage validator rejects an input, so the *old* codes keep authenticating the user indefinitely even after the user regenerated codes. The helper should delete existing local credentials of this type when the provider takes over (and vice versa), otherwise credential rotation can be bypassed.

Undocumented and asymmetric value format passed to user storage providers for recovery codes

The credential value handed to the user storage provider is a Jackson-serialized JSON array of the raw recovery codes (`JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)`), whereas validation of the very same credential type passes a *single* raw code (`UserCredentialModel.buildFromBackupAuthnCode(...)` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`). This asymmetric wire format is not documented anywhere (no javadoc on the new method, no provider documentation in this PR). Any existing third-party `CredentialInputUpdater` that returns true from `supportsCredentialType("recovery-authn-codes")` - which today is only needed for validation - will now silently receive the JSON blob in `updateCredential` and will most likely store it as if it were a single code, corrupting the user's credential. The contract (JSON array of raw, unhashed codes on update; single raw code on validate) must be documented, or a dedicated structured input type used.

User label and generation timestamp are dropped when the credential goes to user storage

`createRecoveryCodesCredential` receives a fully built `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` (containing the user label entered in the required-action form and the `generatedAt` timestamp validated against the auth-session note), but when delegating to user storage it only forwards the codes JSON in `new UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson)`. The provider therefore cannot store the label or creation date (the test provider in this PR invents `Time.currentTimeMillis()` and leaves the label null), so the label a user typed is silently lost and credential metadata shown in the account console differs from the local-storage behaviour.

Reference user-storage implementation never consumes a recovery code, and no test covers single use

`isValid` for `recovery-authn-codes` only checks membership in the stored list and never invalidates the matched code; `getCredentials` additionally rebuilds the credential from the raw list each time, so every code is always reported as unused and the login form always requests code #0. Recovery codes are single-use by definition, so this provider (which is the de-facto reference implementation other provider authors will copy) accepts the same code an unlimited number of times. The new `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only logs in once and therefore does not verify that a used code is rejected, nor that the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-triggered once all codes are consumed - exactly the behaviour that distinguishes recovery codes from a static secret.

getCredentials dereferences a possibly null MyUser

`var myUser = getMyUser(user);` is used without a null check at line 235 (`myUser.recoveryCodes`), while every other method in this class (`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`) explicitly guards against `getMyUser(user) == null`. If `getCredentials` is invoked for a user that is no longer in the in-memory map (e.g. after `removeUser`, or for a cached `UserModel`), the provider throws a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream, which will surface as a server error in whatever credential listing triggered the call.

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin never completes the login and ignores the logout result

Unlike the sibling tests (`testOTPUpdateAndLogin`, `testLoginSuccess`), this test calls `testAppHelper.startLogin(...)` but never calls `testAppHelper.completeLogin()`, so the authorization code is never exchanged and the test only checks the redirect URL rather than that the login actually produced tokens. It then calls `testAppHelper.logout()` without asserting the result; since no id token/refresh token was obtained, the logout can silently fail, leaving the SSO cookie and user session alive for the following tests in this class (which reuse the same realm, browser and username `otp1`), making those tests order-dependent.

Before this change, exit code 4 meant "recreate upgrade required"; after this change 4 means "the rolling-updates feature is disabled" and recreate is signalled with 3. Any existing automation or operator logic that was written against the implemented behaviour (4 == recreate) will now silently interpret "feature disabled" as "recreate required", and will not react to the new code 3 at all. Since the value is being recycled rather than a fresh code allocated, consider using an unused code (e.g. 5) for the new condition, or at minimum call out the incompatible exit-code change in the release notes / upgrade guide for this preview tool.

false_positives.candidate:
Feature `rolling-updates` is only enabled for the non-null update strategy in UpgradeTest

`createInitialDeployment()` returns early (`return kc;`) when `updateStrategy == null`, so the `spec.features.enabled: [rolling-updates]` block is only added for the `RECREATE` parameter. Both parameterized tests (`testImageChange`, `testCacheMaxCount`) therefore run the default/unset-strategy case with the preview feature disabled in the CR, which directly contradicts the new documentation added in this PR ("While on preview stage, the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail."). Either the default strategy path is being tested in an unsupported configuration (and may pass only by accident, e.g. because the test image happens to have the feature built in), or the documented requirement is wrong. In addition, the null and RECREATE runs now differ in two dimensions (strategy *and* feature set), making any failure ambiguous.

No test covers the changed/added exit codes (3 for recreate, 4 for feature disabled)

This PR changes `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` from 4 to 3 and introduces `FEATURE_DISABLED = 4`, and the documentation explicitly tells users to script against these exit codes. However, `testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the stderr text and never asserts `exitCode() == 4`, and `testWrongVersions` never asserts `exitCode() == 3`. Note also that `@Launch`-based tests in this suite do not validate the exit code (see the pre-existing `testMissingSubCommand` which really exits with 2). As a result, a regression in the documented exit-code contract — the only thing automation is supposed to rely on — would go unnoticed. The feature gate is also only exercised for the `metadata` subcommand; the identical gate added to `check` is untested.

Documented command passes the build-time option `--features` at runtime

The `updatecompatibility` macro now renders every documented invocation as `bin/kc.[sh|bat] update-compatibility <args> --features=rolling-updates`. `features` is a build-time option: on a distribution/container that was already built (`kc.sh build`, or any optimized image) specifying it on a runtime command either forces a re-augmentation on every invocation (slow, and impossible on a read-only container filesystem) or is rejected when `--optimized` is in effect. The guide should instead instruct users to enable `rolling-updates` at build time (as this PR does for `operator/scripts/Dockerfile-custom-image`), otherwise the copy-pasteable commands in the guide will not work in the main production deployment style. There is also a correctness trap: the guide elsewhere insists the metadata/check commands be run with exactly the deployment's configuration, yet here it tells users to add a feature the running deployment does not have.

Operator preview note does not cover custom images and is vague about the failure

The new CAUTION states only that "the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail", and the example enables it via `spec.features.enabled`. Consequences: (a) a process detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`, i.e. it is still alive but has not updated `healthy_since`) is left running while a replacement process is spawned for the *same* shards — two flushers then flush/produce the same shard set, risking duplicate and/or fragmented segments on `buffered-segments`; (b) dead processes are never reaped (no `kill`/`join`/`close`), leaving zombies; (c) the same broken check at line 346 in `join()` means `terminate()` is never called on shutdown. Defaults to 1' implies), and passing a negative number yields `num_processes <= 0`, so `process_to_shards_map` is empty and **no flusher process is started at all**. In that case spans keep being written to Redis but no segments are ever flushed or produced, until Redis memory backpressure stalls the consumer. The same happens if `assigned_shards` is empty. Validate the option (require >= 1) and/or clamp `num_processes` to at least 1.

`test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and `sum(len(shards)) == 4`, then immediately joins without submitting any spans. It never verifies the behaviour the PR introduces: that spans landing on each of the 4 shards are actually flushed and produced by the two flusher workers, and that shards are partitioned without overlap (the `sum == 4` assertion would also pass for a duplicated mapping such as `{0: [0, 0], 1: [1, 1]}`, which would cause double-production). It also exercises only the thread path (`produce_to_pipe` is set), so the real spawn-process path with multiple workers remains untested. Add a test that writes spans for several shards, advances the drift, and asserts every segment is produced exactly once, plus an assertion that the union of `process_to_shards_map` values equals `assigned_shards` with no duplicates.

`_create_process_for_shards` constructs `shard_buffer = SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent process and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, replacing the previous instance without closing it. Each restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per worker) therefore leaks the Redis client/connection pool of the discarded buffer in the consumer process. In addition, the parent now holds one buffer per worker group on top of the buffer passed in from the factory, so `submit()` performs N `record_stored_segments()`/`get_memory_info()` round trips per call instead of one. Consider reusing a single parent-side buffer for stats/memory checks and only creating per-shard buffers for the children.

The result is `ErrorEvent.id` values attached to the wrong title/message/timestamp, which is then fed to Seer for summarization. `gen_request_data()` interleaves errors and replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamps come from the nodestore event payload (epoch **seconds**, e.g. 1.75e9), while the top-level timestamp of an rrweb replay event is epoch **milliseconds** (e.g. 1.75e12). The comparison is therefore always true for real data, so every error is emitted before the first breadcrumb instead of being interleaved chronologically, defeating the purpose of the merge. The new unit tests use hand-written second-based event timestamps (1.5, 2.0), which hides the mismatch. Normalize both sides to the same unit before comparing.

That helper runs a Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch per issue, so building a comment for the top 5 issues now issues up to 5 extra event lookups (each able to time out or return a stale 'recommended' event) inside the PR comment task, for a single word of decoration in the comment. Every bullet is therefore separated by a blank line (which Markdown renders as a 'loose' list with extra paragraph spacing) and the list ends with an extra newline immediately before the `<sub>Did you find this useful?</sub>` footer. Previously `attributes` was derived through a `useMemo` that always produced a `TagCollection` object (`{}` when there was no data). Callers that are not updated in this PR and treat the value as always-present (spreading is fine, but `Object.keys(attributes)` / `attributes[key]` is not) can now hit runtime errors, in particular when the hook is used with `enabled: false`. `Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields)` mixes optional chaining with a non-guarded member access and an unguarded `Object.keys`. If `tableData` is ever undefined (the surrounding code defends against it with `tableData?.data ?? []`), this throws `Cannot convert undefined or null to object` instead of rendering an empty table. This endpoint has `permission_classes = ()` and is CSRF exempt, yet the new code iterates the entire posted array with no cap on the number of reports: it logs the full request body, logs each invalid report (`extra={"raw_report": report}`) and emits one metric per valid report at `sample_rate=1.0`. The rewritten `test_basic` and `test_handles_multiple_reports_both_specs` post without `content_type="application/reports+json"` (the previous tests passed it explicitly). For forward cursors an invalid negative offset is now silently clamped to 0, so a malformed/tampered cursor returns page 1 instead of surfacing an error - and the `next`/`prev` cursors are then built from `cursor.offset` (still negative) in `build_cursor`, producing further inconsistent cursors. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed straight into `queryset[offset:stop]`, which raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` and yields a 500. Negative offsets should be rejected explicitly (e.g. `raise BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`, as `OffsetPaginator` and `ChainPaginator` already do) rather than half-clamped; the comment claiming "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is incorrect.

Nothing exercises the optimized path, which is why the datetime/`math.ceil` TypeError and the negative-slice ValueError went unnoticed; there is also no test asserting that unprivileged callers cannot activate the path. The added comment in `Cursor.__init__` states "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but the code is unchanged (`self.offset = int(offset)`) - no validation was removed or added, and nothing in `Cursor` makes negative offsets usable (consumers slice QuerySets, which reject negative starts). A comment that describes a non-existent feature will mislead future readers into assuming negative offsets are a supported, safe input. Remove it or replace it with an accurate note (ideally a validation that rejects negative offsets).

With the lock now only held around the cache write, two concurrent callers that both saw `GetIndex() == nil` (e.g. two Search requests for the same namespace/group/resource, or a watch event racing with a search) can run `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory at the same time when `size > FileThreshold`. false_positives.candidate:
Data race and lost errors in the index-build errgroup

In `searchSupport.init`, the goroutines started via `group.Go` all write to the function-scoped variables `err` (line 190: `_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and `totalBatchesIndexed` (line 189) without synchronization. Worse, each goroutine returns the shared `err`, so one goroutine can observe another goroutine's value: a real build failure can be clobbered by a concurrent `nil` assignment (startup then proceeds with a partially built index) or a successful goroutine can return someone else's error (startup aborts spuriously). After `Stop()` cancels the background context, `Create`/`Update`/`Delete`/`List`/`Watch`/`Search` etc. will happily keep executing against a backend whose watcher/poller has been shut down: writes still reach the DB but no write events are broadcast or indexed, and watchers silently receive nothing. `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created at line 229, but the new error path `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err }` returns without calling `cancel()`. Anything already started during `Init` (the sql backend poller started by `search.init`'s `WatchWriteEvents`, and `initWatcher`'s broadcaster goroutine if it got that far) keeps running for the lifetime of the process, and the context is leaked (this is also what `go vet`'s lostcancel check flags). Two consequences the PR should address explicitly: (1) startup latency - the PR itself states the build exceeds a gRPC request deadline, so Grafana/the storage-server target will not accept any request (not even `/metrics` via the gRPC health service) until indexing finishes; (2) a single transient failure (DB not reachable yet, one namespace failing to index) now aborts `NewResourceServer` and therefore the whole process startup, whereas previously only the first request failed and the next one retried via `sync.Once`... note that with `sync.Once` a retry was never possible either, but at least the server existed. `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages" but then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing is committed. The test only passes because its wait loop exits after ~0.3s, before the first commit tick. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same core problem in test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling: its documented intent does not match what the test actually asserts/implements. The candidate correctly describes a mismatch with the defined error-handling behavior, even though it adds timing details.

false_positives.candidate:
Queue pool is permanently shut down on the first rebalance, then reused

`create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` hands the single, factory-owned `self.queue_pool` to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` it creates. Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops all worker threads and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The factory still holds a non-None reference, so the next `create_with_partitions()` after the rebalance returns a strategy backed by a dead pool: `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`, where the offset is immediately marked added+complete and therefore committed. The result is that after the first rebalance the consumer silently drops every message while advancing offsets, i.e. permanent data loss. The pool needs to be created per strategy (or recreated on assignment) rather than shared across the factory lifetime.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `Commit` callback (`StreamProcessor.__commit` -> `consumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets`). That callback and the underlying consumer state are only safe to touch from the thread running the processor loop; calling it concurrently with `poll()`/`submit()`/rebalance handling can corrupt the staged-offset bookkeeping or raise (e.g. staging an offset for a partition that was just revoked). Because the exception is caught and only logged in the loop, such failures would be invisible and offsets would silently stop advancing. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread (e.g. collected in `poll()`) instead of committed from the commit thread.

Shutdown drops all queued work instead of draining it; join() ignores timeout

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` *before* calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Each worker checks `self.shutdown` at the top of its loop, so after finishing its current item it exits immediately and never drains the remaining queued items, defeating the point of `immediate=False`. Combined with `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` which just delegates to `close()` and ignores the timeout entirely, a normal shutdown or rebalance discards everything still queued. Those offsets stay uncommitted so the messages are re-delivered, but arroyo's `join(timeout)` contract (flush outstanding work within the timeout) is broken and every restart/rebalance causes a burst of duplicate processing proportional to the queue depth.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring claim

Each queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever fills up: if a result processor is slower than the Kafka consumption rate, the strategy will keep accepting messages and grow memory without bound. Each `WorkItem` also retains the full `Message[KafkaPayload]` (field `message`, which is never read anywhere), so the retained payload bytes are kept alive as well, plus one entry per offset in `OffsetTracker.all_offsets`. A bounded queue plus `MessageRejected` (or an explicit limit) is needed to get real backpressure.

OffsetTracker state is never reset across partition assignments

`OffsetTracker` lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool` and keeps `last_committed`/`all_offsets` forever; `create_with_partitions()` never resets it for the newly assigned partition set. If a partition is revoked and later re-assigned to this consumer at a lower offset (rewind, other consumer committed less far, offset reset), `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` from the stale `last_committed`, finds no offsets at or above it, and therefore never produces a committable offset for that partition again - the consumer processes messages but silently stops committing, so the lag grows without bound and everything is reprocessed on restart. The tracker should be reset (or scoped per assignment) when partitions are assigned/revoked.

Offset-gap test does not actually verify gap blocking and is timing-dependent

`test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` submits offsets 100, 102, 103 and asserts that no commit ever exceeds 101. The tracker blocks at the gap only for the first commit tick: after `mark_committed(100)` removes offsets <= 100, the next call to `get_committable_offsets()` uses `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset) = 102` and will therefore commit 103 (reported as 104). The test passes only because the wait loop breaks ~0.2s after the first commit, before the next 1-second tick, making it flaky; and the `for commit in all_commits: assert <= 101` loop gives a false sense that committing past gaps is prevented. Either the skip-the-gap behaviour should be asserted explicitly, or the loop should keep observing commits for more than one tick.

Strategy docstring guarantees do not match behaviour

The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring claims "No item is lost or processed out of order", "Natural backpressure when queues fill up" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing". None of those hold: queues are unbounded (no backpressure), items still queued at close are discarded, and the worker marks an offset complete in its `finally` block even when `result_processor` raised, so failed items are committed and never retried. Leaving these claims in place will mislead operators about the delivery semantics of the new mode.

FilteredPayload messages are funneled through the generic exception handler

`ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload` starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, and that assert is outside its try/except. When this strategy is wrapped by something that emits `FilteredPayload` (e.g. the stale-message DLQ wrapper used via `--stale-threshold-sec`), every filtered message raises an AssertionError that lands in `submit()`'s `except Exception`, logging "Error submitting message to queue" at exception level for each one. Offsets are still advanced, so this is noise rather than data loss, but it will flood error logs/Sentry. `submit()` should handle `FilteredPayload` explicitly (track and complete the offset) instead of relying on the catch-all.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offsets are passed straight into a Django queryset slice and raise ValueError

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects this with `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for any slice whose start or stop is negative, so the request ends in an unhandled exception / HTTP 500. The inline comment “The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically” is factually wrong, and the comment “enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds … safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level” documents behaviour that does not exist. Since `Cursor.from_string` accepts any integer offset from the `cursor` query parameter, this is a user-triggerable error path. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset is negative, the negative offset is passed directly as the slice start, which Django rejects with ValueError.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silently clamping negative cursor offsets masks invalid cursors and is inconsistent for prev cursors

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` in `BasePaginator.get_result` silently rewrites an invalid (negative) forward cursor offset to 0, so the caller gets page 1 data while `build_cursor` still derives the next/prev cursors from the original negative `cursor.offset` (e.g. `next_offset = offset + limit`), producing further bogus cursors. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still handed to the Django slice, which raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so the fix is only half applied. Other paginators in this file (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`) raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`; `BasePaginator` should do the same rather than clamp.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same bug in BasePaginator.get_result(): for cursor.is_prev, the negative offset is not clamped and is passed to the Django queryset slice. The additional discussion of forward-cursor clamping is consistent with the same underlying pagination issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is an integer paginator but is used with a datetime sort key

The endpoint sorts by `-datetime` (a `DateTimeField`). `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — i.e. the integer semantics of `Paginator`, not the millisecond-timestamp conversion that `DateTimePaginator` implements. Consequently, when `optimized_pagination=true` is honored, `build_cursor` calls `get_item_key` on a `datetime` and raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, and any follow-up cursor value is injected raw into the `WHERE datetime >= %s` clause built by `build_queryset`, comparing an integer against a timestamp column. The optimized path therefore cannot work for this endpoint at all; it only produces 500s (and would silently mis-page if it did not crash).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies integer floor/ceil semantics to a datetime sort key from order_by='-datetime', causing TypeError. Extra cursor/query details do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member` can be None, causing a 500 on every audit-log request

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET, before it is known whether the optimized path is even requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` and is None whenever the caller is not an organization member of record — e.g. requests authenticated with an organization auth token / API token that carries `org:write`/`org:admin`, which `OrganizationAuditPermission` accepts. For those callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False (AnonymousUser), so the right-hand side is evaluated and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working endpoint into a hard 500. At minimum the check must be guarded (`organization_context.member and ...`) and only evaluated when `use_optimized` is true.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the unconditional access to organization_context.member.has_global_access can raise AttributeError for non-superuser callers who are not organization members, causing a 500. The candidate's wording focuses on member being None rather than organization_context, but it points to the same code path and failure mode.

false_positives.candidate:
New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a brand-new public paginator wired into a production endpoint, but no tests were added in this PR (neither for the paginator itself nor for the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch of `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`). As a result the broken datetime key handling and the negative-offset ValueError path described in the other findings would not be caught by CI. Tests should cover: default behaviour parity with `DateTimePaginator` for the audit log ordering, and the behaviour for negative/invalid cursor offsets.

Misleading comment added to Cursor.__init__

The added comment claims that `self.offset = int(offset)` is a “performance optimization” that “allows negative offsets … enables efficient reverse pagination”. No code changed here; `int(offset)` has always accepted negative values, and negative offsets are not a supported feature — most paginators reject them and Django refuses negative slices. The comment documents a non-existent and unsafe capability and will mislead the next reader into thinking negative offsets are intentional and handled.

zunionstore defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting the end-timestamp scores used for eviction

Both merge steps use `redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` without an `AGGREGATE` option, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both sorted sets. Scores here are `end_timestamp_precise` values, so a span payload that happens to exist in both the destination set and the merged set (e.g. a duplicate delivery, or a span already zadd'ed under the top-most parent key by `process_spans` and also present under its own span key) ends up with a score of roughly 2×1.7e9. That value is no longer a timestamp, and because the new trimming logic uses `zpopmin` (lowest score evicted first), duplicated spans become effectively un-evictable while legitimate newer spans are dropped. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep scores meaningful.

Segment span limit hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, conflicting with the now-dead max_segment_spans setting

The new eviction uses the literal `1000` in two places (`if span_count > 1000` / `zpopmin set_key, span_count - 1000`), while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still exposes `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, which this PR leaves completely unused after removing the span-count check in `_load_segment_data`. The effective limit is therefore no longer configurable, differs from the previous 1001 threshold, and the stale constructor parameter will mislead operators who try to tune it. Either pass the configured limit into the script as an ARGV, or remove `max_segment_spans` from the buffer.

Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the explanatory comment deleted

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence (“theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly”) was removed. With the lower bound, traces whose redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to their real root set and will be emitted as separate, incorrectly split segments. This is a behavioural change unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (eviction on insert), is not mentioned in the description, and now has no comment documenting the limitation.

max_segment_spans is now dead code and the over-size-segment metric/log was dropped

`_load_segment_data` no longer checks `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, so the constructor parameter `max_segment_spans` is unused, and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric plus the accompanying `logger.error` are gone. Any dashboards/alerts built on that metric will silently go to zero, and there is no longer any signal when a segment is truncated — trimming now happens silently inside the Lua script. Add an equivalent metric for evicted spans (e.g. the `zpopmin` count) and remove or honor the unused parameter.

Module docstring still describes plain Redis sets and no eviction

The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted on insert once a segment exceeds 1000 members, but the module docstring was not updated: step 3 still says “Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`” and the glossary still says “span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys”. Nothing documents that spans can now be silently dropped from a segment, which is the most important semantic change in this PR for anyone debugging missing spans.

No test covers the new eviction-on-insert behaviour

The PR's headline change is trimming segments to 1000 spans during insert (`zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua) and the switch from sets to sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, yet the only test changes are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to existing fixtures. There is no test that pushes more than the limit of spans into one segment and asserts that the oldest-ending spans are the ones dropped, nor any test that the score is preserved correctly across the `zunionstore` merges. The previously-tested-by-implication span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed with no replacement coverage, so a regression in the eviction logic (wrong aggregate, wrong pop count, off-by-one on the threshold) would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility computed from outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument and runs the query against it, but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)`. In the dashboard discover-split path (`get_event_stats_factory.fn`) `_get_event_stats` is deliberately called with a different dataset (`discover` for the errors-only probe, `split_dataset`, etc.), so the decision whether to rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count()` is made for the wrong dataset. Result: the errors-only split probe against `discover` will not be upsampled when the request dataset is metrics/transactions, and conversely a transform decided for `errors` can be applied to a query actually executed against another dataset. Use `scoped_dataset` for the check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: upsampling eligibility is checked against the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset, causing discover-split queries to skip upsampling when the original dataset is metrics/transactions.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental git submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed

This PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d2909 (the PR's own base commit) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. A gitlink without submodule configuration leaves the repository in a broken state: `git submodule update --init --recursive` fails or silently leaves an empty directory, tooling that walks the worktree sees a phantom directory, and CI checkouts can fail. This is clearly an accidental artifact of local development and must be removed from the PR.

Comment claims cached/consistent decision, but eligibility is re-evaluated per call and can flip mid-request

The comments say "Early upsampling eligibility check ... This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution" and "Store the upsampling decision to apply later", but `should_upsample` is recomputed on every invocation of `_get_event_stats`, and the helper's cache has a 60s TTL. In the discover-split flow `_get_event_stats` is called 2–3 times per request (errors-only probe, original query, transactions-only probe). If the cached entry expires or the allowlist option changes between those calls, one series will be `sum(sample_weight)` based and another plain `count()`, so `check_if_results_have_data` / `save_split_decision` compares incomparable magnitudes and the widget split decision is made on inconsistent data. The decision should be computed once per request and passed down.

Cache key built from `hash()` of project ids and omits the allowlist value

The cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}"`. Two different project-id sets in the same organization that hash to the same value will share a cache entry, which can make a query over non-allowlisted projects be treated as eligible and silently multiply reported error counts by the sample weight (or vice versa, suppressing upsampling). The key also does not incorporate the allowlist option value, so the cached answer is not tied to the input that produced it. Use the explicit sorted project id list (or a stable digest such as md5 of the joined ids) in the key, and include an allowlist version/hash.

60s eligibility cache with no invalidation path returns stale upsampling decisions

`cache.set(cache_key, is_eligible, 60)` caches the allowlist decision for 60 seconds, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (defined below at line 67) is never called from anywhere in the codebase — nothing hooks option updates for `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. Consequently, after a project is removed from the allowlist, event-stats responses keep returning upsampled (inflated by 1/sample_rate) counts for up to a minute, and after a project is added the counts stay un-upsampled. Given `options.get` is already option-cached in Sentry, the extra cache buys little while introducing a correctness window; either drop the cache or wire the invalidation to option changes.

Docstring states allowlist is read fresh every call, contradicting the new cache

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`'s docstring says the function "reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time ... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state", but its only caller caches the result for 60 seconds, so callers do not see the latest configuration. The docstring will mislead the next person debugging stale upsampling behaviour and should be corrected or removed.

`_is_error_focused_query` substring match also matches negated/unrelated queries

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the lowercased raw query string contains the substring `event.type:error`. A query such as `!event.type:error` (an explicitly non-error query) or a free-text/message search that happens to contain that substring also matches, so `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (i.e. `sum(sample_weight)`) for a result set that includes transactions/other event types. That yields wrong numbers, and on entities where `sample_weight` is unavailable it can fail the Snuba query outright. Parse the search query (e.g. with the event search parser) and require a positive `event.type:error` term instead of a substring check.

`upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` with no null/zero fallback

The new SnQLFunction resolves to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no `ifNull`/default. Events in an allowlisted project that were ingested without a client sample rate (older events already in retention, SDKs that don't emit `contexts.error_sampling`, or server-side generated events) have no sample weight, so they contribute 0 to the sum and vanish from the chart entirely — an undercount that looks like data loss. The helper docstring in error_upsampling.py ("We rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, so no additional null checks are needed") is an assumption, not an enforced invariant. Use something like `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` or an explicit default.

`upsampled_count` is exposed publicly in the discover function registry

Unlike the neighbouring internal helper functions, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, so it immediately becomes a user-callable aggregate on every endpoint using the discover dataset config (events, events-stats, dashboards, alerts). Users can request `upsampled_count()` for projects that are not allowlisted (producing meaningless or inflated numbers), and for queries that include transaction events, where `sample_weight` is not available — the very case `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` deliberately avoids — which surfaces as a Snuba error rather than a validation error. Mark it `private=True` since the only intended caller is the internal column transform.

`upsampled_count` declares `default_result_type="number"` for an integer aggregate

The aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` and it replaces `count()` (which declares `integer`), yet it declares `default_result_type="number"`. The declared result type is echoed in the response `meta`, so the frontend will format the upsampled count as a float/number rather than an integer, making charts and tables render differently depending on whether upsampling was applied. Use `"integer"`.

Added lines contain trailing whitespace that will fail lint/black checks

Several newly added lines consist of or end with trailing whitespace (e.g. line 223 after the `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)` call, line 234 after the first `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling(...)` assignment, and line 278 in the RPC branch); the same pattern exists in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` docstrings/blank lines. The repository enforces black and flake8 via pre-commit, so CI will reject these as formatting failures until the files are reformatted.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` swallows all exceptions, silently dropping the sample rate

Both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion are wrapped in bare `except Exception: pass`. If a test supplies `client_sample_rate` in an unexpected shape (string, nested differently, typo'd context key), the sample rate is silently not set, the event is stored with weight 1, and the upsampling assertions in tests degrade to asserting the non-upsampled path without any signal that the fixture was wrong. Validate/convert explicitly and let bad fixture data raise, or at minimum narrow the exception types.

No test covers the new public entry point or its caching logic

The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The actually new and risky behaviour introduced by this PR — `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` with its cache key derivation, 60s TTL staleness, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` — has no coverage at all, so regressions such as a cached `True` being returned after a project is removed from the allowlist, or a cache key collision, would not be caught. Note also that cached entries persist across tests in the same process, so any future test of this function must clear the cache in `setUp`.

Upsampling end-to-end tests only cover the default discover dataset

`OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` only issues requests without `dataset` (discover) plus one `dataset=discover` transaction case. The `errors` dataset — for which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` unconditionally returns True and which is the primary production path for error charts — is never exercised, nor is the `topEvents` branch where the transform is also applied. This matters because the `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction was registered only in the discover dataset config; if the errors dataset config does not inherit that registry, every upsampled errors-dataset request would fail with an unknown-function error and no test would notice. Add coverage for `dataset=errors` and for a `topEvents` request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every denied Check now triggers a full permission re-query from the DB

The cache read was removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` and `Check` now only returns early from the cache when the cached scope map *allows* the request. Any request that is not allowed by the cached permissions falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which always queries the permission store. Combined with a denial cache that is keyed per (action, name, parentFolder), this means every distinct resource a user is denied on causes a fresh DB round-trip (user permissions, and on a cold cache basic roles and teams) once per 30s TTL window. Deny-heavy workloads (UI browsing/filtering that issues many per-resource Checks) will see a large increase in authz DB queries compared to before this change. Consider bounding the re-query (e.g. only re-query if the permission cache entry is older than some threshold, or a short negative-result TTL on the permission fetch itself).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same asymmetric Check cache logic: cached grants are trusted and returned early, while cached denials are ignored and trigger a fresh permission lookup. The candidate emphasizes the resulting DB-query overhead, while the golden comment emphasizes the stale-grant security risk, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not actually prove the short-circuit

The subtest "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" comments "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but seeds the permission cache with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, i.e. the scope map does *not* grant access. With or without the `permDenialCache` entry the request would be denied (the default fake store returns no permissions), so the test passes even if the denial-cache short-circuit is removed. Set the scope to `true` so the test fails if the denial cache is not consulted, and additionally assert that the store was not queried (e.g. `fakeStore.calls == 0`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the denial-cache test seeding dashboards:uid:dash1 as false despite claiming it allows access, so the request is denied even without the short-circuit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous: name/parent concatenation can collide

`userPermDenialCacheKey` builds the key as `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Because `_` is a legal character in Grafana resource/folder UIDs, different (name, parent) pairs map to the same key: e.g. name="a_b", parent="c" and name="a", parent="b_c" both yield `...action_a_b_c`. Since `Check` now short-circuits to `Allowed: false` on any hit in this cache (service.go:117), a denial recorded for one resource can silently deny access to a completely different resource the user is actually permitted to see, for up to the 30s TTL. Use an unambiguous encoding (e.g. length-prefixed or a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions, or hash the tuple).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in userPermDenialCacheKey: underscore-concatenated components can collide when values contain underscores or are empty, causing incorrect denial cache hits and wrong permission denials.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial is cached even when it is caused by a stale folder tree

The fallback path re-queries permissions from the database, but `checkPermission` -> `checkInheritedPermissions` -> `buildFolderTree` still uses `folderCache` (30s TTL). If a folder was just created/moved and is missing from the cached tree, the inherited-permission check fails and the resulting denial is then written into `permDenialCache` for another 30s. So a denial caused purely by a stale folder tree gets pinned for up to ~2x the folder cache TTL, and the problem this PR is meant to fix (access to just-created folders/dashboards) still reproduces for resources whose access is inherited through a newly created folder. Either skip caching the denial when the decision depended on the (possibly stale) folder tree, or refresh/bypass the folder cache on the fallback path.

permissionCacheUsage metric no longer measures cache hit rate

`permissionCacheUsage` is incremented with "true" only when the cached permissions allow the request, and the unconditional `WithLabelValues("false", ...)` at this line is also reached when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` *succeeded* but the decision was deny. A permission-cache hit that results in a deny is therefore reported as a cache miss. In addition, a hit in the new `permDenialCache` (line 118) is reported as a `permissionCacheUsage` hit, conflating two different caches. The metric no longer reflects the permission cache hit rate, which makes it useless for tuning TTLs and for detecting cache regressions; it should either count hits/misses of the permission cache independently of the decision, or use a separate label/metric for the denial cache.

In-proc authz client loses all client-side result caching

Replacing the authlib local cache with `NoopCache` for the in-proc client means every `Check` and every `Compile`/List performed by API handlers now goes through the in-proc gRPC channel and is fully re-evaluated server-side on every request; previously results were cached for 30s on the client. Server-side caching only covers the raw permission/identity lookups, not the per-request work: building the allowed folder/item sets in `listPermission` walks the whole scope map and folder subtree on every call, and (per the server change) any denied Check falls through to a DB query. For instances with many permissions/folders this is a noticeable per-request CPU and DB cost increase. If the goal is only freshness for newly created resources, consider a very short client TTL rather than disabling the cache entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is the pipeline signature, not a per-session nonce

`state` is set to `pipeline.signature` and later compared against `request.GET["state"]`. The pipeline signature is derived from the pipeline's view set, so it is a constant value shared by every user and every organization — the tests hard-code it (`state=9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). A constant, publicly discoverable `state` provides no CSRF / authorization-code-injection protection for the OAuth callback: an attacker can always craft a callback URL with the correct `state`. The PR description lists this as one of the security checks, which overstates what it provides. Generate a random nonce per pipeline run, store it with `pipeline.bind_state(...)`, and compare that instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OAuth state is set to the static pipeline.signature rather than a per-request random nonce, so the callback comparison provides no CSRF protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when integration metadata has no `sender` (500 during install)

`GitHubInstallation.dispatch` compares the pipeline-stored GitHub login against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with direct subscripting. `sender` is only ever written by `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` when the incoming state carries it (`if state.get("sender")`), i.e. only for Integrations created from the GitHub `installation` webhook. Integrations created through the install pipeline itself have no `sender` key (see `test_basic_flow`, which asserts metadata without `sender`), and all Integration rows that pre-date the webhook handler also lack it. Any time this branch is reached for such a row (Integration exists, no OrganizationIntegration — e.g. a re-install after the org integration was removed, or a self-hosted instance where webhooks are not delivered), the view raises `KeyError` and the user gets an unhandled 500 instead of the intended error page. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide explicitly how to behave when it is absent.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same unguarded metadata['sender']['login'] access causing KeyError when sender is absent.

false_positives.candidate:
Identity check uses mutable GitHub login instead of immutable user id

The new authenticity check compares the OAuth-authenticated GitHub `login` string to the `login` stored in `integration.metadata["sender"]` at webhook time. GitHub usernames are renameable and, once freed, re-registerable by anyone. Consequences: (a) a legitimate installer who renames their GitHub account is permanently locked out of re-installing (generic "Invalid installation request."), and (b) an attacker who registers the installer's abandoned username passes the check. The webhook stores the sender's numeric `id` alongside the login and `get_user_info()` returns `id` as well; comparing the immutable numeric ids would close both holes.

User validation is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet

The GitHub-user equality check only runs in the branch where an `Integration` row for the `installation_id` already exists. If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` (line 481-482) the pipeline advances with no validation at all, so a caller who supplies someone else's `installation_id` can still bind that installation to their own Sentry org. This happens whenever the `installation` webhook has not been processed yet (race between the user finishing the pipeline and webhook delivery), was never delivered, or webhooks are not configured (self-hosted). A validation that does not depend on previously stored webhook data — e.g. calling `GET /user/installations` with the freshly obtained user access token and asserting the `installation_id` is listed — would cover this branch too.

Unhandled exception from get_user_info on GitHub API failure

`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (from `sentry.identity.github`) performs a `GET /user` and raises on a non-2xx response rather than returning a payload. Unlike the surrounding code paths (bad state, missing access token), this call is not wrapped in try/except, so a transient GitHub 5xx, rate limit, or revoked token turns the install flow into an unhandled 500 instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." page. Wrap the call and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` (ideally with logging/metrics so these failures are observable).

Hard-coded redirect_uri must be registered as the GitHub App callback URL

The authorize redirect sends `redirect_uri=<absolute_uri>/extensions/github/setup/`. GitHub rejects an authorize request whose `redirect_uri` is not under the callback URL registered for the app ("The redirect_uri MUST match the registered callback URL for this application"). Instances whose GitHub App/OAuth App is configured with a different callback URL (self-hosted setups are documented to point the user-authorization callback elsewhere, and single-tenant deployments use custom apps) will fail at the very first step of the integration install after this change. The PR contains no documentation or setup-instruction update for the newly required callback URL.

Re-install now blocked for non-ACTIVE integrations

After the `installations_exist` check, the code re-fetches the integration with `status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE` and renders the generic error if it is missing. Previously this branch (Integration row exists, no OrganizationIntegration) simply advanced the pipeline, so an Integration left in `PENDING_DELETION`/`DISABLED` with its org integrations already removed could be re-installed. Now such users get "We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request", which does not describe the real cause and gives them no actionable path. Either reuse the row already fetched on line 478 or report a status-specific message.

The test passes `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which differs from the valid pipeline signature used by every other test in this file (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). The request therefore short-circuits in `OAuthLoginView` on the state-mismatch branch and the assertion `b"Invalid installation request."` passes for that reason alone. The behaviour the test is named for — `get_installation_info` returning 404 and `build_integration` raising `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")`, previously asserted — is now completely uncovered, and the 404 `responses.replace` setup is dead. Either use the correct state so the flow reaches `build_integration`, or rename the test to reflect that it only exercises state mismatch and add a separate test for the 404 case.

No coverage for token-exchange failure branches

The PR introduces two new failure branches in `OAuthLoginView` — the access-token exchange returning a body without `access_token` (wrong or reused `code`) and `get_user_info` returning a payload without `login` — and both are listed as intended failure modes in the description, but no test stubs a failing `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` or `/user` response. Regressions in these paths (e.g. an exception leaking a 500 instead of the error page) would go unnoticed.

error_short strings are not extractable for translation

`error()` takes `error_short` as a plain string and calls `_(error_short)` at runtime (line 141). Because the argument is a variable, `makemessages` cannot extract the literals ("Invalid installation request.", "GitHub installation pending deletion.", "Github installed on another Sentry organization."), so these user-facing strings will never be translated even though the code implies they are. Mark the literals with `_()` at their definition/call sites and pass the already-lazy objects through.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation decision uses the organization-aware wrapper, so updates can be silently skipped

`update()` obtains `original` from `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which (when the ORGANIZATION feature is on) returns the anonymous wrapper created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the realm's organization support) is disabled, while `updated` is the raw model. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` therefore compares a model whose enabled state depends on *external* org state against a raw model, and bails out of invalidating when both sides fail the login predicate.

Concrete failure: organization X is disabled; IDP `idp1` is linked to X with `BROKER_PUBLIC=true`, raw `enabled=true`, `hideOnLogin=false`. The login caches were populated from the JPA query (which filters on the raw DB columns), so `idp1`'s id is in the `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL` entries. An admin now sets `hideOnLogin=true`: `test(original)` is false (org disabled ⇒ wrapper reports disabled) and `test(updated)` is false (hidden), so the first early-return triggers and no login cache is invalidated. When organization X is re-enabled, `getForLogin` keeps returning `idp1`'s id and `getById` returns a non-null model, so the IDP that is explicitly hidden on login is rendered on the login page (the bean only re-checks `isEnabled()`, not `hideOnLogin`/`linkOnly`).

Use the unwrapped model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`) or compare the raw fields (`enabled`, `linkOnly`, `hideOnLogin`, `organizationId`, `BROKER_PUBLIC`) when deciding whether to invalidate. Note `remove()` correctly uses the raw delegate model, so the two paths are inconsistent today. There is also no test covering a disabled organization combined with a cached login list.

`getForLogin` uses one cache key per realm+FetchMode (`cacheKeyForLogin`) and stores the per-organization result sets inside a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` under `searchKey = organizationId`. When a request arrives with an organizationId that is not yet present in that entry, the code calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` (bumping the revision) and re-adds a merged query containing all previously cached search keys plus the new one.

On the login hot path this means: (a) the first login for each of N organizations in a realm invalidates and rebuilds the shared entry, so the realm's login IDP lookup is re-queried and the entry re-serialized O(N) times, and concurrent first-logins for different orgs will repeatedly drop each other's entry and re-hit the DB; (b) the entry grows monotonically with the number of organizations, so a realm with thousands of orgs ends up with one very large cache object that the realm cache's eviction policy treats as a single element. For `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the problem is gratuitous: `organizationId` is ignored by the query, yet it is still used as `searchKey`, so each distinct org id creates another identical result set (and another invalidate/rebuild cycle). Consider putting the organization id in the Infinispan key itself, or at least using a constant search key for `REALM_ONLY`.

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425) references a hard-coded alias `"alias"` instead of the alias that was just created (`idp-alias-<i>` / `idp-alias-20`). Because the test realm is imported once per class, this leaks state into the other methods of this class: `testCacheIDPByOrg` asserts exact counts (`assertEquals(6, ...)`, `assertEquals(2/4, ...)`) for the IDPs of orga/orgb, and `testCacheIDPForLogin` itself asserts exact counts (5/5/10, 6/5/11, 5/6/11) that are only valid in a clean realm. true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions() contains dead and inverted logic

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` on both branches, so the computed value and the `if` are dead code and the function is a constant `false`. Two problems: (1) the polarity is inverted — `enabled` is true when the flag is *disabled* — so if anyone later re-enables the feature by deleting the trailing `return false`, SQL expressions would be permitted exactly when the toggle is off and rejected when it is on; (2) static analysis / linters commonly flag the unreachable branch and unused assignment, which can fail CI. Since this is the kill-switch for CVE-2024-9264, it should be written unambiguously (e.g. `return false` with a comment explaining that SQL expressions are disabled for security reasons), or the flag check removed entirely.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in enableSqlExpressions: its logic is dead/inverted and it unconditionally returns false, disabling SQL expressions. The candidate adds extra context but points to the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Error text "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading for an intentionally disabled feature

When a query of type `QueryTypeSQL` arrives, the reader returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. The feature *is* implemented in the codebase and the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle still exists and is documented as enabling it; the code path is deliberately disabled for security. Users who enable the toggle will get an error claiming the feature does not exist, with no hint that it was disabled on purpose, making the behaviour hard to diagnose and contradicting the toggle documentation. Either reword the error (e.g. "SQL expressions are currently disabled") or update/remove the toggle documentation accordingly.

This PR disables SQL expressions (the fix for CVE-2024-9264) by stubbing `sql.DB` so every method returns "not implemented" and by short-circuiting `QueryTypeSQL` in `pkg/expr/reader.go`, but it adds no test. There is nothing that asserts that `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` rejects a `sql` query (including when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled) or that `NewSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` fail, so a future refactor could silently re-enable the vulnerable path. Conversely, any pre-existing unit tests that exercise `sql.TablesList` or the SQL command end-to-end will now fail because `RunCommands` always errors — those need to be updated in this PR as well.

Dead DuckDB-specific SQL string interpolation left behind in parser

`TablesList` still builds `SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')` by interpolating the user-supplied `rawSQL` after only replacing `'` with `''`. This is unreachable today (the stubbed `DB.RunCommands` always errors), but it is the exact pattern that made arbitrary SQL/DuckDB execution possible, and the escaping is engine-specific and incomplete (it does not handle backslash escapes or dollar-quoting). Leaving it in place means that whenever a real `DB` implementation is wired back into `NewInMemoryDB`, the injection surface is restored silently. Consider deleting the DuckDB AST parsing code along with the dependency, or at minimum parameterising the statement and adding a comment that this code is intentionally inert.
